    val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("$base/$route")).header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .method(method, body?.let { HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(it) } ?: HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody()).build()
    return http.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()
}
log(send("POST", "teach", """{"text": "lamp please", "label": "lights"}"""))   // {"model": …, "label": "lights", "labeled": 1}
log(send("DELETE", "teach", """{"text": "lamp please"}"""))                     // {"removed": true, …}
log(send("POST", "teach", """{"text": "lamp please", "label": "lights"}"""))
log(send("POST", "retrain?wait=true"))                                          // {"status": "done", "from": 1, "to": 2, "detail": "fine-tune v1 → v2 · …"}
log(ask("lamp please"))                                                         // answered by v2: "version": 2

retrain without wait answers 202 at once; GET …/retrain says running, done or failed. The rows go to the model's queue, AMP/<name>-to-label.csv, the same one Teach on the page fills, and the retrain is a fine-tune on it: Teaching a model while it listens.

docs.title: 13. Teach a model more: fine-tune, versions, rollback
docs.text:
A trained model learns a new label, or a few corrections, without a new build. fineTune keeps the head it has, gives each new label an output of its own, and replays the rows it was trained on so it keeps what it knew (details in Fine-tuning). This one teaches "intents" from §3 a label it doesn't know:

val music = listOf(
    "play some jazz" to "music",
    "put on my running playlist" to "music",
    "next song please" to "music",
    "turn the music up" to "music",
    "play the new album" to "music",
    "pause the song" to "music",
    "what is this song" to "music",
    "shuffle my favourites" to "music",
)
val tuned = fineTune("intents", music)              // replays sample-intents.csv, so the old labels stay
tuned.modelStatus()                                 // after, and the head before on the same rows

val m = initMod("intents")                          // opens on the new head
log(m.predict("play something relaxing"))           // music
log(m.predict("switch off the kitchen light"))      // still lights

versions("intents").forEach { log(it.describe()) }  // v2 · fine-tune of v1 …, v1 · build …

A correction is a row it gets wrong with the right label; the new row wins over the one it learned. The model it replaced is one call away:

fineTune("intents", listOf("is it bright outside" to "weather"), fineTuneOptions(epochs = 60))

if (!rollback("intents", 1)) error("no v1 to go back to")   // v1's head again, as the next version
log(initMod("intents").predict("play some jazz"))           // not music any more: v1 never learned it

docs.title: 14. Scores you can trust: cross-validation, calibration, mistakes
docs.text:
On a small file one validation split is luck, and a softmax head is surer than it is right. Cross-validation compares the heads on rows they did not see, five times over; calibration makes a score of 0.8 right about 80% of the time; the analysis says which rows it got wrong and which labels look wrong. The tables are internal lines (turn the level on, on the console strip):

val train = source("sample-intents.csv")
val options = buildOptions(
    candidates = searchSpace(hidden = listOf(emptyList(), listOf(32)), dropouts = listOf(0.0, 0.2), patience = 10),
    folds = 5,
    calibrate = true,
)
modelBuilder("intents-checked", train, options)
suspects("intents-checked")                         // training rows whose label looks wrong
mistakes("intents-checked")                         // validation rows it got wrong, the surest first
calibrationChart("intents-checked")                 // how often each score is right, and a gate worth using
trainingCurves("intents-checked")                   // loss and accuracy by epoch

// The gate the chart suggests: below it, say so instead of guessing
val m = initMod("intents-checked")
val (label, score) = m.scores("dim the lights a bit").entries.first()
log(if (score >= 0.8) label else "not sure ($label ${"%.2f".format(score)})")

What to label next: the texts it is least sure about, with its guess, in AMP/<name>-to-label.csv.

val asked = java.io.File.createTempFile("asked", ".txt")
asked.writeText("is it bright out\ndim it a little\nhey\nwill I need sunglasses\nmake it cosy in here")
val file = textsToLabel("intents", asked.path, limit = 3)   // diverse = true: three unlike each other among its closest calls
log(file ?: "nothing to label")
// fill in its label column, then: fineTune("intents", source("intents-to-label.csv"))

The Improve tab's teach loop, from a script: a correction goes to the top of the queue, labeled, as the chips under the Try line put it there; the plan says in the strip's words what a fine-tune on the labeled rows would do, training nothing (an internal line, and an error line when it would not start); after the fine-tune the queue is graded again by the head that answers since:

val queued = teach("intents", "put the radio on", "music")   // the queue's path; null for a model that keeps no texts
teach("intents", "play my road trip songs", "music")
teach("intents", "some music for the kitchen", "music")
queue("intents").forEach { log("${it.label.ifBlank { "?" }} · ${it.text}") }

val plan = planFineTune("intents")                           // on the labeled rows of its queue
if (plan.ok && queued != null) {
    fineTune("intents", source(queued))                      // as Fine-tune on the Improve tab's queue
    val graded = regradeQueue("intents")                     // what the new head answers to each text of the queue
    log("${graded.count { it.labeled && it.guess == it.label }} of ${graded.count { it.labeled }} corrections answered right")
} else log("not yet: ${plan.problems + plan.tooFew}")

planFineTune("intents", source("more.csv")) plans on a file instead, as the strip does before a fine-tune on one.

The vectors of every text embedded so far are kept, so the second build of the same file is mostly training: embeddingCache.print() shows them, embeddingCache.clear() frees the disk.

docs.title: 15. When something goes wrong
docs.text:
• A script that throws stops with Error: … in red and failed after 3s on the console strip; the error level turns itself on. The tooltip of the status keeps the last error.
  • A model that is not there: initMod("nope") throws Module 'nope' not found in …/AMP/models/intents. Wrap it when the script should go on:
val m = runCatching { initMod("intents") }.getOrElse { e ->
    error("no 'intents' model yet (${e.message}); building one")
    modelBuilder("intents", source("sample-intents.csv"))
    initMod("intents")
}
  • A terminated session: an inference on a session terminated from the Models page throws Model intents (#2) is closed; call initMod again to get a fresh one.
  • A second Run while a script runs only logs "Script is already running"; there is no stop. A script that loops forever is stopped by terminating the session it uses, or by closing the app.
  • importPlugin, saveState, loadState, listStates, packages.fetch and importModelOnnx never throw: they log one Error line and return nothing (null, an empty list). Database calls and initMod do throw, so that the script does not go on with no data; the examples above show the try.

docs.title: 16. Shell commands: look something up on the computer
docs.text:
shell runs a command in your login shell and gives back what it printed. A command that fails is not an exception, so the script decides what it means. The console shows each command as an info line; turn on data and error to read its output there as it runs.

val du = shell("du -sh .", dir = "~/Documents", timeoutSeconds = 60)
log("Documents: ${du.out}")

val found = shell("grep -rl TODO ~/notes")
when {
    found.timedOut -> error("grep took too long")
    found.exit == 1 -> log("nothing found")             // how grep says so
    !found.ok -> error("grep failed: ${found.err}")
    else -> found.lines.forEach { log(it) }
}

A script file gets its arguments one by one, whatever is in them. Use it for text the script did not write itself, which in the command line of shell would be read as a command:

val text = queue("intents").firstOrNull()?.text ?: "nothing yet"
val r = shellScript("~/bin/lookup.sh", listOf(text, "it's a second argument"))
if (r.ok) log("$r") else error("lookup.sh: exit ${r.exit}: ${r.err}")

A template from someone else runs its commands with your rights, so read it before you press Run.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: The Dashboard (route home1/) lists the devices you configured as cards. It is not reachable at the moment: no sidebar icon leads to it and the route sends you on to the sandbox, so what follows describes the screens as they are built, for when it is wired back in. Devices are stored in AMP/componentSettings.json and, when the Amie backend is reachable, synced to the backend under the signed-in user (a guest syncs under a fixed guest id).

docs.title: Adding a device
docs.text:
Press + in the window header. The Add Device screen asks for:

Field Meaning Device name How the card is titled Port The port the device listens on, typed (the serial ports the machine sees are listed under the card's configuration, port) Endpoint The device's address

docs.title: A device card
docs.text:
Each card shows the name, endpoint and port, and four actions:

Action Screen Connect The connection panel: shows the endpoint and status, with a Connect / Disconnect switch Manage A terminal bound to the device (source terminal/<deviceId>, shown by the console's columns switch) where you can send commands and see its output Configure The device's configuration page Remove Deletes the device from the configuration and refreshes the dashboard

Device terminals write to the same AMP/logs.txt as the sandbox console, tagged with their device id, so their history comes back when you reopen them.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Requirement Why Notes JDK 21 The desktop module pins a Java 21 toolchain Gradle's foojay resolver downloads one if it is missing Gradle wrapper ./gradlew from the repository root Gradle 9.3, configuration cache on BERT models modelBuilder and initMod embed text with the bge encoder; initMod() runs the NER model The NER folder (model.onnx, tokenizer.json) with bge/ inside it: AMP/models/bert for a Gradle run, where ./scripts/setup.sh downloads them, or AMIE_MODELS_DIR (BundledModels.kt). The packaged app ships them in app/resources/models/bert/ Keycloak (off) Sign-in, backups and publishing The desktop app has no accounts for now; AMIE_ACCOUNTS=1 turns them on, with Keycloak in Docker on http://localhost:8080 Amie backend (optional) Devices, packages, Publish Address in AMP/backend.json; see Amie backend Android SDK (optional) Only for the Android app sdk.dir=... in local.properties

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
All commands run from the repository root.

./gradlew :desktopApp:run                 # run the desktop app
./gradlew :desktopApp:compileKotlin       # compile only (fast check)
./gradlew :desktopApp:packageDistributionForCurrentOS   # DMG / MSI / DEB under amieApplication/desktopApp/build/compose/binaries/main/, BERT models included

Packaging copies the BERT models into the app (the bundleModels task) and fails when they are not there: point it at your copy with -Pamie.modelsDir=<folder> or AMIE_MODELS_DIR (the folder with model.onnx and bge/model.onnx). A package is built for the system it is built on, so the DEB comes from a Linux machine.

The lightweight build (-Pamie.lightweight=true, the default on an Apple Silicon Mac and on arm64 Linux such as a Raspberry Pi 5) leaves out TensorFlow 1.15, KotlinDL and their JavaCPP, about 700 MB of jars that are mostly native libraries for other systems. Training, fine-tuning, calibrating and serving are the app's own Kotlin heads on ONNX Runtime and work the same. It carries DJL's TensorFlow 2 engine instead, so importModel and initMod open TensorFlow SavedModels in it (the full build can't, as TensorFlow 1.15's classes clash with it); both builds open TorchScript on PyTorch (Models from outside). Settings shows Build · Lightweight · no TensorFlow 1.15 in it. The arm64 DEB can be made on an Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux container (eclipse-temurin:21-jdk with fakeroot and dpkg-dev, the models mounted and named with AMIE_MODELS_DIR, then ./gradlew :desktopApp:packageDeb); it installs into /opt/amie-pilot with a menu entry, and keeps AMP/ in ~/.local/share/amie-pilot/AMP.

In IntelliJ or Android Studio open the repository root and use the run configurations in the toolbar.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
./gradlew :desktopApp:test

The desktop module's tests need no services and never touch your AMP/ folder: the test task points AMIE_AMP_DIR at build/test-amp and the backend, site and Keycloak addresses at fake hosts, and the HTTP clients under test get a mock engine. They cover the editor (folding, formatting), the prediction helpers, the Postgres driver and config, every script of the cookbook and the starter templates (compiled through the sandbox's assembler), the templates store (save, replace, seed once), the serving access log (one line a request, never a text), the Keycloak client (password grant, refresh, logout, what each failure says, issuer, signature and expiry checks on the token), the backend client (profile, upload, publishing, the SSO handoff, saved states, error reports, an unreachable backend), a model session over a Mockito model, and the training kit (regularisation, schedules, early stopping, cross-validation, the head search, fine-tuning, calibration, versions and rollback, the texts to label, the embedding cache and the charts) over a fake encoder. TrainingGoldenTest holds the weights a default fit gives to the bit, so a change that moves the default training fails there. Five test classes have cases that run the real BERT encoder, so those only run when asked (the rest of each class runs always):

AMIE_E2E_ENCODER=1 ./gradlew :desktopApp:test --tests '*TrainingGoldenTest' --tests '*RealEncoderFineTuneTest' --tests '*EncoderLifecycleTest' --tests '*OrtScopesScriptTest' --tests '*ModelGroupsScriptTest' --tests '*VersionCompareTest' --no-configuration-cache --rerun

The first checks that a default build on the sample data still writes the same model.onnx, byte for byte; the second builds on the sample data, teaches the model a music label from a dozen sentences, checks it still answers the old labels and rolls it back. The third opens and closes a model session 30 times and checks that the shared encoder is given back each time, that a model closed twice gives it back once, that a cancelled encoder or head is opened again on the next text, and that a listener, a rename and a destroy let go of the encoder and the port. (ModelServerListenerTest starts and stops a listener 20 times on a free port without the encoder, in the normal run.)

PageKeyboardTest, in the normal run, opens the real Models page off-screen on three small models built with the fake encoder and presses every shortcut of the page (the list's moves, Enter to the Try line, ⌘F, ⌘1 to ⌘4, and Esc on each kind of thing it closes, the command palette, and Enter to a group's Try line), checking where the selection and the keyboard end up. It lists no GitHub jars while it runs, so it needs no network. TryPasteTest pastes into the Try line with the paste key, from a clipboard of its own: several lines after a sentence asked are a batch of the lines pasted alone, the field keeps what it held but for a selection pasted over, and a paste while it is asking starts nothing and says so. SelectionStaysTest checks that the palette's lit line stays on its item when the page lists the items again in another order, and that a list scrolls its selection into view once, at its first copy, and not again when a fold opens on it. FirstStepsPageTest opens the page from the empty snapshot of the app's first start on a model built, fine-tuned, asked and corrected with the fake encoder, and checks that the first steps stay hidden, also once the correction is taken away; then it opens the page again (the strip shows that step), gives the correction back (all done) and dismisses them. FirstStepsStripTest checks the strip alone; with AMIE_PAGE_SHOTS set it also saves it fresh, half done and done. NewModelPanelTest checks that a csv a first step asks for goes into an open New model form with what was typed in it kept. MixUpsPageTest gives two models built with the fake encoder a validation run with lights and weather swapped: What would help names the pairs, Show the rows opens the Metrics tab on the chosen pair's rows, brought into view in a window too low to show them otherwise, its chip shows them all again, and the model that keeps no texts gets the counts and no rows. FocusRingTest checks the ring Tab gives a control (and that a click leaves none, Space and Enter press it, and on the Models page Enter presses the control Tab moved to rather than going to the Try line, goes on to the Try line from text that presses nothing, and held down on a button presses only the button); ContrastTest computes WCAG's ratio for every colour against each surface it is drawn on, and for a heatmap's text on every shade of the ramp. SandboxJumpTest checks the sandbox's places: a console line's place calls back with its line and column (also while its tooltip shows, which used to throw), the editor puts the caret on a place, opens the fold over it and brings it into view, and in the real sandbox a script that doesn't compile names its own line, not one of assembly.kts, and is kept as a failed run. SandboxEditorWidthTest checks that the editor lays its text out as wide as its view, narrower once the console comes up beside it, and wider, unwrapped, for a line longer than the view, the width read off the field's own lines being the text's measured unwrapped. ConsoleFollowTest checks that a console opened on more lines than it shows starts at the newest and follows the next.

PageShotsTest renders the real Models page off-screen and uses it the way a person would: it clicks rows, tabs and buttons by their text, types on the Try line, and saves a PNG of every state worth a look. It builds two showcase models with the real encoder in the test AMP folder (a minute or two) and a group of the two, so it only runs when given a folder for the pictures. The harness itself (the window, the showcase models, the shots) is ui/PageHarness.kt, which CodingSandboxTourTest extends too:

AMIE_PAGE_SHOTS=/tmp/shots ./gradlew :desktopApp:test --tests 'org.example.project.ui.PageShotsTest' --tests 'org.example.project.ui.CodingSandboxTourTest' --no-configuration-cache --rerun

The tour starts with the first steps, on a page of their own opened with the queue's labels taken away, so correct an answer is the step to take: taken on the Try line (all done, the bar green), then Dismiss, and Settings with the toggle that shows them again. Then it goes through the model list and a model's About and Metrics tabs, its Improve tab with the queue half labeled, its first version compared with the head that answers now on what its fine-tune taught it (the figure, then the rows that changed), a Try answer corrected with a new label, the fine-tune plan blocked and then ready, the notice with Undo after the fine-tune, the ⋯ menu, New model (Train on a csv…) with the sample data, a batch of sentences pasted on the Try line (copied as csv, which it checks, and its unsure answers queued), a model that keeps no texts with a sentence and a batch (checking on the way that nothing it was asked was written anywhere in AMP), the Groups tab with the group of the two asked a sentence on its Try line (the same check after it), the Packages and Sessions tabs, and Settings. Last, on a page of its own as it adds a run, both models are validated on the sample data with five lights rows labeled weather and three weather rows labeled lights: the Improve tab names what it mixes up, Show the rows opens one pair's rows, and the model that keeps no texts gets the counts (the same check after it, its csv holding a sentence nothing may keep). What the page copies goes to the harness, never to your clipboard. AMIE_PAGE_STEPS runs steps of your own instead, separated by ;, such as click:Metrics;wait:1000;shot:metrics or ask:turn the lights on;until:wrong? it is;shot:answer. The other steps are named:text (a click on the first control whose screen-reader name holds that text, as an icon-only control's tip does: named:Where Listen serves), at:x,y (a click there), hover:x,y (the next shot keeps the pointer there, so its tooltip shows), type:text, key:Enter (key:Cmd+F holds ⌘, Ctrl off macOS; key:Tab moves the keyboard on, its ring showing, as in the app), paste:one|two|three (those lines into the Try line at once, as a paste gives them), clipboard:name (what the page copied, as name.txt), scroll:text (scrolls until what shows that text, or has it as its description, is in view: scroll:Versions), menu (the selected model's ⋯ menu), building:showcase:fineTune and built (the page sees a build, fine-tune or calibration of that model start and end, without training anything), busy:ms and tree:name, which writes the page's semantics tree as text so you can see what there is to click. The showcase models are removed at the end; AMIE_PAGE_KEEP=1 keeps them for the next run. AMIE_PAGE_HEIGHT sets the window's height (1000 by default; the window is 1500 wide). show:sandbox (or show:settings, show:models) switches the window as the sidebar would; in the sandbox, code:one|two puts those lines in the editor in place of its text, and run presses Run.

CodingSandboxTourTest (part of the same command, or alone with --tests 'org.example.project.ui.CodingSandboxTourTest') shoots the sandbox and needs no showcase model: three runs of main.kts (one that finishes, one that throws in an API call, one that doesn't compile), the console's places, the tooltip of one, the caret put on its line, and Recent runs. The script, assembly.kts and the recent runs of the test AMP folder are put back as they were after.

While the harness runs, AMP/github.json lists no repositories, so the Packages tab stays off the network.

docs.title: UI goldens
docs.text:
The tour's shots are also a visual regression check. amieApplication/desktopApp/src/test/resources/ui-goldens/ keeps a golden PNG of every state the tour shoots, and this compares a new tour with them:

AMIE_UI_GOLDENS=check ./gradlew :desktopApp:testGoldens --no-configuration-cache --rerun

It runs in an AMP folder of its own, build/golden-amp, emptied first and given the seed's demo jar as its one package, so nothing other tests leave in build/test-amp shows in a golden, and in a JVM of its own, so nothing another test did once per JVM (the backend's file, the ORT cache) is missing from it either. AMIE_UI_GOLDENS=check ./gradlew :desktopApp:testUi takes the tour too, after the suite; the shots go to build/ui-goldens (or where AMIE_PAGE_SHOTS says). A pixel has changed when one of its channels moved by more than 2 (of 255), and a shot passes while no more than 0.002% of its pixels changed: about 30 of a 1500×1000 shot, a stray pixel but never a word. What shows a value of the run, which the next run shows otherwise (a time, how long a thing took, the memory figure of the status strip, a session's number, a folder's path), is marked on the page with Modifier.variesByRun() and left out, both where the golden had it and where the shot has it. A check that fails names each shot that changed, how many pixels and where, and saves <name>.diff.png beside the shots: the shot dimmed, what changed in red, what was left out in dark blue.

When the change is meant, make the goldens again and commit them with it:

AMIE_UI_GOLDENS=update ./gradlew :desktopApp:testGoldens --no-configuration-cache --rerun

update writes the goldens, and marks.json with where each one showed something of its run, only once the tour got to its end, and drops the golden of a state the tour no longer shoots. Something new on the page that changes from run to run needs variesByRun(), or every check after it fails there. The goldens hold this machine's fonts and text rendering (macOS); on another system, make them there first.

Two more switches turn on checks that need something outside the repository: AMIE_CHECK_JARS=<folder> checks every jar in that folder as initMod and a fetch would (JarPackagesScriptTest, nothing of the jars is run), and AMIE_LIVE_GITHUB=1 lists the jars of the real GitHub repository (GitHubJarsTest). Coverage is on only when asked for:

./gradlew :desktopApp:test -Pcoverage && ./gradlew :desktopApp:jacocoTestReport -Pcoverage   # build/reports/jacoco/test

The services themselves are tested in the Amie repository (README.md there, "Testing"): unit tests for the backend and the S3 service, and scripts/e2e-auth-publish.py, which runs sign-in, registration, publishing and SSO against the running stack.

docs.title: First start
docs.text:
1. The app opens on the sandbox with main.kts open. No account is needed: the sandbox, the models and the metrics work on this machine. A session saved in AMP/session.json signs you back in without asking; otherwise you are a guest, and signing in is under Account in Settings for when you want publishing, backups or the package repository; see Signing in.
  2. Open the templates (the disk icon on the strip over the editor) and press Load on Ask the dummy model, then press Run. Everything the app writes goes into its AMP folder, which is ~/Library/Application Support/amie pilot/AMP on macOS whether it was started with Gradle or installed; see The AMP folder.

docs.title: The three screens
docs.text:
• Sandbox (the prompt icon, >_, first in the left sidebar): the editor with Run over it, and the output console. The sandbox.
  • Models (the cube, second sidebar icon): every intent model with its metrics, data, requirements, console and sessions; the package jars and their collections; and every open session. Open to everyone; only Publish needs a sign-in. Models page, Models and metrics.
  • Settings (the gears at the foot of the sidebar): your account with its backup and package search, UI scale, the editor, the AMP files. Settings.

The device dashboard (route home1/) is not reachable at the moment: no sidebar icon leads to it and the route sends you on to the sandbox. Its screens are described in Devices.

The window's top bar (30dp, dragging it moves the window) is the page's own toolbar, as an IDE's, with no title: the sandbox has its script's name, +, the env, Run and export there; the Models page its tabs; Settings a back chevron and its sections as tabs. On Windows and Linux the window's minimize, full screen (F11 too) and close end it. On a Mac the window is the system's, its title bar see-through under the bar: the red, yellow and green buttons sit at its left, the green one (or View → Enter Full Screen, ⌃⌘F) gives full screen in its own Space, and Esc or the same again leaves it. The account isn't there: who is signed in, Sign in, Create account and Log out are all under Account in Settings.

At the foot of the window a 22dp status strip, as in VS Code, shows the process memory and the heap as text at the right. Its ✕ hides it until the app closes, and Memory then appears in the sidebar to bring it back.

docs.title: Learn amie
docs.text: An interpreter for scripts that train, ask and serve intent models, from the first line at the prompt to a model served over HTTP, one chapter at a time. Every example runs as it is written.

docs.title: What amie is
docs.text:
______     __    __     __     ______
/\  __ \   /\ "-./  \   /\ \   /\  ___\
\ \  __ \  \ \ \-./\ \  \ \ \  \ \  __\
 \ \_\ \_\  \ \_\ \ \_\  \ \_\  \ \_____\
  \/_/\/_/   \/_/  \/_/   \/_/   \/_____/

amie trains small intent models on your own labeled text, runs them, groups them, serves them over HTTP and scripts all of it in Kotlin. A script is main.kts, and the functions it calls (initMod, modelBuilder, group, database, log and the rest) are in scope with nothing to import.

It works the way the Python interpreter does: a prompt where each line runs as you type it, script files, -c for a line of code, and a command for every feature. Everything a script makes lives in one folder, the AMP, so a model built by one script is there for the next, and a package added at the command line opens in a script.

amie is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later. The full text is the LICENSE file at the root of the repository; amie --version says so too.

docs.title: Install and the first run
docs.text:
The install script builds the interpreter and puts it on the PATH: the distribution under ~/.local/lib/amie, and ~/.local/bin/amie linked to it.

$ amie/install.sh
Building amie...
Installed amie 1.0.0 (Kotlin 2.1.0) on OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 21.0.5, Mac OS X aarch64 at /Users/me/.local/bin/amie

--prefix /usr/local installs it for every user (build as yourself first, then sudo it with --no-build); --uninstall takes it out again. A JDK 21 is needed, to run as well as to build, and amie finds one on its own: AMIE_JAVA_HOME, JAVA_HOME when it is one, the Mac's java_home, Homebrew's openjdk@21, sdkman's, /usr/lib/jvm, or one Gradle downloaded.

From the checkout, the launcher at the root of the repository runs it without installing, building it the first time and again whenever the sources changed:

./amie --version
amie 1.0.0 (Kotlin 2.1.0) on OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 21.0.5, Mac OS X aarch64
amie is free software under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later: see LICENSE.

Built by hand, ./gradlew :amie:installDist at the repository root leaves it in amie/build/install/amie, the folder the install script copies. The rest of this book writes amie for any of these.

docs.title: The AMP folder
docs.text:
Everything amie knows is in one folder, the AMP: models, envs, packages, templates, the log. By default:

Where Folder macOS ~/Library/Application Support/amie pilot/AMP Windows %APPDATA%\amie pilot\AMP Elsewhere ~/.local/share/amie-pilot/AMP

Another folder is one option away: amie --amp ~/scratch/amp, or the environment variable AMIE_AMP_DIR. A folder that doesn't exist yet is made, empty, which is a fine way to try things without touching the default one. The greeting at the prompt says which AMP is in use.

Intent models train on a BERT encoder, read from AMP/models/bert, or from the folder AMIE_MODELS_DIR names. A scratch AMP needs one or the other before its first build.

docs.title: The first run
docs.text:
$ amie
 ______     __    __     __     ______
/\  __ \   /\ "-./  \   /\ \   /\  ___\
\ \  __ \  \ \ \-./\ \  \ \ \  \ \  __\
 \ \_\ \_\  \ \_\ \ \_\  \ \_\  \ \_____\
  \/_/\/_/   \/_/  \/_/   \/_/   \/_____/
amie 1.0.0 (Kotlin 2.1.0) on OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM 21.0.5, Mac OS X aarch64
Type :help for the commands, :api for the script's functions, :learn for the book, :quit to leave. AMP: /Users/me/Library/Application Support/amie pilot/AMP
>>> log("hello")
hello
>>> :quit

amie -h prints the whole command line, and every command prints its own help with --help.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text:
At >>> each line is a piece of script, run in one interpreter kept from line to line. What a line defines (a val, a fun, a class, an import) is there for the lines after it. The value a line ends with is printed.

>>> val texts = listOf("turn the lights on", "is it raining")
>>> texts.size
2
>>> fun shout(s: String) = s.uppercase() + "!"
>>> shout(texts.first())
TURN THE LIGHTS ON!

A line that isn't whole waits at ... for the rest. A block whose brackets are closed is sent by a blank line, so a for or a function over several lines goes in as one piece:

>>> for (t in texts) {
...     log(t.length)
... }
...
18
13

Lines are edited and recalled with the arrow keys, and the history lives in ~/.amie_history between runs. Ctrl-C stops the line that is running, or drops the block being typed. Ctrl-D leaves, as :quit does.

docs.title: The prompt's own commands
docs.text:
A line that starts with a colon is for the prompt itself, not the script:

Command What it does :help These commands :api [word] The script's functions, with the word in their name or description: :api group :learn This book, in the browser :env [name] The env the lines run in; with a name, that env from now on :load file.kts Runs the file's lines here, so what it defines stays :sessions Every open session: models, groups, packages, templates in the background :config [x.jar] Package config files: every jar's and whether each is filled in, or one jar's keys; key=value sets keys; :config --help lists all of it :setup x.jar Asks for each config key of the jar with its hint; Enter keeps a value :terminate x Closes the session named x, or #id; :terminate all closes every one :runs The recorded runs of main.kts, AMP/pluginDir/runs.jsonl :reset Forgets what the lines typed here defined :clear Clears the screen :quit Leaves; :exit, :q and Ctrl-D do too

help, help(group), quit and exit work without the colon too, with or without the parentheses, as they do at Python's prompt. A line that starts with amie and a space is amie's own command line, run right here: amie envs new prod, amie models list, amie hf search bert. On a terminal the banner is in the pride flag's colors, the commands and the prompt have a color each and errors are red; a piped output or NO_COLOR in the environment leaves everything plain.

:api is the fastest way to find a function. The description of each comes from the list the script API is generated from, so what it says is what the function does:

>>> :api vote
fun group(name: String): ModelSwarm
    The models of a group opened together: predict is the best score across them, vote the label most give, ...

docs.title: The first lines of script
docs.text:
The console has levels. log and info are the script's own output, data is what it produced, error is a problem. Internal lines, the engine's own, are hidden unless amie runs with -v.

>>> log("hello from amie")
hello from amie
>>> data(mapOf("lights" to 0.9f, "weather" to 0.1f))
lights: 0.9
weather: 0.1
>>> error("how a problem looks")
how a problem looks

Errors go to standard error, everything else to standard output, so a script's results can be piped and its complaints still reach the terminal. Every line also goes to AMP/logs.txt.

docs.title: Ask a model
docs.text:
A model is opened by name with initMod, which gives a session: one per model, kept open until it is closed. Every session answers through the same three calls.

>>> val m = initMod("intents")
>>> m.predict("switch off the kitchen light")
lights
>>> m.scores("is it going to rain")
{weather=0.93, lights=0.04, greeting=0.03}
>>> m.answer("good morning")
greeting:0.97
Call Returns predict(text) The best label, nothing else; throws when the model answers nothing scores(text) Every label with its score, best first, a Map<String, Float> predictions(text) The answers as Prediction(label, score), in the model's order inference(text), run(text) The raw lines the model answers, label:score answer(text) The first raw answer as it came, or null

Each call runs the model once, so ask once and keep the result. The chapter on models trains the intents model these lines use.

docs.title: A confidence gate
docs.text:
The scores let a script say "not sure" instead of guessing:

>>> val threshold = 0.5f
>>> for (text in listOf("turn the lights on", "asdf qwerty")) {
...     val (label, score) = m.scores(text).entries.first()
...     if (score < threshold) log("$text: not sure ($label ${"%.2f".format(score)})")
...     else log("$text: $label ${"%.2f".format(score)}")
... }
...
turn the lights on: lights 0.97
asdf qwerty: not sure (greeting 0.41)

docs.title: A model for one block
docs.text:
sessionMod gives a snapshot of a model's head, kept in memory and gone when the block ends. Inside the block its functions need no name in front, and what the block ends on is what the call returns:

>>> val answers = sessionMod("intents") {
...     listOf("hello there", "lights off").map { predict(it) }
... }
...
>>> answers
[greeting, lights]

docs.title: Scripts in files
docs.text:
A file of script runs as main.kts, with the same API in scope and nothing to import:

// label.kts
val m = initMod("intents")
val lines = generateSequence { input() }        // standard input, a line at a time, until it ends
lines.forEach { log("${m.predict(it)}\t$it") }

$ printf 'lights off\nis it raining\n' | amie label.kts
lights  lights off
weather is it raining

The forms of a run:

Command line What happens amie label.kts Runs the file amie label.kts a b With arguments, read as System.getProperty("amie.args"), one a line amie -c 'log(initMod("intents").predict("hi"))' Runs the code given amie -i label.kts Runs it, then opens the prompt with its models still open and its values defined amie -e prod label.kts In the env prod, over the one the script names amie -v label.kts With the internal lines: the env sourcing, a build's phases, what the run used amie run label.kts The same as the bare file amie new reader A project: AMP/projects/reader/main.kts to start from, in an env named reader amie run reader Runs the project by its name, as a starter or a template by its title

Standard output carries the console, standard error the errors, with the script's line in front:

$ amie bad.kts
main.kts:2:5: Unresolved reference: initMode
$ echo $?
1

The exit code is 0 when the script finished, 1 when it failed, and 2 for a command line amie can't read. A script that leaves a model serving keeps the process up until Ctrl-C.

-i is the way to work on a script: run it, then poke at what it built from the prompt, and :load runs a file into the prompt the same way without leaving.

docs.title: Train a model
docs.text:
An intent model is trained from a csv with a text column and a label column, whatever they are called. A handful of rows for each label is enough to start; more rows make a better model.

text,label
turn the lights on,lights
switch off the kitchen light,lights
lights out please,lights
is it going to rain,weather
what's the weather like today,weather
will it be sunny tomorrow,weather
hello there,greeting
good morning,greeting
hi how are you,greeting

The command does the whole thing and prints the validation:

$ amie models build intents.csv --name intents
Building intents: embedding 9 rows, training, exporting
accuracy 1.00  macro F1 1.00
label     precision  recall  f1  support
greeting  1.00       1.00    1.00  3
lights    1.00       1.00    1.00  3
weather   1.00       1.00    1.00  3

The model is in AMP/models/intents/intents, ready for initMod("intents"). Validated on a split of its own rows by default, it validates on a test file instead with --test test.csv.

The same build as script, which is what the command runs for you. intents.csv stands for your own file: source() finds it as given, relative to the folder amie was started in, then in AMP/, then in AMP/pluginDir/. A new AMP folder has sample-intents.csv to try.

val train = source("intents.csv")          // the text and label columns are inferred
relate(train, "intents-test.csv")          // optional: a test file to validate on
val built = modelBuilder("intents", train)  // embeds with BERT, trains a small head, exports ONNX
built.modelStatus()                         // precision, recall, F1 for each label

A file named in a script is looked up as given, then in the AMP folder, then in AMP/pluginDir.

docs.title: Look at what was built
docs.text:
$ amie models list
intent    intents    3 labels    v1
$ amie models validate intents
$ amie models info intents
$ amie models remove intents

validate prints the stored validation again; info the labels, the encoder, the version, how it was trained, the groups it is in and where it is served, if anywhere. In script, validateMetrics("intents"), confusionMatrix("intents") and mistakes("intents") show the same as tables.

docs.title: Teach it more
docs.text:
A trained model learns from new rows without starting over. Rows of labels it knows correct it, a label it doesn't know gets an output of its own, and what it knew is replayed so it keeps it. The model before stays as a version.

>>> fineTune("intents", source("more.csv"))
>>> versions("intents")
>>> rollback("intents", 1)

buildOptions opens the rest: your own head architectures, cross-validation over folds, calibration so the scores mean what they say, and a search over candidates. :api buildOptions lists what it takes.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group is a named set of models, kept in the env, that is asked as one. vote is the label most of them give, predict the best score across them, each every model's own answer.

$ amie groups add house intents dummy
$ amie groups list
house    intents, dummy    env default
$ amie groups open house "turn the lights on"
intents: lights
dummy: lights
vote: lights

Without texts, groups open reads them from standard input, a line each. groups remove house dummy takes a model out, and without a model removes the group.

In script:

>>> val swarm = group("house")
>>> swarm.vote("is it raining")
weather
>>> swarm.each("is it raining")
{intents=weather, dummy=weather}
>>> swarm.close()

Opening a group opens a session of each model; closing the swarm closes the ones it opened.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
A package is a jar with a class that answers text, kept in AMP/pluginDir. It is opened like a model, by its file name, and asked with run or answer, since it has no labels of its own:

$ amie packages search google
6 jars in samging/jar-jar matching 'google'
$ amie packages add spotify.jar
$ amie packages add ~/build/greeter.jar
greeter.jar: Greeter 1.2, a package class found
$ amie packages test greeter.jar
$ amie packages info greeter.jar
$ amie packages setup spotify.jar
    clientId: 
    clientSecret:

A jar's settings are files in AMP/pluginDir/config/<jar>/. amie packages setup asks for each key with the hint the file gives, Enter keeping a value, and offers the values another jar already has, so one Google client fills every Google package. amie packages config spotify.jar clientId=abc sets a key from a script, --all-jars sets it for every jar with that file, and amie packages config alone shows every jar's files and whether each is filled in.

>>> val greeter = initMod("greeter.jar")
>>> greeter.answer("hello")
Hello to you

add checks that the jar has a package class before copying it in. test runs the tests the jar declares in META-INF/amie/package.json, or one call with "hello" when it declares none. info says what the jar is, where it came from, whether it opens here and how its last test went.

docs.title: Writing a package: run and close
docs.text:
A package class fulfils the AmiePackage interface: List<String> run(String) and close(), both required, and a public no-arg constructor. Implementing the interface is the easiest way, but any class with the same methods qualifies, so a jar needs no amie library to compile against:

Member What amie does with it The no-arg constructor Every initMod("x.jar") makes a new instance, in a class loader of its own configure(File dir), if there Called after the constructor with AMP/pluginDir/config/<jar>/; Path, String and Map work too List<String> run(String text) What .run and .answer call; each element is one line void close() Called once, by .close(), :terminate or the end of a scope, to release what run opened; then the class loader is dropped 
public class Greeter {
    public java.util.List<String> run(String text) {
        return java.util.List.of("Hello to you");
    }

    public void close() {}
}

Two sessions of one jar never share an instance or a static field. run runs on amie's amie-package-call thread while the script waits; Ctrl-C interrupts it, and an exception it throws becomes the script's error. The classes must be compiled for Java 21 or older, and a Kotlin package can rely on amie's own standard library. When a jar has several classes that fit, "entry" in its META-INF/amie/package.json names the one.

docs.title: Packages from GitHub
docs.text:
A script asks for a jar in a GitHub repository with github:. amie downloads it, checks it as packages add does, and keeps it in AMP/pluginDir with where it came from:

>>> val notes = initMod("github:samging/jar-jar/memory.jar")
>>> notes.answer("help")
remember <text>  keeps it
>>> val files = initMod("files.jar")

A plain name like files.jar is looked for in the env, AMP/pluginDir, as a path, and last in the repositories of AMP/github.json, which starts with samging/jar-jar. @main, a tag or a commit after the name pins a version, and a release's assets are found too. A github: open downloads again only when the file changed; a plain name uses the copy already in AMP/pluginDir. A private repository needs GITHUB_TOKEN or a "token" in AMP/github.json; without one the jar is reported as not found. amie packages search lists what those repositories hold, and amie packages add <x.jar> downloads one by its name.

To upload a jar, check it with amie packages add and amie packages test, then open a pull request that adds it at the top of samging/jar-jar. Its Check jars workflow first checks every jar the way amie checks a download, running none of its code, then opens each one as amie packages test does: it calls run() with every test the jar declares and then close(). The jar is there for everyone once the pull request is merged.

docs.title: Maven packages
docs.text:
A library from Maven Central goes into the env, so a script can import it:

$ amie packages maven org.jsoup:jsoup:1.17.2
$ amie packages list

>>> import org.jsoup.Jsoup
>>> Jsoup.parse("<p>hi</p>").text()
hi

In a script file the same is one line, read before the script compiles: implementation("org.jsoup:jsoup:1.17.2"). What was ever imported into an env is kept in its lock file, like a virtualenv.

docs.title: Envs
docs.text:
An env is a folder under AMP/env holding its Maven packages and its groups. Scripts run in default unless told otherwise. A second env keeps one project's packages away from another's.

$ amie envs new prod
$ amie envs list
default    2 packages    1 group    AMP/env/default
prod       0 packages    0 groups   AMP/env/prod
$ amie envs show prod

Three ways to run in an env:

  • amie -e prod script.kts, or -e prod before any command, for this run.

  • :env prod at the prompt, for the lines after it.

  • amie envs use prod, which rewrites the environment(...) line of the saved main.kts in AMP/pluginDir, or makes one with it.

A script names its own env with environment(SettingsEnv("prod")), read before it compiles; -e wins over it.

docs.title: Templates and the background
docs.text:
A template is a script saved under a name in AMP/templates: the starters that come with amie, and the scripts you save.

$ amie templates list
Hello: log at every level          first steps, starter
Train a model from a csv           models, starter
Serve a model and call it          serving, starter
$ amie templates show "Train a model from a csv"
$ amie templates run "Train a model from a csv"

export turns a template into a bundle that runs on its own, a folder with a run.jar:

$ amie templates save reader ~/reader.kts     keeps the file as the template "reader"; a name taken is saved again
$ amie templates edit reader                  opens it in $VISUAL or $EDITOR, or prints the path when neither is set
$ amie templates delete reader                removes it

$ amie templates export talk --out ~/bundles/talk
$ java -jar ~/bundles/talk/run.jar

The bundle carries the env's Maven jars and the package jars the script uses. --no-jars leaves them out, for a bundle to send where they are already, or to keep it small: require.txt then lists each file with the path to put it at under the bundle (a Maven jar from Maven Central or the exporting machine's AMP/env/caches, a package jar from its AMP/pluginDir), run.jar --check says which are still missing, and a run with a Maven jar missing fetches it from Maven Central when it can reach it; with a package jar missing it stops and names it.

$ amie templates export talk --out ~/bundles/talk --no-jars
$ cat ~/bundles/talk/require.txt
$ java -jar ~/bundles/talk/run.jar --check

docs.title: A template in the background
docs.text:
A script can start a template beside itself and talk to it. The template reads its caller's lines with input() and answers with output(...); the caller sends and receives.

// the template, saved as "reader"
val model = initMod("intents")
while (true) {
    val text = input() ?: break        // null once the caller closes its input
    output(model.predict(text))
}

>>> val job = coroutineTemplate("reader")
>>> job.send("turn the lights on")
>>> job.receive()
lights
>>> job.closeInput()
>>> job.await()
finished

By delegation the same template is called like a function, started on the first call and reused after:

>>> val reader by template("reader")
>>> reader("is it raining")
weather
>>> reader.close()

A template that fails makes the call throw, with its name and its error, so a failure never passes for an answer. :sessions lists the runs in the background, and a script that ends waits for the ones it started.

docs.title: Serve a model
docs.text:
A model served answers over HTTP. The command keeps the process up until Ctrl-C:

$ amie models serve intents --port 8765
Serving intents at http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict
Serving. Stop with Ctrl-C or SIGTERM.

From another terminal:

$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict -d '{"text": "turn the lights on"}'
lights:0.97
$ curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict?text=is+it+raining'

Every request is appended to the model's incoming.jsonl. In script, serve("intents", port = 8765) returns the address or null when it couldn't start, and stopServing("intents") ends it; a script that leaves a model serving keeps amie running after its last line.

docs.title: Models from the Hub
docs.text:
Models of the Hugging Face Hub that run here, ONNX among them, are searched, looked at and imported into AMP/models/imported:

$ amie hf search sentiment --format onnx
$ amie hf search whisper --task asr --limit 5
$ amie hf info onnx-community/whisper-tiny.en
$ amie hf import onnx-community/whisper-tiny.en --model-name whisper-tiny

>>> val whisper = initMod("whisper-tiny")
>>> huggingFace.search("bert", format = "onnx")
>>> val m = huggingFace("owner/repo")

The tasks narrow a search: text-classification, ner, tts, asr, embeddings and more; info says which files run here and which one an import takes. A repo with several files that run here (a full model.onnx beside quantized and fp16 ones, say) is picked at the terminal with the arrow keys: the same list, the one import takes under the cursor, up and down move it, Enter imports, n leaves. --take 3 picks for a pipe or a script. A gated repo needs HF_TOKEN in the environment. An ONNX, TorchScript or TensorFlow model already on disk is opened by its path with importModel("/path/model.onnx").

docs.title: Encoder and decoder pairs
docs.text:
A sequence-to-sequence export (T5, BART, Marian translation, Whisper) is two ONNX files in one folder, encoder_model.onnx with decoder_model.onnx and often decoder_with_past_model.onnx. Neither answers a text alone: the encoder turns the input into hidden states, the decoder takes those with the ids written so far and gives the next token's scores, one step at a time. The import offers every encoder and decoder of the folder as a numbered menu, the companion files beneath, and at a terminal waits for the choice:

$ amie hf import google-t5/t5-small
google-t5/t5-small is an encoder and decoder pair; the import takes the files marked:
  encoders
  [x]  1  onnx/encoder_model.onnx (134.9 MB)
> [ ]  2  onnx/encoder_model_quantized.onnx (33.9 MB)
  decoders
  [x]  3  onnx/decoder_model.onnx (221.7 MB)
  [ ]  4  onnx/decoder_model_merged.onnx (221.9 MB)
  [ ]  5  onnx/decoder_model_merged_quantized.onnx (56.0 MB)
  [ ]  6  onnx/decoder_model_quantized.onnx (55.7 MB)
  [x]  7  onnx/decoder_with_past_model.onnx (209.7 MB)
  [ ]  8  onnx/decoder_with_past_model_quantized.onnx (52.7 MB)
  with: config.json, generation_config.json, spiece.model, tokenizer.json, tokenizer_config.json
Take 1 3 7, 568.3 MB
up and down move, space takes or leaves a file, Enter imports, n leaves

The marked files are the default: the full variant, with the merged decoder left out when the plain and the with-past ones are there. Space takes or leaves the file under the cursor, the quantized ones here, at least one encoder and one decoder; the size line follows. --take "2 6 8" picks for a pipe or a script's huggingFace("…"), which otherwise take the marked files without asking.

initMod("opus-mt-en-de") then opens both sessions, and the script wires them. .inference, .predict and .answer refuse on a pair, saying how.

Member What it is Comes from m.encoder The encoder session, run with tensors: .inputs, .outputs, .run(mapOf(…)) encoder_model.onnx m.decoder The decoder session, the same way decoder_model.onnx m.decoderWithPast The decoder that takes the past attention state back, or null when the export has none decoder_with_past_model.onnx m.tokens(text) The token ids and the attention mask of a text, as .ids and .mask tokenizer.json beside the models m.text(ids) The words of a list of ids The same tokenizer m.startToken The id the decoder starts from, or null when no config names one decoder_start_token_id, else bos_token_id, of generation_config.json, then config.json m.endToken The id that ends the decoding, or null eos_token_id of the same files m.encode(text), m.encode(file) The encoder run: a text through the tokenizer, or an audio or image file through the preprocessor; .hidden the states, .mask the text's mask tokenizer.json, or preprocessor_config.json m.decoderFeeds(encoded, ids) The decoder's inputs for one step: the ids so far, the hidden states, and the encoder's mask when the decoder names one m.decoder.inputs m.startTokens(encoded?, vararg tokens) The ids the decoder starts from: the start id and the forced ones after it, each replaceable by a name the config knows: a language ("de"), a task ("translate", "transcribe"), "timestamps" or "notimestamps". A language left open and not named is detected from the encoding, else English forced_decoder_ids, lang_to_id, task_to_id, no_timestamps_token_id of the config files m.preprocessor The preprocessor_config.json as JSON: sampling rate, mel bins, image size, mean and std That file m.abilities encoder, decoder, and decoderWithPast, tokens, startToken when the folder has them; text, audio or image for what the encoder takes The folder m.getStatus(), m.close() Each session's status by name; every session closed Both sessions

What the encoder takes is read off the folder: a text pair has no preprocessor_config.json and takes text through its tokenizer; one whose file names a feature extractor (Whisper) takes an audio file, wav or aiff at any rate, turned into the log-mel spectrogram that file describes; one naming an image processor (TrOCR, Donut, Nougat) takes an image file, resized and normalized as it says. encode does whichever applies, and decoderFeeds fills the decoder's inputs by their names, Marian's encoder_attention_mask among them. The same greedy loop then translates or transcribes:

>>> val m = initMod("t5-small")                 // or "whisper-tiny", with a wav in place of the text
>>> val e = m.encode("translate English to German: The house is wonderful.")
>>> val starts = m.startTokens(e)               // Whisper: start, language (detected, or startTokens(e, "de")), transcribe, no timestamps
>>> val ids = starts.toMutableList()
>>> for (i in 1..40) {
...     val logits = m.decoder.run(m.decoderFeeds(e, ids.toLongArray())).getValue("logits")   // [1, ids so far, vocabulary]
...     val vocab = logits.shape.last().toInt()
...     val last = logits.floats().takeLast(vocab)                 // the scores at the last place
...     val best = last.indices.maxBy { last[it] }
...     if (best.toLong() == m.endToken) break
...     ids.add(best.toLong())
... }
>>> log(m.text(ids.drop(starts.size).toLongArray()))
Das Haus ist wunderbar.

The sessions are still there raw: m.tokens(text) and m.encoder.run(mapOf("input_ids" to t.ids, "attention_mask" to t.mask)) are what encode(text) does, and m.encoder.inputs names what a file becomes (input_ids, input_features, pixel_values). Running the whole id list each step is simple, not fast. A faster loop runs m.decoder once, then m.decoderWithPast with each step's present.* outputs fed back as its past_key_values.* inputs, which its .inputs name.

docs.title: Sessions and housekeeping
docs.text:
Whatever a script opens is a session: a model, a group, a package, a template in the background. Sessions stay open after the line that opened them, which is what makes the second predict fast.

>>> :sessions
#1  intents  model    running  opened 14:02:11
#2  house    group    running  opened 14:05:40
>>> :terminate house
>>> :terminate all

From the command line, amie sessions list shows the sessions of that process, and amie sessions runs the recorded runs of main.kts.

docs.title: Scope functions
docs.text:
A block decides how long what it opens lives:

Block What it opens is ortClosable { } Closed with the block ortStatic("name") { } Kept across runs under that name ortRequired("name") { } Kept while anything else is in session, freed once nothing else is open; its block opens it again ortLimited("name", 3) { } Capped at that many ortAsync { } Run in the background 
>>> ortClosable {
...     val m = initMod("intents")
...     listOf("hi", "lights off").map { m.predict(it) }
... }
...
[greeting, lights]

docs.title: Data and the shell
docs.text:
A Postgres database named in AMP/databases.json is one call away, and so is the login shell:

>>> val db = database("main")
>>> db.print("select label, count(*) from answers group by label")
>>> shell("ls ~/data").out

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
initMod and database throw when what they name isn't there, so a script doesn't go on without data. Wrap what may be missing:

val m = runCatching { initMod("intents") }.getOrElse { e ->
    error("no intents model yet (${e.message}); building one")
    modelBuilder("intents", source("intents.csv"))
    initMod("intents")
}

importModel, importPlugin and the save and load of states never throw: they log one error line and return nothing, so test their value.

At the prompt an error prints and the prompt comes back, with everything defined before it still there. In a file the run stops, the line is on standard error and the exit code is 1. handleBy(handler) { } runs a block on after an error with the handler's value, and errorLog() is what the local text model makes of the last one.

When a build or a run does something you didn't expect, -v shows the internal lines: which env was sourced, the build's phases, what the run used.

The amie reference has the command line, every command, the script API in brief and the exit codes; the Scripting API has every function in full.

docs.title: Models page
docs.text:
Route models, opened from the second icon in the sidebar (the cube), which the arrow chip at the far left of the tab strip, right where the sidebar meets it, hides and shows (the arrow turns round while the sidebar is away) (the choice is kept in AMP/settings.json, as the sandbox's is). It is a full page (not a side panel) in components/terminal/window/controller/ModelsPage.kt (its state and what each action does; each area of it is a file beside it: ModelsList.kt, ModelDetail.kt, ModelTabs.kt, ModelTry.kt, ModelImprove.kt, NewModelPanel.kt, GroupsTab.kt (a group's Try line in GroupTry.kt), PackagesTab.kt, SessionsTab.kt, Notices.kt, ModelIcons.kt, ModelsSnapshot.kt for what it reads, ModelsDecisions.kt for what it decides (the list's order, what Improve suggests, a queue row's chips, how a plan is worded), FirstSteps.kt for the first steps over the Models tab, PageWidgets.kt), and it re-reads its state while open. What it showed last is kept for the life of the app (ModelsCache), so coming back to the page shows the models at once; the first read after start-up is local only (files, sessions, listeners) and the one slow read, the server's jar listing, is fetched right after and cached for a minute by JarPackages. Nothing on the page waits for the network.

The page keeps to one quiet scheme, the same grays as the sandbox, and everything on it is square: no rounded corners anywhere, in the window frame, the sidebar, the header, the chips, the status marks or the charts. There are three kinds of button: one filled dark-blue button per place for the action that creates, builds, validates, opens or fetches (New model, Build, Open session, Validate, Add, Create, Fetch, Save), a dark-red one for what ends or removes something (Stop, Terminate, Destroy), and bare text for everything else (the Save under ⚙ too), with a faint square under the pointer. The chips that are on or off (methods, run numbers, console scope) are bare text too, lit in the tab strip's gray when on; the label chips under a wrong answer and in the queue (and + new label) have a thin outline while off, and ⋯ shows a bordered square under the pointer. The icon chips (the sidebar's arrow, and the sandbox's) are white icons on no square. Two hues sit on the grays, as accents and never as fills: blue for what is primary, chosen or focused (the filled button, a link, the focus ring, a focused field's border, the open tab's bar, the selected row's edge and its faint wash, the line of a build or a download under way) and green for what runs, succeeded or is done (the status marks, the Run icon, the bar of a notice that ended well); red stays for what ends, removes or failed. Nothing is vivid: the tokens the rest of the app shares (AccentColor, AccentInk, AccentWash, SuccessColor, DangerColor in ui/theme/Color.kt) are muted too, so every screen calms down with the page. Muted is not faint, though: every word reaches 4.5:1 against what it is drawn on, and the icons, the status marks and the focus ring 3:1 (WCAG 2 AA; ContrastTest holds each colour where it is used, the muted words of a lit line one step lighter than the rest). On-screen words are kept short; the explanations live in the tooltips.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
• Every button, tab and status word has a tooltip (components/ui/viewport/Tooltip.kt, AppTooltip): rest the pointer on it for half a second and a square dark box says what it does, or, on a disabled button, what is still missing. The status words (inferring, 2 open, on server, on GitHub, missing) say what they mean for that row (a quiet state such as idle is only the gray mark and its tooltip); the status strip at the foot of the window explains its numbers.
  • Almost nothing is reachable only by right-click. Every model, group and package row has a ⋯ button (shown while the pointer is over the row and on the selected row) and every detail panel header has one at its right end; a session row's Copy log and Copy #id, and a Maven Central hit's actions, are on right-click only. Both open the same square menu the right-click opens (SquareContextMenu), with the actions that end or remove something in red. A model's menu groups its actions under small headings (Check, Improve, Groups, Share, Manage). Esc or a click elsewhere closes it.
  • Slow actions say so on their button: Opening…, Starting…, Stopping…, Publishing…, Fetching…, Saving… (then saved for a moment), Rolling back…, Picking…, Asking…, Teaching…, Building…, Terminating…, Comparing…, Queueing…, Testing…, Removing…, Adding…, and the button is disabled until the action ends.
  • Notices are readable: what an action did, or why it failed, appears in a strip under the tabs with the whole text (it wraps and can be selected), a bar at its left edge that is red for a failure, and Dismiss. A notice after a change to a model's head (a fine-tune, calibration, retrain or rollback) also has Undo, which makes the head before it the model again; that notice has an Undo in turn. Destroying a model asks first in the same kind of strip, with the full consequence spelled out and a red Destroy button.
  • Forms open in the panel, not above the page. New model and New collection take the place of the detail panel on the right while they are open, so the list never moves. While New model's form is open its button is a red Close (hidden while a build runs), and every form has a red × at the right of its hint line; either brings the selected item back. A form has no title, only a muted line saying what it takes. Everything that closes something inside the page (a form, the Try table, a comparison, a collection's jar list) is red, like the window's own close button, and the window header shows no page title. A build in progress is one line at the top of the list with a thin progress bar; a fine-tune or a calibration shows there the same way (fine-tuning name, calibrating name).
  • Empty states say the next step: a filter that matches nothing names the query and offers Clear; the Sessions tab with nothing open says how a session is opened; the server group of the packages list says it is still asking the server; a model without a run says no validation yet beside Validate.
  • The first steps show someone new where to begin (FirstSteps.kt): a strip over the Models tab names four, build one from the sample data, ask it something, correct an answer and fine-tune it, and ticks each once AMP shows it done, whatever did it (a script counts as much as the page): a model trained on data or scored (the dummy, only written, doesn't count, even validated); a run line in a model's sessions.log or a request its server answered; a labeled row in a model's queue, or a fine-tune on one; a fine-tuned head (or a fine-tune run, after a rollback past it). A step not done yet is a button that goes where it is done: the first opens New model with the sample data chosen, the second and third put the keyboard on the Try line of the selected model (the third on one that keeps texts, the only ones that take corrections; the first such in the list when the selected one doesn't), the fourth opens its Improve tab. Its tooltip names the model, or says what the step waits for. The strip shows while a step is undone; once all four are done its bar turns green and it says all done until the page closes, so an AMP where everything was done before never shows it (nor are the steps read again on that page, so one coming undone later doesn't bring it back). Dismiss hides it for good, kept in AMP/settings.json; Settings shows it again (first steps under Models page).
  • The command palette finds anything (CommandPalette.kt): ⌘K (Ctrl+K), or the icon at the right end of the tab strip, opens one field over the top of the page. What you type picks among every model, group, package and session (choosing one goes to its row; a session goes to its model, group or package, an ONNX session to the Sessions tab) and the actions of the item whose panel is open, the same ones its ⋯ menu lists, which run exactly as from the menu. The letters of each word you type have to come in order (ftf finds Fine-tune on file…), words in any order, and a word may also match the item an action belongs to (file showcase); the start of a name or of a word counts most. Up and Down move the lit line and Enter runs it (the lit line stays on its item while the lists change under it, a model added or a session opened); a click runs the line clicked; Esc or a click outside closes the palette.
  • The keyboard reaches the lists, the filters, the Try line and the tabs (PageKeys.kt). While a text field has the keyboard, the keys it uses stay its own: only Esc and the ⌘ shortcuts reach the page. A click on a row takes the keyboard back to the list, and the tooltips of the tabs and the filters name their shortcut. Tab and Shift+Tab move between the page's controls, and the one that has the keyboard shows a thin blue square round it (only after Tab: a click leaves none; on a filled button a dark line keeps it apart from the fill); Space or Enter presses it (FocusRing.kt, the same on every page). For a screen reader, an icon that stands alone says what its tooltip says, an icon beside its own words says nothing more, and the filters are called "filter".
Keys Action Up / Down Select the row above or below in the list on show (models, groups or packages); the rows of a folded section are skipped, a package listed twice (in a collection and where it lives) is visited where it first shows, and the selected row scrolls into view once (opening a fold doesn't scroll the list back to it) Home / End Select the first or the last row of the list Enter Put the keyboard on the selected model's Try line (Models tab), or the selected group's (Groups tab); Enter there asks. On a control Tab moved to, Enter presses that control instead; on text Tab moved to (which presses nothing), it goes to the Try line as before Tab / Shift+Tab Move the keyboard to the next or the previous control; it shows a thin ring, and Space or Enter presses it ⌘F (Ctrl+F) Put the keyboard on the list's filter; Enter there goes back to the list with the filter kept ⌘1 to ⌘4 (Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4) Models, Groups, Packages, Sessions ⌘K (Ctrl+K) Open the command palette Esc Close what is open, one thing per press: a menu; then a strip (the fine-tune plan, a flag, a new group, a rename, a destroy); then a form in the panel (New model, From Hugging Face, New collection, From Maven Central); then the filter's text; then leave the text field

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The page's tabs are in the window's top bar, as the sandbox's tools are, so there is no row over the page: four tabs with their counts, Models, Groups, Packages and Sessions, after the arrow chip that hides the sidebar, and the command palette's icon at the right end. There is no back button: the sidebar leads to the other pages. Signing in happens under Account in Settings and on this page is only needed for Publish; everything else works without an account. (The website is not opened from the page any more; a publish notice names the address that lists what you published.) Each tab but Sessions is a flat list on the left, a 1dp rule that can be dragged to resize the list, and one bordered detail panel on the right for the selected item; the Sessions tab is one full-width list. The tab strip already names the section and counts its items, so there is no title above the list: its first line is the filter box (its tooltip says what it matches) with the one action of the list beside it (New model, whose form starts with where the model comes from, a csv or Hugging Face; New group; Add, which offers a jar from this machine or a new collection; Terminate all on the Sessions tab, shown while something is open, its filter only past four sessions).

At the foot of the window sits the status strip: what the process holds of the machine's memory, the heap against its -Xmx limit, the native memory, and the BERT encoders loaded (the heavy part, shared by every session; one that was cancelled is left out until its next text loads it again). It turns red near the limit. Its ✕ hides it until the app closes and Memory in the sidebar brings it back; while it is hidden nothing reads the memory.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
The list has one line per module in AMP/models/intents: the name, its last accuracy (or not validated), its version once it has more than one (v3), serving :port while it listens, in group… for the groups it is in, its open sessions, the status word at the right and the ⋯ button; a running one is underlined in green. Models are grouped by the data they were trained on (the csv name the builder records in module.json; the dummy sits under written, not trained, older models under unknown data), so the same data trained twice sits together. Groups with a running model come first; inside a group the running models come first, then the most accurate. The filter box matches the name, a label, the status, the data and the file a model was validated on. Clicking a line selects it; the panel on the right shows that model only, with the status line (listening address or not serving, the version once there is more than one, the data it was trained on, in group1, group2; its tooltip counts a listener's requests, abstentions and errors) under its name and the actions at the right of the header:

Action What it does Open session / Terminate session The filled button. Loads the model (encoder and head) as a session, the same as initMod("name") in the sandbox, or closes it. A model has one session at most Listen on :port / Stop Starts or stops the HTTP listener (runtime/ModelServer.kt) with the settings as shown; the label names the port it will use ⚙ Opens the serving settings under the header: Host / Port / Path / Methods, Min score and Fallback (under the min score the model abstains, answering the fallback label or none: Serving a model), with the min score its last run suggests and Use, then Access, folded until one of its fields is set: Key (shown as dots, with New key and Copy), Origins, Max bytes and Per minute (who may ask and how much); Save writes them all to AMP/models/intents/<name>/serving.json; a port outside 1–65535, a min score that isn't a number from 0 to 1, an origin that isn't one or a limit under 1 is named and keeps Save and Listen disabled (a min score of 0 is none); the order is Host, Port, Path, Min score (with its suggestion and Use), Fallback, Access, then Methods (POST/GET) on one row with Save, the POST and GET URLs with Copy and Copy curl, applies after Stop and Listen while it listens, and last Requests, folded: the last twelve lines of the model's access.log, newest first (time, status, ms, method and path, outcome), errors in red, the whole line with its request id in the tooltip (Serving a model). The gear stays lit while the block is open Publish Uploads the model as <name>.onnx, <name>.module.json and <name>.guide.md to the Amie backend (POST /upload, progLanguage=onnx) with the Keycloak token, then asks the website to refresh its listing and says in the notice strip whether /dashboard?username=<you> lists the files, naming that address; a guest is sent to Account in Settings. A backend that cannot be reached ("Host is down", "Connection refused") is an address problem in AMP/backend.json, not a sign-in one ⋯ The whole menu: Open session, Listen/Stop; Check: Validate on sample data, Validate on file…; Improve: Fine-tune on file…, Calibrate on file…, Texts to label from file…, Roll back to v<n> (the newest kept head), Retrain on <data>.csv, Retrain on file…; Groups: Add to group …, New group with …; Share: Publish to the website, Remove from the website; Manage: Rename…, Reveal folder, Copy initMod("name"), Terminate model, Destroy model…. Only what applies shows: Open session without a session, Stop listening while it listens, Fine-tune, Calibrate and the two Retrains not during a build, Texts to label only for a model that keeps texts, Roll back only with a kept head, Terminate model only while it runs; for a guest Publish and Remove read (sign in)

Try is the line under the header, above the tabs (Ask it something): type a sentence and press Enter (or Ask). The answer shows under it: the label, its score, the next three labels with theirs, and how long it took. The first question opens the model's session if none is open (the button says Opening…), as Open session does, and the session's log keeps the line. When the answer is wrong, the line under it, wrong? it is, has a chip for each of the other labels (the likelier first, the rest behind more) and + new label for one the model doesn't have yet. A chip puts the sentence in the model's queue with that label (teach in jetbrainDLBuilder/LabelQueue.kt), and the line then says taught, with Show the queue, which opens the Improve tab. A model that doesn't keep texts answers the same way but offers no correction, since nothing it is asked may be written down; the line says so.

Several lines pasted into the Try field at once are a batch, asked one by one: only the lines pasted, not the sentence the field held, which stays in the field (less whatever the paste replaced, so a paste over a selection takes the selection away); blank lines and repeats are left out, and past 200 lines the rest are too (the line says how many). One line pasted goes into the field as text. Lines pasted while a sentence or a batch is still being asked start nothing, and still asking: paste once it ends shows beside the field for a moment. The answers show as a table under the field in place of a single answer: each sentence with its answer and score, the runner-up and its score, and the milliseconds, with unsure beside the answers whose two best scores are less than 0.2 apart (the row's tooltip says how far apart). Past eight rows the table scrolls, so the tabs under it stay where they are. The line over it says how far it got (asking 4 of 10…, with Stop), then how many were asked, how many it was unsure of and the mean time of an answer. Copy as csv copies the table as text,answer,score,runner-up,runner-up score,ms, quoted where needed. For a model that keeps texts, Queue the 3 unsure puts those sentences in its queue as rows to label, each with its guess, its score and the runner-up, after the rows there; a text the queue has already stays as it is. The line then says how many went in, with Show the queue. A model that doesn't keep texts is never offered this. × closes the table, and a sentence asked on its own takes its place. Rename and Destroy wait while a batch is asked; Stop ends it, keeping the answers so far, as does Terminate session.

Rename… opens a strip at the top of the page with the current name in a field; Rename is enabled once the new name is a module name (letters, digits, dots, dashes, underscores) no other model has. The folder under AMP/models/intents moves, module.json, the guide's title and modules.json say the new name, its queue of texts to label (AMP/<name>-to-label.csv) is renamed with it, labels and all, the sessions on it are closed, and a listener comes back under the new name (a serving path that was the old default becomes the new default). A trained model can be renamed like any other; scripts then open it with initMod("newname"). A name whose queue file is in AMP/ already, one no model owns (left by hand, or by a model of that name destroyed before destroying removed queues), is refused rather than merged: the renamed model would take those labels for its own and fine-tune on them. Move or delete that file first.

Destroy model… asks first: the strip names the folder that goes, with every run and its logs, and the model's queue when it has one. The csv files it was trained on stay in AMP/, since other models may use them.

Neither is offered in the middle of something: while the model is being built, trained again, fine-tuned, calibrated or validated, Rename… and Destroy model… say to wait for that to end, and so do Rename and Destroy in their strips when one of those began while the strip was open (the strip stays, for once the model is free). Roll back and a notice's Undo wait the same way.
