Whatever still ends after a rename or a destroy (a fine-tune started from a script, a regrade of the queue, texts to label being picked) writes nothing back under the old name, so a destroyed model doesn't come back and a renamed one gets no twin; its console line says why. A build doesn't write over a model renamed to its name meanwhile either, and a fine-tune or a calibration doesn't write over a head the model got meanwhile (rolled back, trained again, or destroyed and built anew).

Retrain trains the model again under the same name: on the csv it was trained on as it is now (edit or add rows to the file, then retrain), or on another csv (Retrain on file…, also Other file… on the Data tab). Nothing that opens the model has to change: the head is rebuilt in place, the sessions on the old head are closed so the next initMod opens the new one, a listener comes back on it, the description, icon and guide stay (also ones changed while it trains, as with a fine-tune or a calibration), and the Metrics tab keeps every earlier run beside the new one, so the runs show whether the new data helped. Only one build runs at a time; the line at the top of the list follows it as for a new model.

Fine-tune on file… (⋯ menu, the Improve tab, and at the right of Files on the Data tab) teaches the trained model more from a csv instead of training it again: a label it doesn't know yet (three rows of it at least) gets an output of its own, and rows it got wrong move it towards the right answer, while the rows it learned from before are replayed and its weights are held near where they were, so what it knew stays. Nothing starts at once: a strip at the top of the page first says what it would do (planFineTune in jetbrainDLBuilder/FineTune.kt, worked out without training): the rows and which of its labels they are, the new labels and their rows, the earlier rows it would replay and from which files, the rows the preprocessor would drop, and that the version it has now stays. It warns about a new label spelled like one it has (light beside lights), rows that give a text it learned under another label, and files it was trained on that are gone from AMP/ (nothing to replay). A new label with fewer than three rows is named in red, and so is anything that keeps the fine-tune from starting; Fine-tune stays disabled then, and its tooltip says why. Fine-tune starts it, Cancel changes nothing. The notice says the versions and the accuracy before and after on the same held-out rows, with Undo, and the Metrics tab has the run. It is fineTuneClassifier, the same as fineTune(...) in a script, with its default options (Fine-tuning).

Calibrate on file… fits one temperature on labeled rows the model hasn't learned from and folds it into the head, so a score of 0.8 is right about 80% of the time; the answers, and so the accuracy, stay the same. The notice says the temperature and the calibration error before and after, with Undo.

Every retrain, fine-tune and calibration keeps the head it replaces (the ten newest, in AMP/models/intents/<name>/versions/). Roll back (on a kept head under Versions on the About tab, or Roll back to v<n> in the ⋯ menu for the newest one, and under Versions on the Improve tab) makes that head the model again as a new version, with the labels and the scores it had; the head that answered is kept in turn, so a rollback is undone the same way, which is what the notice's Undo does.

Compare on a kept head asks it and the head that answers now about the same labeled rows, changing nothing: no run is added and no session opened. It offers the csv the model was trained on, the one it was last validated on and the ones fine-tunes taught it (those still in AMP/), or On a file…. Under the list then: v1 → v3 on 40 rows of check.csv, one line with accuracy and macro F1 then and now and how many rows it answers right now that it didn't and wrong now that it got right (every row answered as before when none moved), and one figure (plots/compare.png): each label's F1 then (a dark square) and now (a light dot) on one axis, with accuracy and macro F1 under them, and the confusion change, how many more or fewer rows of each label got each answer (then→now in the cell; on the diagonal more is better, off it fewer). Both heads are scored over the labels of both, so a label one of them doesn't have reads new or gone, and its rows count as answered wrong by that head; rows of labels neither has are left out and counted. For a model that keeps texts the rows answered differently follow, those it gets wrong now first (fifty show; the tooltip has both scores); one that keeps no texts gets the counts only. The comparison stays until × or until the model's head changes, and shows on both tabs. One comparison runs at a time: Compare waits while another runs (of any model), while a build runs and while the model rolls back, and Roll back, Undo, Rename and Destroy wait while a kept head of the model is compared. A fine-tune or retrain started meanwhile isn't held up; the comparison, of the head before it, then doesn't show. The rows' vectors go to the embedding cache only when both heads keep texts.

Texts to label writes the texts the model is least sure about, closest calls first, to AMP/<name>-to-label.csv with its guess beside an empty label column: from what it was asked over HTTP (the button at the right of Ran on on the Data tab, shown once it has requests) or from a csv or txt of texts (Texts to label from file… in the ⋯ menu, Find texts to label on the Improve tab, whose menu also offers Varied close calls: texts unlike each other among the closest calls, What to label next). That file is the model's queue: the Improve tab lists it to label with a click, and corrections made on the Try line land in it too. It also shows under Files as to label, with how many rows have a label so far, Open in viewer to fill them in by hand, and Fine-tune on it once at least one has. Rows labeled already stay at the top when you ask again. A model that doesn't keep texts has neither action and no queue.

Under the header the panel has its own tabs, each with a tooltip that says what it holds:

Tab What it shows About The description (editable; Save description appears under it once it has changed and writes module.json), then the Icon, Details, Training and Versions blocks (Icon: a glyph from the set, or Upload image, kept as models/intents/<name>/icon.<ext>; Training also has its validation rows, the heads tried and what the preprocessor did). Every uppercase block title on these tabs is a line that folds its block away and back (open by default): Details: created / encoder / head / labels (the model's folder is in Settings, Model folders); Training: architecture, data, the version and what made it (v3 · fine-tune of v2), the files it was fine-tuned on, the temperature when it is calibrated, whether it keeps texts, rows, epochs, batch size, learning rate, hidden units, final loss, train accuracy; Versions: the head that answers now and every kept one, each with what made it, when, its labels and accuracy (the tooltip has its head and note), and Compare and Roll back on the kept ones Improve Making the model better in one place; its count is the labeled texts of the queue it still answers otherwise. What would help (shown when something would): what its last run and its requests suggest, each with the button that does it: the dummy's fixed weights (Fine-tune on the sample data), labels with an F1 under 0.6 (Fine-tune on file…), the labels it takes for others (“lights” taken for “weather” 6×: every pair of the last run's confusion matrix off the diagonal with two rows or more, the most first, three named; a model that keeps texts gets Show the rows, a menu of the pairs when there are several, which opens the Metrics tab on that run with answered wrong open on the pair's rows and brought into view, and a model that keeps none gets the counts and Fine-tune on file…), scores that don't say how often it is right (calibration error 0.1 or more and not calibrated: Calibrate on file…), requests over HTTP not looked at (Pick texts to label), training rows that look mislabeled (Open the csv). Teach it, with Find texts to label (from its requests or from a file, under Closest calls or Varied close calls, texts unlike each other among them) and Fine-tune on file… at the right: the queue, one line per text with what the model guessed and its score, a chip per label (the one it has lit; a click labels it, a second click takes the label away; with many labels only the likely ones are chips and other label has the rest), + new label, and × to take the text out; the first eight show, then Show all. A labeled text the model answers right shows ✓ answers it. Under the queue, how many texts are labeled and how many of them it answers right, and Fine-tune on n rows, which fine-tunes on the labeled rows of the queue through the same strip as any fine-tune; once it answers every labeled text right the button steps back to Fine-tune again. After every change of the head made on the page (a fine-tune, calibration, retrain, rollback or undo) the queue's guesses are worked out again with the new head (regradeQueue, texts embedded before come from the cache), so the queue shows what the model answers now. Versions: the same list as on the About tab, with Compare and Roll back. Scores: whether it is calibrated, its calibration error on the last run, and Calibrate on file…. Retrain: Retrain on <data>.csv and Other file…. A model that doesn't keep texts has no queue; Teach it says to fine-tune it from a csv Guide AMP/models/intents/<name>/guide.md, the guide shipped inside the model, rendered as light markdown; Edit and Save change it (Cancel while editing; before a guide exists it reads default guide, not saved yet with Edit and save), and it goes along when the model is published. It holds the model card (version, data and rows per label, earlier versions, the last run's scores, calibration, what it mixes up, its texts), written again after every run and on Save between two marker lines the tab doesn't show (the model card); what is being typed stays as typed when a run writes it Metrics One line: the run chips (the latest first, each chip's tooltip names what made the run, its data, rows, accuracy and time) and Validate, which offers On the sample data and On a file… and adds a run (metrics/ModelValidation.kt). Under it the run: when, made by (build, fine-tune, calibration, validation or rollback, and the version), the rows, the scores (in brackets, where each fell in 1,000 resamples of the rows, so how far it can be trusted: how far the scores hold), before for a fine-tune or calibration (the head before it on the same rows), calibration (its calibration error and temperature) and a note, then the run's warnings, a line each (the one about rows that repeat a row it learned from names them in its tooltip, or says that a model that keeps no texts keeps only their count: rows it learned from). A run that came from a build has Heads compared: every head the build trained, with accuracy, macro F1, train accuracy and loss on the same validation rows (and cv F1, the mean over the folds ± their spread, when it cross-validated), F1 per label under each, what the diagnostics said of it, and the chosen one marked; a head's tooltip adds its cross-validation and where early stopping stopped. The chosen run's charts follow: scores per label (with macro F1's range as a bar under its mark), the confusion matrix, how the heads learned (every head's accuracy on its training and validation rows, epoch by epoch, the kept epoch outlined) and how far the scores can be trusted (reliability bars against the diagonal, and what answering only above a score keeps), then answered wrong (the validation rows it got wrong, the surest first; a run keeps the 25 it was surest about. Opened from Show the rows it lists one pair's rows under a chip, lights → weather, that shows them all again, as does choosing another run; when the run kept fewer of the pair's rows than it got wrong, a line says how many) and labels that look wrong (training rows the cross-validated heads doubt), both folded, then scores by run and, under its own From the sessions block, how sure the model is and how long an answer takes, from the sessions log. While a validation runs, Validate reads validating n/total. The charts are PNG files drawn by metrics/MetricsImages.kt into AMP/models/intents/<name>/plots/ whenever the metrics or the log change, in one muted slate hue; a run from before the curves and calibration were kept draws its two charts as before Data Files, with Fine-tune on file… at the right: the csv files it was trained, validated and fine-tuned on and the queue to label, each with rows per label and text lengths as bars, a folded preview and Open in viewer; the trained-on file has Retrain (the same name, on the file as it is now) and Other file…, the queue to label has how many rows are labeled and Fine-tune on it; then Ran on: what its sessions answered and what the server served, with Texts to label once it has requests Requirements metrics/ModelRequirements.kt: everything it needs to run, checked on this machine, each line marked met / not met / information (the mark's tooltip says which). initMod, Open session and Listen refuse a model on the lines about the model itself, the encoder, the head and the labels Console The console lines that name the model, or with all models everything the models, packages and sessions logged; the box's height can be dragged Sessions The sessions it owns, each with Log and Terminate

docs.title: Icons and groups
docs.text:
Every model has an icon: the chip by default, or one from a small catalog (lightbulb, cloud, chat, home, music, shield, star, bolt, heart, language, science, work, pets, school, cart, hub, groups) chosen under Icon on the About tab and kept in module.json, or an image of your own: Upload image there copies a png, jpg or svg into the model's folder as icon.<ext>, which then shows in the list, on the panel header and in groups (and goes along when the model is published); Remove image goes back to the catalog icon.

No row says idle, running, stopped, open or closed: the green underline under a row is running (a session open, a listener on, a swarm open), its absence idle. Only the other states keep a word (inferring, on server, 2 open, missing).

Groups have their own Groups tab: every group of every env in a list (icon, how many models, which, the underline while its swarm is open), folded by env, and the selected one in the panel. + New group there makes an empty one to fill with Add model.

A group is a named set of models that are asked together: a swarm. A model's ⋯ menu offers Add to group for every group it is not in and New group with …, which opens a strip at the top of the page asking for the name and the env the group belongs to. Groups live in the env, as packages do: each env keeps its own in AMP/env/<env>/groups.json, a script sourced in that env finds them with group("name") (the default env first, then any), and internalEnv() lists them with the packages. Selecting a group on the Groups tab shows its panel: Open swarm / Terminate swarm, the models (a row each; Detach takes one out; Add model adds one), the icon picker, where it lives and, while open, the swarm's session with its log. Remove group leaves the models alone. A destroyed or renamed model is taken out of (or renamed in) every group. A group with a model that keeps no texts keeps what it is asked out of every log: its own, its console lines, and those of its other models, which write each text's length instead; a text asked of one of those models directly is logged as its own module.json says.

A group's panel has a Try line under its header, as a model's has: a sentence asked of all its models at once, the way its swarm asks them (the first question opens the swarm, as Open swarm does, and Enter on the list comes here). Under it shows the group's answer, each label's best score across its models (what predict and inference give in a script) with the three labels after it; then the vote, the label most of its models give (a tie goes to the higher best score), with how many give it; then a row per model with its own answer and score and the two labels after them. A model that gave none says so: it couldn't be opened, it failed (its Console tab says why), or it joined the group after the swarm opened. The answer goes once a model is added to the group or detached from it, since its rows and vote were of the models before. A group's answers aren't corrected here; each model is taught on its own page.

Groups are also made by dragging on the Models tab: take a model's row and drop it on another model's row to open the new-group strip with the two of them, or on the zone that appears over the list while you drag ("drop here for a new group") for a new group with that one; adding to a group that exists is Add to group in the ⋯ menu or Add model on the Groups tab. The ghost beside the pointer says what the drop would do, and the row under it is lit. A click without movement still selects the row.

docs.title: New model
docs.text:
Check data next to Build runs the preprocessor on the chosen file without training and shows its report under the fields: what it would clean, drop (with the reason) and refuse, and whether a build could start. The reasons are explained in Models and metrics.

New model beside the filter box opens the form in the place of the detail panel, and Close stands where the button was while it is open. The form's first line, From, says where the model comes from: A csv (the form below) or Hugging Face (the one in From Hugging Face); the chip switches the form, and while a build runs only Hugging Face is offered. The csv form is open on its own when there are no models: Name, About (a sentence kept in module.json), Data (Choose a csv with a text column and a label column, or Sample data for AMP/sample-intents.csv, 45 rows over greeting, lights and weather; the name is filled from the file name) and an optional Test file to validate on instead of a 20% split. Options are chips, all off but keep texts, which is the build as it always was: cross-validate scores every head over 5 folds and keeps the best mean (and lists the rows whose label the heads doubt), more heads compares 12 heads instead of 4, stop early ends a head's training once it stops improving and keeps its best epoch, calibrate fits the temperature as part of the build, and turning keep texts off makes a model that never writes a text down, for one that answers other people. Each chip's tooltip says what it costs. As soon as the data file is chosen the form reads it and shows how many samples and which labels it holds, with rows per label as bars, the most first, so a label with few rows shows before the build. While Build is disabled the line beside it (and its tooltip) says what is still missing: a data file, a name, or a csv without the two columns. Build runs the same buildClassifier the sandbox's modelBuilder runs, on a background thread; while it runs one line at the top of the list shows the phase, step and a thin progress bar, and under it every head scored so far (architecture, accuracy, macro F1, train accuracy, loss, the chosen one marked once all are compared; the tooltip of a line has its F1 per label), so the comparison is visible while the next head trains. When it ends the new model is selected. Only one build runs at a time. Close brings the selected model back.

A csv chosen from anywhere else on the machine (Data, Test, Validate on file…, Retrain on file…) is copied into AMP/ first (a newer copy replaces the one there), so the model finds its data again by its name later: the Data tab, the list's grouping and a retrain all look the file up in AMP/. A file already under AMP/ is used where it is.

A fresh checkout has one component already: the dummy model (modules/AmpModules.kt, ensureDummyModule), a fixed one-layer head over the encoder with the labels greeting, lights, weather. It is written when AMP/models/intents is empty, so the page always has something to configure and initMod("dummy") works before any training. The sample csv (ensureSampleData) has the same labels, so the first thing to try is Validate on sample data on the dummy (its weights are fixed, so expect poor numbers) and then + New model with Sample data to see what a trained model's metrics look like.

docs.title: From Hugging Face
docs.text:
The Hugging Face chip on the first line of the New model form opens this one in the place of the detail panel.

Search finds models on the Hub in the formats initMod opens. Under it, a menu picks the task, as the Hub files models (Any task, the default; Text classification, Token classification, Feature extraction, Text generation, Text to speech, Speech recognition, Audio classification, Image classification), and the chips narrow the format: All supported (the default), ONNX, TorchScript, TensorFlow and TFLite. A task with no words lists the most downloaded models of it, so the speech models or the classifiers of the Hub are a click away. The search waits until typing pauses (300 ms), and a new search cancels the one under way. Each row is a repo: its id, its task, downloads and likes, and at the right the formats it has. The formats are read off the repo's files, so a repo that only has weights is left out. TorchScript has no tag of its own on the Hub (pytorch mostly means weights), so a TorchScript search keeps only repos with a .pt or .pth file. When the Hub doesn't list a repo's files, the row says Check the files. Show more brings the next results. A search with no results says so, and so does one that can't reach the Hub. Clicking a row looks that repo up.

Repo takes a repo id (owner/name) or a huggingface.co address, including a folder's (/tree/main/onnx) or a file's (/blob/main/onnx/model_quantized.onnx). Look up asks the Hub what the repo holds at that revision (the default branch unless the address names another). Nothing is downloaded at this point, beyond the repo's config.json when it has one (read for the model's kind and its labels). The panel then shows:

  • the repo, its commit, its Task as the Hub files it, and from its config the Model type and the Labels it answers with (id2label, the first twelve and how many more), so a classifier's labels are known before it is downloaded;
  • the runnable files by format, each with its size: ONNX (*.onnx, the onnx/ folder and the quantized variants, with an ONNX file's external data), TorchScript (*.pt, *.pth), TensorFlow SavedModel (saved_model.pb with variables/) and TFLite (*.tflite);
  • Not runnable here: weights-only files (*.safetensors, pytorch_model.bin, *.gguf, *.h5), each with a short reason, shards counted as one row;
  • the default pick, already chosen. That is the file an address named, or else a plain model.onnx (the root's before onnx/'s), a full model before an 8-bit variant and an 8-bit variant before fp16, then the other formats. Click another file to change it. An encoder and decoder pair (encoder_model.onnx with decoder_model.onnx, a T5, BART, Marian or Whisper export) is taken whole, the full variant of each; amie hf import lists every encoder and decoder of the folder to pick with the arrow keys, the default already marked, and initMod opens the pair as two sessions (see Encoder and decoder pairs);
  • Comes with: the config and tokenizer files that go along with the pick (config.json, tokenizer.json, tokenizer_config.json, special_tokens_map.json, vocab and merges files, generation_config.json), from its folder and the folders above it, and what a speech or an image model needs besides: a voices/ folder (a Kokoro export's voices), the .onnx.json of a Piper voice, tokens.txt, lexicon.txt and espeak-ng-data/ of a VITS export, a labels.txt or classes.txt, and a pair's preprocessor_config.json, which says how a sound or an image becomes its encoder's input;
  • Name: the folder under AMP/models/imported, which defaults to the repo's last part, made a folder name.

Download runs in the background, apart from the page, so leaving the page leaves it running. A line at the top of the list shows the file coming in, how much has come and a progress bar, with Cancel, which throws away what came. Each file arrives as <path>.part under AMP/models/imported/.incoming/<name>/. Its size is checked against the Hub's before it takes its name, and only once every file is in does the folder move to AMP/models/imported/<name>, in one rename. A closed app, a lost connection or a full disk never leaves a half file under its real name. The next download of the same commit goes on from what came: a whole file isn't asked for again, and a .part is resumed. When the download ends, the model is selected and a notice gives its initMod line.

Each failure says what happened and what to do: no such model or revision, no connection, a gated or private repo (with or without HF_TOKEN), nothing that runs here, no room on the disk or a folder that can't be written, a file that came in short. A token for a gated or private repo comes from the HF_TOKEN environment variable alone. It goes only to huggingface.co, never to the storage a big file is sent on to, and it is never logged, printed or stored.

Imported models are listed under their own fold, Imported, after the intent models. Each row shows the model's format, its task when the Hub filed it under one, its source repo and its size, and the filter finds a model by any of them or by one of its labels. Its panel shows the task, the labels its config.json names (written into source.json as the model came in, so nothing is opened to say them), the commit, when it was downloaded, its folder and every file. Delete (or Delete… in its ⋯ menu) asks first, then removes AMP/models/imported/<name>. A folder put there by hand is listed too, its format read off its files.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Jars come from six places, each a fold of the list: AMP/pluginDir, the env, Maven Central, the website's downloads page (On the server), GitHub (On GitHub, the repositories in AMP/github.json) and the website's store: the packages people published under their accounts (/api/all-packages), each with its author (by name on the row). Fetch downloads a store jar from the address its listing gives into AMP/pluginDir, as does the first initMod("name.jar").

The list has one line per package jar a script can open, first under the collections and then under the folding groups by place: In AMP/pluginDir, In the env, From Maven Central, On the server (the website's /api/jars, else the S3 service's /api/aws/jars; a line says so while the server is still being asked), In the store and On GitHub, the last three folded by default. Each line shows the Java the jar needs and its version, and at the right 2 open, inferring, on server or on GitHub (an idle jar has no word) (the tooltip says what that means) and the ⋯ button; an open one is underlined in green. The filter box matches the jar name, version, Java, a collection name, the class a session opens on, and any class or resource name inside the jar, so a class can be found without knowing which jar holds it. Add beside the filter box offers Jar from this machine… (copied into AMP/pluginDir and imported into the env), From Maven Central… and New collection….

docs.title: Repository
docs.text: Under the installed packages, the Repository section searches what the Amie server offers (JarPackages.listing, the jars of the website's downloads page and its store, and of the GitHub repositories in AMP/github.json), by name, version or author. Fetch on a result downloads the jar into AMP/pluginDir, where a script opens it with initMod("x.jar"); a jar already there says on this machine. When the repository can't be reached the section says why, naming the addresses it tried, instead of showing an empty list, and Try again asks again at once; what could be read still shows beside the reason. It needs an account: a guest sees why, with Sign in to search, which leads to Account in Settings, and the repository is asked nothing.

docs.title: What a package needs
docs.text:
A package jar's panel has three blocks the libraries do not: Requirements, every line marked met, not met or information: the Java it needs against the Java this app runs, its package class, whether it ships metadata, its config folder, each config file and environment variable it declares, and what its last test run came to. A required file that is missing or still its template, or a required variable that is not set, is not met, and initMod refuses the jar until it is; Config, the folder AMP/pluginDir/config/<jar>/ with Reveal folder, where the package's files are read from (as resources, through the amie.package.config property and a configure(...) method; templates for the missing files are written on the first open) and the declared files with their state; and Tests, the test runs the jar declares and the last run's answers, each marked pass or fail. Test run in the header (also in the ⋯ menu) opens a fresh session with the configuration in place, runs the declared tests (or one call with "hello" when there are none), closes it and reports in the notice strip and the block, where every test shows what it asked (run("…")) and the whole answer line by line, with the reason when it failed.

Under the header the jar's flags say what it works with at a glance, as coloured tags: its version (blue), the Java it needs (slate, red when this app is too old for it), its language (violet) and how its last test run went (green or red), then the jar's own flags from its metadata (flags: [{"text": "stable", "color": "green"}]) and the ones you add with Add flag (also in the ⋯ menu): a word and one of six colours (slate, green, amber, red, violet, blue), kept in the sidecar metadata beside the jar and removable from the ⋯ menu. The same flags show on the jar's row in the list. A jar with no metadata gets Write metadata template in its ⋯ menu, which writes AMP/pluginDir/<jar>.package.json to fill in. The format is in Sandbox scripting.

docs.title: From Maven Central
docs.text: Add → From Maven Central… opens a form in the place of the detail panel with one box. Type a name (gson, okhttp), a class name, group:artifact for the versions of one artifact, or paste a full group:artifact:version as in a Gradle dependency; Maven Central is asked as you type and the hits are ordered here, the artifact named like what you typed and the well-known groups first (the server's own order buries them). Every hit is a row with its newest version and publication date and its own Add, which resolves that version and its dependencies into the env (AMP/env/<env>/env.lock.json, files under AMP/env/caches), exactly what implementation("group:artifact:version") in a script does. A pasted coordinate is the first row. A thin bar shows while the library is being resolved, and the form closes itself when it is done: the library then sits under From Maven Central in the list, selected, with the same Source, Build and Contents sections as any jar (the coordinate is in Source), a Remove button that takes it out of the env (the files stay cached), and a menu that copies the implementation("…") line. A script can import its classes from the next run without declaring it. These are libraries, not packages: nothing opens them with initMod.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
A collection is a folder of jars that belong together, kept in AMP/pluginDir/collections.json (pluginEngine/PackageCollections.kt), typically the jars that run on one Java: "jvm21" with every plugin that fits. Add → New collection… opens the form in the place of the detail panel: a name, the jars to put in (toggles), and a By Java shortcut per Java version found among the jars (jvm17, jvm21, …) that names the collection and picks every jar that runs on that Java or older. Each collection is a fold at the top of the list with its jars as rows; moving the pointer over a row shows Detach, Add jar lists the jars that are not in it yet (and turns into a red Close while that list shows), and Delete folder removes the collection but keeps the jars. A jar can be in several collections, and its panel header says which.

The detail panel describes the selected jar without running anything (pluginEngine/JarInspector.kt, read once per file version). Its header has the status line (status, java 17+, kotlin or java, version), Fetch (filled) for a jar still on the server or Publish for a jar on this machine (uploads it to the website under your account; the server refuses a jar without run(String): List and close(), with the reasons in the notice), and the ⋯ menu with the same plus Open its page on the website, Reveal file and Copy initMod("name.jar"); its ⋯ also has Reveal config folder, Detach from collection and Remove flag … when they apply. Under it a row of the jar's flags, the initMod("name.jar") call, then folding sections, closed until opened, except Requirements when something is unmet or the jar ships metadata, Config when it declares files and Tests once they ran:

Section What it shows Source where it is, the website page, the exact download URL, when it was fetched and published (from <jar>.source.json), the file Build what built it (the manifest's Created-By, Build-Jdk-Spec), the class file version and the Java it needs, whether this app's Java can load it, language, size Contents the class a session opens on (the one with run(String) and close()) and the Main-Class; a filter box; Classes grouped by package and Resources grouped by folder, each group folding; the entry class and main class are marked; clicking a line copies its full name

Then Sessions: the sessions open on it, each with Log and Terminate. There are no Run or Quit buttons: a package is a bottle, not something the page controls. A script opens its own instance with initMod("name.jar"), calls run(text) (or answer(text)) and close(), and a jar that is only on the server is fetched into AMP/pluginDir on first open (see Packages).

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
(What a session is and how to use one from a script is in Running sessions; this is the tab.)

The tab lists everything that is open as flat rows named after the owner (dummy #3, echo-1.0.jar #1) with what it is (intent model, package, model group for a swarm, ONNX session, session model, background template), the script block that holds it (static search, timed search, 40s left, closable; see Scope functions), inferring while it answers (idle is the gray mark), how many runs it has done and for how long it has been open; with more than a few, a filter box matches owner, kind or #id, and Terminate all sits at the right of that first line. Log unfolds what the session was asked and answered: one line per inference call ("turn the lights on" -> lights:0.97, weather:0.02 (12 ms)), plus open, close and error lines, with the time of each. The same lines are appended to the owner's file, AMP/models/intents/<name>/sessions.log for a model and AMP/pluginDir/<jar>.sessions.log for a package, so the history of a terminated session is not lost (runtime/SessionLog.kt). Terminate ends a session: intent model sessions (from Open session or initMod("name"); runtime/ModelSessions.kt), package sessions (pluginEngine/JarPackages.kt; terminating calls the package's close() and drops its class loader) and ONNX Runtime sessions opened on a bare file with importModelOnnx (modelLoaders/OrtSessions.kt; terminating cancels in-flight runs; these keep no log). The ORT session inside a model session is not listed twice; it goes with the model session. A template running in the background has a row as well, with its name and how long it has run, no count of runs and no log; Terminate cancels it. Terminate all ends all of them, the swarms first. Right-click a row for Terminate, Show log (Hide log once shown), Copy log and Copy #id; a session row has no ⋯ button.

Each row has a resources line under it: for a model its head and its encoder on disk, the encoder said once with how many share it, the time a run takes and when it was last used (head 9 KB · encoder 415.6 MB, shared by 3 · 12 ms a run · last used 3s ago); for a package its jar, for a bare ONNX session its file, for a group its heads together, and for a background template what its meter reads now (memory 1.20 GB, peak 1.40 GB · heap 340.0 MB of 4.00 GB · cpu 2.10 s · ort 12 runs in 640 ms). Over the rows a totals line says what the process holds, how much of it is the encoders, the heap against its limit, and how many sessions are open and what they weigh together (Process 1.85 GB, of which encoders 415.6 MB · heap 340.0 MB of 4.00 GB · 20 sessions weigh 436.0 MB); what each figure is, in Running sessions. A session model is a snapshot from sessionMod("name") (modules/SharedModels.kt): Terminate ends it for whatever holds it and leaves the model alone. Over the sessions, Scripts lists every script running and each that left something open (runtime/ScriptRuns.kt), named after the template it is word for word, else main.kts, with what it holds, its answers, its CPU and what it allocated, and its sessions under it; what the figures are is in Running sessions.

docs.title: Models and metrics
docs.text: A model is an intent classifier: a small dense network trained on BERT embeddings of your texts. Everything about a model lives in AMP/models/intents/<name>/, so building, inspecting and serving one needs no account; only publishing does. A fresh checkout starts with a fixed dummy model (labels greeting, lights, weather) that is written when AMP/models/intents is empty, so initMod("dummy") and the Models page work before any training.

docs.title: Building one
docs.text:
From the Models page: New model, pick the csv (or Sample data, AMP/sample-intents.csv), Build. From a script:

val train = source("intents.csv")        // columns: text,label (header names like text/label/intent are detected)
relate(train, "intents-test.csv")        // optional: validate on this file instead of a 20% split
val model = modelBuilder("intents", train)
model.modelStatus()                      // the validation table
model.modelChart()                       // bars, history and confusion matrix

intents.csv stands for your own file. source() finds it as given, relative to the folder amie was started in, then in AMP/, then in AMP/pluginDir/; an absolute path is taken as it is. A new AMP folder has sample-intents.csv (45 rows) to try, and a name that is not found is reported with the folders looked in and the csv files of AMP whose names come closest.

modelBuilder runs the preprocessor over the rows, embeds every text once, trains every candidate head on the same rows, keeps the best one by macro F1 on the validation rows, and exports it:

File Content model.onnx The trained layers, written as ONNX (opset 13) module.json Encoder path, input and output sizes, pooling, the label list, the data file it was trained on metrics.json One entry per build: accuracy and macro F1 (with how far they hold, below), per-label precision / recall / F1 / support, the confusion matrix, warnings, what it was validated on serving.json Host, port, path, methods and whether it listens incoming.jsonl Every request the served model received versions/v<N>/ The heads it had before, with their module.json and scores: the ten newest, for a rollback

Accepted data shapes: a DataSource from source(...), List<Pair<text, label>>, Map<label, List<text>>, or rows of [text, …, label].

docs.title: Before training: the preprocessor
docs.text:
Nothing is embedded before the rows are cleaned and measured. The preprocessor writes what it did to the console (the info lines that begin with modelBuilder:), keeps the same lines with the model (metrics.json, shown under About → Training on the Models page), and stops the build when the set cannot give a usable classifier. What it does, in order:

  1. Cleans every row. Control characters go, runs of whitespace become one space, text and label are trimmed.
  2. Unifies label spellings. Lights and lights are one label; the more frequent spelling wins and the console says label 'Lights' read as 'lights'.
  3. Drops rows that cannot be learned from, each with its reason: an empty text, an empty label, a text with no letters or digits (???), a single character.
  4. Drops repeats and conflicts. The same text twice under one label keeps one copy (repeated row). The same text under two labels keeps the label with the majority (same text under another label, kept as 'lights'); with no majority both rows go, because neither label can be right.
  5. Measures what is left: rows per label, distinct texts per label, words per text and the spread of lengths.

A build stops, with the sentence below in red and the model not written, when:

The console says Why training would be pointless What to do no labeled rows at all Nothing came out of the data shape Return rows of [text, label], pairs, or a map; check the csv's header names almost every row has its own label (… labels for … rows): the text and label columns are probably swapped A classifier learns a few labels from many texts, not the reverse Swap the columns, or name them text and label label '…' is … characters long, which looks like a text Same as above, seen from the label's side Same a classifier needs at least 2 labels With one label there is nothing to decide Add rows of another label label 'x' has 3 rows after cleaning, at least 5 are needed Too few to train on and hold some out to validate Add rows of that label, or drop the label label 'x' has only 1 distinct text; the rest differ only in case or punctuation The encoder sees one sentence; the head would memorise it, not the label Write different sentences for that label nothing is left after cleaning Every row was empty, repeated or in conflict Look at the dropped lines above it embeddings are nearly identical (after embedding) The encoder cannot tell the texts apart, so no head can tell the labels apart Use texts that differ in more than a word

Softer problems become warnings, stored with the metrics and printed, and training goes on: labels imbalanced more than 10×, texts of under two words on average, texts longer than 1000 characters (the encoder reads the first 512 tokens), many texts that differ only in case or punctuation, every text of the same length.

buildOptions(preprocess = false) skips the cleaning; only the hard checks of the old builder run then.

For a model that keeps no texts (buildOptions(keepTexts = false)) the lines count the dropped rows without quoting them, and a label longer than 60 characters, which is a text when the columns are swapped, is named by its length alone (a label is 87 characters long, which looks like a text); with the columns swapped no line names a label at all, for any model.

The dropped rows are written to AMP/models/intents/<name>/dropped.csv (text,label,reason), so they can be fixed in the source file. A related test file is cleaned the same way, and a test row whose text also appears in the training rows is left out of the validation (the console says how many), because it would be scored on what was memorised.

Check before building. checkData(source("intents.csv")) in a script runs the preprocessor alone and prints the same report, ending with whether a build could start; on the Models page the New model form has Check data next to Build, which shows the report under the fields.

docs.title: After validating: what the scores say
docs.text:
Once the chosen head is validated, a few more lines are added to the warnings (printed, and kept with the build):

The console says What it means the validation has only 7 rows; its scores are rough Each row moves accuracy by a seventh; add rows or a test file before trusting a number labels with fewer than 2 validation rows: weather That label's precision and recall come from one row the head fits the training rows much better than the validation rows (0.99 vs 0.80): it memorises Overfitting: more varied rows, or a smaller head (architecture(hidden = emptyList())), would generalise better accuracy 0.62 is barely above always answering 'lights' (0.58) The head learned little beyond the majority label; the texts may not separate the labels label 'weather' is weak (F1 0.40); it is mostly taken for 'lights' (4 of 6 rows) The confusion matrix's worst row in a sentence; those two labels need more distinct examples 3 of 48 validation rows repeat a training row (2 the same text, ignoring case and punctuation; 1 nearly the same to the encoder): scores on rows it learned from flatter it Those rows test what it remembers, not what it learned: rows it learned from

Two more options help with awkward data: buildOptions(balanceClasses = true) weights the loss so every label counts the same, which lifts a rare label the head would otherwise learn last; buildOptions(seed = 7) changes the split, the initial weights and the shuffles (the same data and seed always give the same model, so a comparison between two runs is a comparison of the data or the options, not of luck).

docs.title: Which head: the architecture search
docs.text:
On top of the encoder's 768 numbers per text sits a small head. By default four are trained on the same training rows and scored on the same validation rows, and the best macro F1 wins (ties: the better accuracy, then the smaller head):

Candidate Head linear dense[768 -> labels] softmax dense[16] one hidden layer of 16 relu units dense[32] one of 32 dense[64, 16] two hidden layers

As each head finishes the console shows its accuracy, macro F1, train accuracy, loss and parameter count, then its F1, precision and recall per label, then what the diagnostics make of it (memorising, barely above the majority label, a weak label and what it is taken for), and the Models page lists it under the build line at once. Once every head is in, one line ranks them (compared 4 heads by macro F1: dense[16] 0.950 · dense[32] 0.912 …) and chosen: dense[16], the best macro F1 on the validation rows (next: dense[32] 0.912) says which is kept. The chosen head is then validated once more on every validation row (the Validating phase), so what is stored, charted and exported is that head's own run. The comparison is kept with the build in metrics.json (candidates, with perLabelF1 and insights per head; Heads compared on the Metrics tab) and in one line of the manifest (search, shown as heads tried under About → Training). Each candidate costs its epochs; on a few hundred rows the whole search takes seconds.

docs.title: Training again
docs.text: modelBuilder("intents", train) with the name of a model that exists trains it again in place, which is how a model follows its data: add or fix rows in the csv and build under the same name. Nothing that runs on the old head is cut off: the session open on it and its listener each open the new head beside the old one, swap it in once their answers in flight are done, and close the old one after, under the same session id and on the same port (a script holding the session, a swarm over it or a client of the listener sees the old answers up to the swap and the new ones from it; sessions.log has a swap line, access.log too). The icon, the guide and the description (unless the build gives one) are kept, and metrics.json keeps every earlier run, so the runs show whether the new rows helped. Only a model that stops keeping texts closes its session instead, so no log goes on keeping them. A fine-tune and a rollback swap the same way. The Models page's Retrain does the same. The head it replaces is kept under versions/ (Versions and rollback); to add a label or a few corrections without training from scratch, fine-tune instead.

docs.title: Your own head
docs.text:
val options = buildOptions(
    candidates = listOf(
        architecture(hidden = listOf(32, 16), epochs = 200, learningRate = 0.005),
        architecture(hidden = emptyList(), epochs = 100),              // a linear head
        architecture(hidden = listOf(64), activation = "Tanh"),
    ),
    pickBy = "accuracy",            // or "macroF1" (the default)
    validationFraction = 0.25,       // how much is held out when there is no related test file
)
val built = modelBuilder("intents", train, options)

architecture(...) takes the hidden layer widths (an empty list is a linear head), epochs, batchSize, learningRate and the hidden activation (Relu or Tanh); a wrong value is refused when the line runs, not after the embedding. One candidate means no comparison, just that head. The Models page's New model uses the defaults.

docs.title: Against memorising: regularisation, schedules, early stopping
docs.text:
architecture(...) takes more than the layers. Every setting below is off unless it is given, so a head that leaves them out trains exactly as it always has:

Setting What it does When it helps weightDecay = 0.01 AdamW's decoupled weight decay: every step pulls the weights (not the biases) a little towards zero The head memorises: its train accuracy is far above the validation's dropout = 0.2 Switches off that share of the hidden units for each row while training; a linear head has none A wide head (dense[128]) on a few hundred rows labelSmoothing = 0.1 Spreads that share of each target over every label, so the head is less sure of rows like its training rows Scores near 1.0 on everything, noisy labels schedule = "cosine" The rate eases from its value down to a hundredth of it over the epochs ("linear" too; "constant" is the default) Long fits, a high starting rate warmupEpochs = 5 The rate climbs to its value over the first epochs A high rate, a deep head patience = 10 Early stopping: a tenth of the training rows is put aside, the fit stops once their loss hasn't improved for 10 epochs, and the best epoch's weights are kept You don't know how many epochs are enough name = "wide" Your name for the head in the console and the charts A search with many similar heads

A head with settings of its own is named after them, dense[32] · lr 0.003 · dropout 0.2 · early stop 10, so the ranking in the console says which variant won. Early stopping prints stopped early at epoch 17 of 150, keeping epoch 7, the lowest loss on the tenth of the training rows put aside.

docs.title: Cross-validation and searching heads
docs.text:
On a small file one 20% split is luck: three validation rows of a label move its F1 by a third. With buildOptions(folds = 5) every candidate is also trained five times on four fifths of the training rows and scored on the fifth it did not see; the heads are compared by the mean of those five scores (with its spread: over 5 folds of the training rows, accuracy 0.872 · macro F1 0.875 ± 0.069), and the chosen one is then trained on all the training rows and validated as before. It costs folds + 1 fits per head.

searchSpace(...) makes the candidates from every combination of the values it is given:

val options = buildOptions(
    candidates = searchSpace(
        hidden = listOf(emptyList(), listOf(32), listOf(64, 16)),
        learningRates = listOf(0.01, 0.003),
        dropouts = listOf(0.0, 0.2),
        patience = 10,
    ),
    folds = 5,
)

That is 2 linear heads (dropout means nothing to them) and 8 others. trials = 12 draws 12 of a bigger grid at random (seed picks which); a search of more than 64 heads is refused. Without arguments it tries six layer shapes, from linear to dense[128, 32], at two rates.

Rows that look mislabeled. In cross-validation every training row is scored by a head that never saw it. A row is a suspect when that head is at least 60% sure of another label and gives the row's own label less than the rows of that label usually get. After the build the console names three (5 training rows look mislabeled … "lights there number 103" is 'weather', they say 'lights' 0.955), and suspects("intents") lists them all, the widest disagreement first, with their texts only when the model keeps texts. A suspect is a wrong label or a hard row: fix it in the csv, or keep it.

docs.title: Scores you can trust: calibration
docs.text:
A softmax head trained to fit is usually surer than it is right: a score of 0.95 may be right 80% of the time. Every run measures this. The expected calibration error (ECE) is the gap between how sure the answers are and how often they are right, averaged over ten bins of the top score. Every score gate from 0 to 0.95 is measured too: how many rows it keeps and how many of those are right. calibrationChart("intents") prints both, and the console names a gate worth using (a gate at 0.95 keeps 20% of the rows and 100% of what it keeps is right).

buildOptions(calibrate = true) fits one temperature on the validation rows (the scores become the softmax of the logits divided by it) and folds it into the last layer. The exported model, initMod and the HTTP server then give the calibrated scores without knowing about it. The answers stay the same: dividing every logit by the same positive number keeps their order. A model that is built already is calibrated on rows it has not seen:

calibrate("intents", source("intents-holdout.csv"))   // at least 10 rows; a new version, the same answers

This fits the temperature on those rows, reports the error before and after on two halves of them, and writes the calibrated head as the next version. Nothing is written when the scores were right already.

docs.title: Mistakes
docs.text: The validation rows a run got wrong are kept with it, the surest mistakes first (buildOptions(keepMistakes = 25); 0 keeps none). mistakes("intents") prints each row's label, the answer, both scores and the text. A model that doesn't keep texts keeps the labels and scores without the texts.

docs.title: The embedding cache
docs.text: Embedding is most of a build's time. Every text's vector is kept in AMP/cache/embeddings/<encoder>/vectors.bin (the SHA-256 of the text, not the text, and its 768 numbers), so building again, a search or a fine-tune embeds only the texts it hasn't seen (fineTune: 40 of 52 texts came from the embedding cache). The store belongs to one encoder folder and changes when the encoder's model or tokenizer file changes, so an old vector never answers for a new encoder. embeddingCache.print() shows what is kept and embeddingCache.clear() frees it; a store that grows past 512 MB starts over. buildOptions(cacheEmbeddings = false) skips it, and a model with keepTexts = false never uses it.

docs.title: Fine-tuning: teaching a model more
docs.text:
A new label, or a few rows the model gets wrong, don't need a new build. fineTune starts from the head the model has, adds an output for every label it doesn't know, and trains on the new rows together with the rows it learned from before:

val tuned = fineTune("intents", source("music.csv"))   // or listOf("play some jazz" to "music", …)
tuned.modelStatus()                                    // after, and the head before on the same rows
versions("intents")                                    // v2 fine-tune of v1, v1 build
rollback("intents", 1)                                 // v1's head again, as v3

A client of a served model can do the same over HTTP without the page or a script: POST <path>/teach puts a sentence and its label in the model's queue, POST <path>/retrain fine-tunes on the queue in the background while the model keeps answering, and the new head is swapped in when it is written (Teaching a model while it listens).

What it does, in order (jetbrainDLBuilder/FineTune.kt):

  1. Maps the labels. A row's label is the model's label when they match in any case (Lights is lights). A label it doesn't know is a new label and needs at least 3 rows, so one can be held out to check it. A label a letter or a plural away from a known one is flagged ('light' is taken as a new label; if it is meant to be 'lights', spell it so in the file). The rows are cleaned as a build cleans them, but one label, or one row of a label it knows, is enough.
  2. Replays what it learned from. The rows of its data file, and of the files it was fine-tuned on, are trained on again (up to 200 per label) when they are still in AMP/, so the labels it knows are not forgotten. When a new row's text was learned under another label, the new row wins: that is how a correction is made.
  3. Grows the head. Each new label's output starts where it will end up (weight imprinting). Its weights point from where the labels it has sit to the mean of the new label's rows, and its bias is set so it answers its own rows without taking the others'. With nothing to replay (a model downloaded from the website), where the labels it has sit is the mean of the training features the build kept in module.json (featureMean), so a new label still lands in the right place.
  4. Trains gently. It runs 40 epochs at a rate of 0.002 (a build runs 150 at 0.01). The loss is weighted so a new label of ten rows counts as much as one of two hundred, and every weight it had is pulled back towards where it started (L2-SP, stayNear = 0.01). The new outputs are free; freeze = 1 keeps the first layer as it is.
  5. Scores before and after on the same held-out rows: a share of the new rows and of the replayed rows, or the related test file. It prints on the 2 held-out new rows: accuracy 0.000 before, 1.000 after, then the earlier rows, then all of them. An old label whose F1 falls by more than 0.1 is a warning (the fine-tune forgets some of what it knew: 'weather' F1 0.950 → 0.710; replay more earlier rows (replayPerLabel), raise stayNear, or roll back). Labels with no rows among the checked ones are left out of the macro F1.
  6. Writes the next version. The head it replaces is kept under versions/ and the guide's label list gets the new labels. module.json records kind: fine-tune, parentVersion and fineTunedOn. The run joins metrics.json with its baseline, so the Metrics tab shows before and after.

fineTuneOptions(...):

Option Default What it does epochs, learningRate, batchSize 40, 0.002, 16 The fit stayNear 0.01 How hard the weights it had are pulled back: higher forgets less and learns the new rows less; 0 lets them go anywhere replay, replayPerLabel true, 200 Train on the earlier rows too, at most this many per label freeze 0 The first n layers keep their weights; at least the last one learns balanceClasses true Every label weighs the same in the loss validationFraction 0.2 The share of the new rows, and of the replayed rows, held out to score before and after patience 0 Early stopping, as in a build calibrate false Fit a new temperature on the held-out rows afterwards (a calibrated model's temperature is taken out before training) minNewLabelRows 3 The rows a new label needs cacheEmbeddings, keepMistakes, seed, preprocess as in a build

A fine-tune is refused, and the model left as it was, when the model doesn't exist, the encoder doesn't fit its head, a new label has too few rows, or freeze covers every layer. The console says which. One that ends after the model got another head meanwhile (rolled back, trained again, or destroyed and built anew under its name) writes nothing, so that head isn't lost and no two heads get one number; run it again on the head it has now. A calibration does the same.

docs.title: Versions and rollback
docs.text:
Every head a model replaces is kept. A build, a fine-tune, a calibration or a rollback copies the head it replaces, its module.json and the run it was scored with into AMP/models/intents/<name>/versions/v<N>/; the ten newest are kept. versions("intents") lists them, the current one first:

versions 'intents' · 3 kept
v3 (current) · v1 brought back · 2026-10-21 10:12 · 3 labels · accuracy 0.933 · macro F1 0.930
v2 · fine-tune of v1 · 2026-10-21 10:05 · 4 labels · accuracy 0.950 · macro F1 0.948 · fine-tuned v1 on music.csv: 8 new rows, 36 replayed; new label music
v1 · build · 2026-10-21 09:58 · 3 labels · accuracy 0.933 · macro F1 0.930

rollback("intents", 1) makes v1's head the model again as a new version (v3), so a rollback can itself be undone. The description, icon and guide stay as they are, and v1's scores are appended to metrics.json, so the page shows the scores of the head that answers. On the Models page the model's About tab lists its versions under Versions, each kept one with Roll back, and its ⋯ menu rolls back to the newest kept one. Compare beside it scores that head and the current one on the same csv without changing anything: each label's F1 then and now, the confusion change, and (for a model that keeps texts) the rows they answer differently (the Models page; util/VersionCompare.kt, which writes nothing of the model but plots/compare.png, and keeps the rows' vectors in the embedding cache only when both heads keep texts). Publishing sends only the current head; the versions stay on this machine.

docs.title: What to label next
docs.text:
Labeling is the expensive part, so label what the model is least sure about:

textsToLabel("intents", "asked.txt", limit = 50)   // or a csv's text column; without a file, what it was asked over HTTP
textsToLabel("intents", "asked.txt", limit = 50, diverse = true)   // texts unlike each other among its closest calls

This ranks the texts by the gap between the model's two best scores, the closest calls first. It leaves out repeats, near-repeats (cosine above 0.98 to one already picked) and the texts it was trained on (a training file that can't be read is passed over). The closest calls are often many wordings of one confusion; with diverse = true (Varied close calls on the Improve tab) it takes the closest calls, five times as many as it is asked for, and picks among them one text at a time: first the closest call, then each time the text least like those picked so far (by the cosine of the encoder's vectors). They are listed closest call first, as always, and a few labels cover more kinds of text. Without it the output is exactly as before. The result goes to AMP/intents-to-label.csv: an empty label column beside the model's guess, its score and the runner-up. Fill in the labels and run fineTune("intents", source("intents-to-label.csv")); rows left blank are dropped. Asking again keeps the rows you labeled already at the top of the file and doesn't pick their texts a second time, so no labeling work is lost. A model that doesn't keep texts writes no such file.

On the Models page this file is the model's queue, on its Improve tab: each text is labeled with a click, a wrong answer on the Try line goes into it with the right label (teach(model, text, label); the text the queue has already is relabeled, and a label the model knows is written in its spelling), the answers of a batch of pasted sentences it was unsure of go into it as rows to label with their guesses (the page's queueGuesses in LabelQueue.kt, not part of the script API; after the rows there, leaving a text it has already as it is), and Fine-tune on n rows fine-tunes on its labeled rows. Before any fine-tune starts, the page shows what it would do: rows per label, new labels, what it would replay, and what blocks it (planFineTune(model, rows), which reads the head and the earlier files without training; a test checks that its counts are the ones the fine-tune then uses). After a change to the head made on the page, regradeQueue(model) rewrites the queue's guess, score and runner-up with the head it has now, keeping the labels, so the page can mark the labeled texts it answers right.

A script runs the same loop with teach, queue, planFineTune (on the labeled rows of the queue when given no data, printed in the strip's words) and regradeQueue; the recipe is in the cookbook.

docs.title: Validating without training
docs.text: A run can be added to metrics.json without rebuilding: on the Models page, Validate on file or Validate on sample data runs the model on every row of a csv and stores accuracy, F1 per label and the confusion matrix as one more run, with the file name as the validation set (metrics/ModelValidation.kt). This is how the dummy model, which is written rather than trained, gets metrics at all. A validation keeps what a build keeps beyond the scores: the calibration error and its gates, and the rows it got wrong.

docs.title: Reading the metrics
docs.text: Metrics are plain local files, so anyone using the app can read them, from the console or from the Models page.

docs.title: In the console, as tables
docs.text:
validateMetrics("intents")                          // all labels
validateMetrics("intents", listOf("lights", "music")) // some labels

metrics 'intents' @ 2026-10-14 16:02:11: 240 samples (192 train / 48 validation on split 20%)
accuracy 0.917 (0.854–0.979)  macro F1 0.905 (0.836–0.966)  (ranges: the middle 95% of 1,000 resamples of its rows)
label   precision  recall  f1     support
lights  0.933      0.933   0.933  15
music   0.875      0.933   0.903  15

docs.title: How far the scores hold
docs.text: A score on 48 rows is not the score on the next 48. Every run a build, fine-tune, calibration or validation adds keeps where its accuracy and macro F1 fell when its rows were drawn again 1,000 times (metrics/ScoreIntervals.kt): each draw takes as many rows of each label as the run had, at random and with repeats, and is scored as the run was (the same F1 rule, so the labels a fine-tune left out of its macro F1 stay out), and the middle 95% of the draws is the range, accuracyRange and macroF1Range in metrics.json. The draws are seeded, so the same rows give the same range every time, and they use random numbers of their own, so training never sees them. The narrower the range, the more the score can be trusted: 0.917 (0.854–0.979) says that another 48 rows like these could score anywhere in there. A run that got every row right, or every row wrong, has no range, since every draw scores the same; runs from before the ranges were kept have none either. A rollback's run keeps the ranges its version had. The Models page gives them in brackets on the Metrics tab's scores line, and the scores chart draws macro F1's as a bar under its mark.

docs.title: Rows it learned from
docs.text:
A row a run is scored on that is also a row the model learned from tests what it remembers, so it flatters the scores. Every run looks for them (jetbrainDLBuilder/Leakage.kt) and says how many it found as a warning of the run, printed and kept with it; nothing that is trained changes. A row repeats one it learned from when it is

  • the same text: the same letters and digits, ignoring case, spaces and punctuation (Turn on the lights! and turn on the lights); a text with no letters or digits is like no other;
  • nearly the same to the encoder: its vector within a cosine of 0.98 of a training row's. The run has the vectors already, so this costs no time in the encoder.
Run Its rows Against Looks for build the validation rows (the split, or the test file) the training rows both fine-tune the rows it is scored on (the held-out rows, or the test file) the rows it trained on, new and replayed, and the files its head learned from before, as a validation looks in them (replay trains on a sample of them only); a held-out replayed row, there to see what it forgot, only among the rows it trained on both, the same text only in those files; a fine-tune with too few rows to hold any out is scored on its training rows and says so instead validation the file's rows of labels it knows the files it learned from: its data and the files fine-tunes taught it, those still in AMP/ (one that can't be read is passed over) the same text: its rows go through a session, which gives no vectors calibration its rows as a validation the same text; past a third of the rows, the warning says the temperature may be too low for new texts instead

A build or fine-tune already leaves out a test file's rows whose text is a training row's in lowercase (the console says how many); the check finds the rows that differ from one in punctuation or that the encoder can hardly tell from one. For a model that keeps texts, the build's console gives a few of the pairs, and the run keeps ten in metrics.json (leakage), which the Metrics tab shows in the warning's tooltip; a model that keeps no texts keeps only the counts.

docs.title: In the console, as ASCII charts
docs.text:
metricsChart("intents")             // accuracy, macro F1 and the F1 of every label as bars
metricsChart("intents", listOf("lights"))
metricsHistory("intents")           // accuracy and macro F1 across every build, as a line chart
confusionMatrix("intents")          // the last validation's confusion matrix as a shaded grid

metricsChart draws one bar per row with precision, recall and support beside it:

metrics 'intents' · build 3 of 3 · 48 validation samples on split 20%
F1 per label (bar), precision p, recall r, support n
accuracy ███████████████████████████░░░ 0.917
macro F1 ███████████████████████████░░░ 0.905
lights   ████████████████████████████░░ 0.933  p 0.933  r 0.933  n 15
music    ███████████████████████████░░░ 0.903  p 0.875  r 0.933  n 15
weather  ██████████████████████████░░░░ 0.880  p 0.917  r 0.846  n 18

metricsHistory plots every build on one canvas (● accuracy, ○ macro F1, ◆ where they meet) with the build numbers under the columns and a dated line per build, so you can see whether a new data file helped.

history 'intents' · 3 builds
1.00 ┤            ◆
     ┤      ●
     ┤      ○
0.50 ┤●
     ┤○
0.00 ┤
     └─────────────
      1     2     3
      ● accuracy   ○ macro F1   ◆ both

confusionMatrix prints truth in rows and prediction in columns; the shade of each cell is its share of the row and ✓ marks the diagonal.

Four more read what a run keeps beyond its scores:

mistakes("intents")            // the validation rows the last run got wrong, the surest first
suspects("intents")            // training rows whose label looks wrong (a build with folds)
calibrationChart("intents")    // how often each score is right, and what a gate keeps
trainingCurves("intents")      // loss and accuracy by epoch of the chosen head, or of the last fine-tune

calibration 'intents' · v1 · build · 10 validation rows on split 20%
expected calibration error 0.176 (0.164 before the temperature 1.623 was folded in); 0 means a score of 0.8 is right 80% of the time
how often right per top score (bar), how sure on average (sure), answers in the bin (n)
0.80–0.90 ██████████████████████████████ 1.000  sure 0.896  n 1
0.90–1.00 █████████████████████████░░░░░ 0.833  sure 0.933  n 6
answer only from  keeps  right
0.00              100%  0.900
0.80               70%  0.857
0.95               20%  1.000
a gate at 0.95 keeps 20% of the rows, and 100% of what it keeps is right

trainingCurves draws the loss and the accuracy by epoch on the training rows (●) and the validation rows (○); a validation loss that rises while the training loss falls is a head memorising. The other heads of the build get a line each (dense[16]: loss 0.990 → 0.055, validation 0.859 → 0.464, lowest validation loss at epoch 8).

Each of these returns the report, so they chain: metricsChart("intents").history().confusion(). A model that was never built logs an error telling you to run modelBuilder first, and a run kept before the analysis was says so (the last run of 'intents' kept no mistakes (it was made before they were kept)).

docs.title: On the Models page
docs.text: The Models page (second sidebar icon) draws the same numbers as charts on the model's Metrics tab: the scores per label (Per label) and the Confusion matrix of a validation run (one run at a time, picked with the run chips), how the heads of a build (or a fine-tune) learned (Training by epoch) and how far a run's scores can be trusted (Calibration), the scores across the runs (Scores over runs), and from the sessions how sure the model is (Confidence by label) and how long an answer takes (Answer time). Each chart has a short title and only the figures it alone shows; what a chart means is in the Guide tab. They are read from metrics.json and sessions.log; the rows it got wrong and the ones whose label looks wrong are listed under the charts. A heatmap cell's numbers are white or black, whichever stands out more from the cell, so they read at 4.5:1 on any shade. The ASCII charts stay in the console. Asking a model a sentence and correcting its answer is the Try line under its header; fine-tuning, calibrating, rolling back and the texts to label are its Improve tab (also its ⋯ menu, its About tab's Versions and its Data tab), and every one of them that changes the head offers Undo in its notice. The page also builds a model from a csv (New model: name, a sentence about it, data file, optional test file), and every model is a component with Open session, Listen, the serving settings behind the gear, and Publish (Keycloak sign-in); every open session can be terminated there and its log (what it was asked and answered) read. Details in Models page.

docs.title: Using a model from a script
docs.text:
val m = initMod("intents")
log(m.predict("turn the lights on"))             // "lights"
log(m.inference("turn the lights on").first())   // "lights:0.97"
m.close()

initMod() with no name opens the bundled NER model; importModelOnnx("path.onnx") opens any ONNX model behind the same inference / getStatus / close interface. Models made elsewhere open the same way: initMod("<name>") for a folder of AMP/models/imported (a Hugging Face repo), importModel("path") or initMod("path") for a file or folder: ONNX, TorchScript on PyTorch, or a TensorFlow SavedModel, with text in through its tokenizer.json, labels from its config.json and a tensor API (.inputs, .outputs, .run(floatArrayOf(…))). TFLite and weights alone (safetensors, pytorch_model.bin, gguf, h5) are refused with the way to ONNX. See Models from outside. Every initMod("name") is a session the Models page lists and can terminate; what it was asked and answered is logged per session (behind Log on the page and in AMP/models/intents/<name>/sessions.log). ORT sessions are also printed with sessions.print(). A blank text has no answer (a listener answers 400 for one): inference gives an empty list, scores an empty map and predict fails with "the model answered nothing", and the console says the text was empty.

docs.title: The model card
docs.text:
A model's guide (AMP/models/intents/<name>/guide.md, its Guide tab, published with it) holds a short model card between two marker lines (metrics/ModelCard.kt), written again after every run of the model (a build, fine-tune, calibration, validation or rollback) and when the guide is saved on the page:

<!-- amie:model-card: written again after every run of the model; your own text goes outside these two lines -->
## Model card

- version: v2, fine-tune of v1, 2026-10-21
- data: intents.csv, 45 rows (greeting 15, lights 15, weather 15)
- fine-tuned on: music.csv, 12 rows (music 12)
- earlier versions: v1 (build)
- last run: validation of v2, 2026-10-21, on 45 rows (sample-intents.csv): accuracy 0.933 (0.867–0.978), macro F1 0.931 (0.862–0.977)
- calibration: none; calibration error 0.041 on the last run
- mixes up: “lights” taken for “weather” 2×
- texts: kept; its logs, runs and queue show the texts it is asked and gets wrong
<!-- /amie:model-card -->

The ranges are how far the scores hold, shown when the resamples didn't all score the same; a last run whose rows repeat rows it learned from says how many (rows it learned from). The rows per label are the ones each version learned from, after cleaning, kept with its head when it was made (dataRows and fineTunedRows in module.json), so a queue that grew afterwards, an edited csv or a file that isn't on this machine doesn't change them; for a model from before they were kept the card counts the file as it is now, and names a file that isn't here without its rows. Rows a script gave without a file read 10 rows a script gave (music 10). The dates are UTC. The card holds no row texts, only counts and label names, so a model that keeps no texts has one too.

Nothing outside the marker lines is changed: write your own text above or below them. A new guide has the card after its description; a guide from before (or written by hand) gets it at its end. What is written between the markers is replaced at the next run, and a guide whose markers don't pair up (one deleted, or a second card pasted in) is left as it is, with a line in the console. The Guide tab doesn't show the marker lines, and while the guide is being edited a run that writes the card leaves what is typed as it is; Save then writes it with the card brought up to date. Everything that writes the guide (Save, the card, a fine-tune adding its labels to the list, a rename changing the title) takes its turn, so none undoes another, and Save never holds the page up while a run writes the card.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text: Signed in with Keycloak, select a model on the Models page and press Publish: the model goes up to your package folder on the Amie backend (POST /upload, progLanguage=onnx) as <name>.onnx, <name>.module.json and <name>.guide.md, so two models never overwrite each other, and the website's dashboard lists them. A guest pressing it is sent to the sign-in page. Requires the backend from Amie backend, which stores the files in the Amie S3 bucket. Package jars go the other way: a script opens one the server lists with initMod("name.jar") (see Packages).

docs.title: Raspberry Pi 5
docs.text: How the app was measured for a Raspberry Pi 5, what that measurement can and cannot say, what it changed, and the one command that measures a real Pi 5.

docs.title: What was measured, and what that is not
docs.text:
The app has a headless benchmark: --bench starts it with no window, measures the parts a person waits for, prints one bench: line for each and writes the same as JSON next to the AMP folder. It runs on a scratch AMP folder (AMIE_AMP_DIR), never on yours.

Part What it is jvm start to main The JVM's start up to the app's main onnx runtime loaded ONNX Runtime's native library, loaded by the first session encoder loaded, first predict The bge encoder opened and shared, then the first answer of the dummy model through it 100 predicts The median and the 95th percentile of a hundred answers, with the threads the app was given and with one 1,000 rows embedded What a build does with its rows, in batches of rows of one token count readSnapshot with 20 models The Models page's read of twenty models with ten runs each, the first time and again; the plots it leaves to a thread of its own are timed on a line of their own script engine, first compile and run The Kotlin compiler a first Run waits for, with a small script compiled and run 8 background templates Eight templates started at once, each with an engine of its own, and how long until all ended compiled bundle A script exported compiled to classes (the export), then java -jar run.jar in a JVM of its own (the run) peak resident, peak heap The most the process held, sampled four times a second; heap against its limit

What the numbers on this page are. They were taken on an Apple M5 Mac with 16 GB and a warm file cache, with the JVM held to a Pi 5's budget as far as a JVM allows: -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=4 (the JVM sees four cores, and sizes its thread pools, its JIT threads and the app's ONNX threads by four) and -Xmx2g or -Xmx4g, which are the heaps the 4 GB and the 8 GB model get. They are not a Pi 5's numbers. A Pi 5's four Cortex-A76 cores at 2.4 GHz are slower than this Mac's cores for this kind of work (by how much, this page cannot say), so every time here is a floor for the Pi, not a forecast of it.
