The figures that are about the app's shape (which part costs most, how much memory it holds, how a change moved a part) carry over; the absolute milliseconds do not.

What cannot be imitated on this Mac:

  • Slower cores. The Mac's cores are faster, and the cap above limits how many the JVM uses, not how quick they are. The encoder's 14 ms answer and 2 ms per row will be longer on a Pi.
  • The SD card. Here the encoder (415 MB) and the libraries came from a warm cache on an NVMe disk. A Pi reads them from an SD card or an SSD, cold on the first start, and the first load of the encoder will be seconds there. Everything below that is "loaded" is the warm figure.
  • Memory pressure and swap. The Mac has 16 GB, so nothing was swapped. The peak resident of 1.7 to 2.0 GB is the figure to hold against a 4 GB Pi's RAM, with the system and the window on top of it.
  • No GPU, and the window. The benchmark has no window. Compose on a Pi's graphics stack (software rendering or the Mesa driver, Skiko's arm64 Linux build) is not exercised, so how the window feels is not measured here.
  • Thermals and the governor. A Pi 5 without a cooler throttles under the load of a build; the script below prints vcgencmd get_throttled and the governor so a throttled run can be told.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Each run was a fresh JVM, one at a time. The first column of figures is the app as it was before the changes below (the two switches that turn them off were set), the second is after them, both with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=4 -Xmx2g; the third is -Xmx4g. "After" is a second start on the same AMP folder, which is what a Pi does every time but its first.

Part Before, 2 GB After, 2 GB After, 4 GB jvm start to main 151 ms 165 ms 165 ms onnx runtime loaded 1,106 ms 36 ms 897 ms (first start) encoder loaded 4,924 ms 775 ms 798 ms first predict 33 ms 35 ms 29 ms 100 predicts, 4 threads (median, p95) 14.2, 15.2 ms 14.1, 17.9 ms 14.1, 15.2 ms 100 predicts, 1 thread (median, p95) 47.4, 47.7 ms 47.4, 47.6 ms 47.3, 47.7 ms 1,000 rows embedded 12,517 ms 12,675 ms 12,320 ms readSnapshot, 20 models, first 259 ms 242 ms 259 ms readSnapshot, again 4 ms 4 ms 4 ms plots drawn in the background 1,761 ms 1,761 ms 1,768 ms script engine, first compile and run 2,175 ms 2,095 ms (365 ms warmed, see below) 2,094 ms a second engine, compile and run 222 ms 242 ms 225 ms 8 background templates, started, finished 36 ms, 1,842 ms 34 ms, 1,596 ms 33 ms, 1,570 ms compiled bundle: export (20 MB) 3,304 ms 3,300 ms 3,485 ms compiled bundle: java -jar run.jar 220 ms 216 ms 224 ms peak resident 1.74 GB 1.99 GB 2.03 GB peak heap 628 MB of 2 GB 805 MB of 2 GB 602 MB of 4 GB total 35.3 s 29.9 s 30.6 s

A run with -Xmx1g -XX:+UseSerialGC -Damie.ort.threads=3 (what the troubleshooting page suggests for a 4 GB Pi) held 455 MB of its 990 MB heap at the peak and 1.67 GB resident; its answers took 18.1 ms at the median and its rows 14.1 ms each, against 14 and 12.7 ms with four threads. Eight templates still fit in that heap.

Where the time goes, from these runs: the encoder's compute is what costs most. A build spends 12.4 ms of every row in ONNX Runtime (a hundred answers took 1.4 s with four threads and 4.7 s with one), so a thousand rows take 12 of the benchmark's 30 seconds. After it come the first script compile (2.1 s) and the export of a compiled bundle (3.3 s, which happens once per export, not per run). The Models page's read, the answers and the bundle's run are small.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
Each of these was measured before and after on the runs above. The switch in the last column turns it off, which is how the "before" column was taken.

Change Before After Switch off No call home from DJL's tokenizer. The tokenizer library, on the first tokenizer, asks the EC2 metadata address who it runs on and then reports to an S3 bucket. Off AWS the first call waits for its connection to time out, which held the encoder's load. The app now sets DJL's own switch (OPT_OUT_TRACKING) before any tokenizer is made, unless the machine set it. encoder loaded 4,924 ms 775 to 823 ms -Damie.djl.telemetry=true ONNX Runtime's native library is unpacked once into AMP/cache/ort/, not into the temp folder on every start (13 MB on a Pi, 26 MB on this Mac, with the JNI library beside it). A Pi on an SD card wrote and read those megabytes before its first session at every start. onnx runtime loaded 1,106 ms 36 ms from the second start (about 920 ms on the first) -Damie.ort.cache=false The script engine is warmed in the background four seconds after the window shows, at the lowest thread priority, so the first Run finds the compiler loaded. first compile 2,095 ms 365 ms (measured with --bench --prewarm; it cost the answers running beside it about 1.5 ms at the median) -Damie.prewarm=false

The first of these is also a privacy change: the app no longer sends anything to Amazon's telemetry bucket through DJL. Setting OPT_OUT_TRACKING=false in the environment or as a property keeps DJL's behaviour.

Also in this branch, from the earlier slow-hardware work: ONNX threads that sleep when idle, plots drawn off the page's read, one-vector-per-row builds and the 35% heap limit (see Troubleshooting).

docs.title: What was left alone
docs.text:
Each of these needs a real Pi to judge, or changes results:

  • Batching the rows of a build (several texts per ONNX run). It may raise throughput on four cores and may not on a Pi's memory bandwidth; the vectors differ in the last digits. Try it on the Pi.
  • An int8 or fp16 encoder. Likely the biggest win on ARM, and it changes the vectors every model is trained on.
  • Other ONNX session options (arena off, a saved optimized graph, ORT's defaults) were measured against the app's options on this Mac and made no difference in the answer time (13.1 to 13.6 ms); the load time of a saved graph is a cold-disk question this Mac cannot answer.
  • JIT and class loading flags (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, class data sharing for the script compiler's 2 seconds, -XX:CICompilerCount): their value depends on the Pi's cores.
  • The thread count of the encoder (-Damie.ort.threads): three threads were slower here (18.1 ms against 14.1 ms, with a 1 GB serial-GC heap beside it); on a Pi, with the window needing a core, it may be better. The benchmark prints both the app's count and one thread.
  • The installed package's layout. The Pi command below uses the DEB's jars under /opt/amie-pilot/lib/app; that layout was not checked on a Pi, and neither was the compiled bundle step with the jars loaded that way. If that step fails the benchmark says so on its line and goes on.

docs.title: Running it on a Raspberry Pi 5
docs.text:
On a 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, with the arm64 DEB of the app installed (see Getting started), or in a checkout of this repository:

./scripts/pi-bench.sh

That one command installs a JDK 21 if the Pi has none (apt, else Temurin 21 from adoptium.net into ~/amie-bench/jdk), picks -Xmx2g on a Pi with under 6 GB and -Xmx4g otherwise, and runs java -Xmx2g -cp '/opt/amie-pilot/lib/app/*' org.example.project.MainKt --bench on a scratch AMP folder in ~/amie-bench/amp. Without the DEB it builds the classes from the checkout with Gradle first and stops Gradle's daemon so it is not in the memory being measured. It prints the Pi's model, cores, RAM, governor and throttling state, then the bench: lines, and keeps them in ~/amie-bench/result-<time>.txt with the JSON next to the AMP folder.

To run it by hand, with the JDK installed (sudo apt install openjdk-21-jdk-headless, or Temurin 21):

AMIE_AMP_DIR=$HOME/amie-bench/amp java -Xmx2g -Dcompose.application.resources.dir=/opt/amie-pilot/lib/app/resources \
  -cp '/opt/amie-pilot/lib/app/*' org.example.project.MainKt --bench

Options after --bench: --stand-in (a small head stands in for the encoder), --no-bundle (skip the export and its run), --rows N, --predicts N, --prewarm. With AMIE_JVM_ARGS="-Xmx1g -XX:+UseSerialGC -Damie.ort.threads=3" the script runs the flags of a 4 GB Pi from the troubleshooting page instead. Run it twice: the first run unpacks ONNX Runtime's library and reads the encoder cold, the second is what every start after it costs. Cool the Pi first, and send back the throttled line with the numbers.

docs.title: Scripting API
docs.text:
Complete scripts for every call below, ready to paste, are in the Cookbook.

The same scripts run outside the app with the amie command line: Learn amie goes through them chapter by chapter, and the amie reference has the commands and the API in brief.

The sandbox is a Kotlin script editor (main.kts) with a console (how to use the editor, the completion dropdown and the console filters is in The sandbox). The script runs inside the app with the sandbox API bound to it; everything it logs shows in the console on the right and is appended to AMP/logs.txt.

Every function below can be called directly (source("x.csv")) or through the amie object (amie.source("x.csv")). The only difference is amie.import: without the prefix write implementation("group:module:version") or dependency(...) for a package and environment(SettingsEnv(...)) for an environment, since a bare import(...) reads as a Kotlin import.

docs.title: Running a script
docs.text:
1. Type in the editor. The script is saved to AMP/pluginDir/main.kts as you type.
  2. Press Run over the editor or ⌘↵ (Ctrl+Enter elsewhere) inside it.
  3. While the script runs the console strip reads running 12s (with the model build's phase and progress when modelBuilder is working) and the Run button reads Running…; pressing Run again only logs "Script is already running".
  4. When it ends the strip shows finished in 41s or failed after 3s, and the console gets the same line.

Started with AMIE_AUTORUN=1, the app opens the sandbox and runs the saved main.kts once, as if Run was pressed (the model site's ample.sh does this for the gateway). Without a saved main.kts nothing runs.

The level toggles on the console strip (internal, error, data, info) filter what is shown; only info is on at start, the counts on the others say what is hidden. Clear empties the view, the log file keeps it all.

docs.title: Run phases
docs.text:
• Configuration. implementation("group:module:version") / amie.import("...") and environment(SettingsEnv("env", "profile")) / amie.import(SettingsEnv(...)) calls are read from the script text before it compiles, the packages are resolved from Maven Central (cached under AMP/env/caches) and put on the script's classpath. Each env (AMP/env/<name>/env.lock.json) keeps what was ever imported into it, like a virtualenv.
  • Execution. The script's own import lines are moved to the top (a trailing // comment on one is fine), LogLevel is imported for you, then val amie = bindings["logger"] as ScriptLogger and a prelude of top-level functions delegating to it (fun source(path: String) = amie.source(path), …) are inserted before the rest of the code, and the whole is evaluated with the Kotlin JSR-223 engine on a background thread. The prelude is generated from one list (SandboxApi.kt), which also feeds the editor's completion dropdown.

docs.title: The API
docs.text:
Defined in ScriptLogger.kt. The most used calls (prefix amie. optional):

Call What it does log("..."), info, error, data Any value, so log(pkg.run("x")) prints every answer: a list, a set or an array one element a line, a map key: value. Console lines at the given level: info for the script's own output (the only level on at start), data for what it produced (every model answer is one), error (turns itself on when a run fails), internal for the app's own lines source("train.csv") Reads a labeled CSV (text and label columns are inferred from headers like text, label, intent). Looked up as given, then in AMP/, then AMP/pluginDir/ relate(train, "test.csv") Attaches a test file to a training source; the model validates on it instead of a split. Remembered in AMP/relations.json sourceFile("file.csv", column = "") Raw rows keyed by index, optionally one column hasModel("name") Whether AMP has that model: built, a text model, a speech model or one imported into AMP/models/imported modelBuilder("name", data) Trains and exports an intent classifier (below) initMod("llama3.2-3b") A text generation model of AMP/models/text, run on the app's own ONNX Runtime and managed as any other session; .answer(text) answers (voice.md) modelBuilder("name") { ... }, modelBuilder("name", buildOptions(...)) { ... } Same, the lambda returns the data; the second with your own options modelBuilder("name", data, buildOptions(...)) The same build with your own options: architecture(hidden, epochs, batchSize, learningRate, activation) candidates, pickBy (macroF1 or accuracy), preprocess, validationFraction, seed, balanceClasses, keepTexts (false for a model trained on other people's data: no row text reaches the console or dropped.csv, and its sessions log each text's length instead of the text), folds (cross-validate every head over 2 to 10 folds and find rows that look mislabeled), calibrate (fold a temperature into the head so the scores mean what they say), cacheEmbeddings (keep the vectors on disk, on by default), keepMistakes. See Models and metrics architecture(..., weightDecay, dropout, labelSmoothing, schedule, warmupEpochs, patience, name) A head with what keeps it from memorising, a cosine or linear rate with a warm-up, and early stopping after patience epochs without progress; all off unless given. See Against memorising searchSpace(hidden, learningRates, epochs, batchSizes, activations, dropouts, weightDecays, patience, trials, seed) The candidates of a search: every combination of the values, or trials of them at random. buildOptions(candidates = searchSpace(...), folds = 5) fineTune("name", data, fineTuneOptions(...)) Teaches a trained model more: rows of labels it knows correct it, a label it doesn't know gets an output of its own, and its earlier data is replayed so it keeps what it knew. The data is what modelBuilder takes; the model before stays a version. Returns what modelBuilder returns. See Fine-tuning fineTuneOptions(epochs, learningRate, batchSize, stayNear, replay, replayPerLabel, freeze, …) How a fine-tune goes; the table is in Fine-tuning calibrate("name", data) Fits a temperature on labeled rows the model hasn't seen (at least 10) so its scores mean what they say; the answers stay the same; a new version versions("name"), rollback("name", 2) The heads the model had (the current one first, the ten before it kept in versions/), and an earlier one made the model again as a new version; rollback returns true when it did textsToLabel("name", path = "asked.txt", limit = 50, diverse = false) The texts the model is least sure about (a csv's text column or a text file's lines; without a path, what it was asked over HTTP) written with its guess to AMP/<name>-to-label.csv, under the rows labeled in that file already; returns the file's path. diverse = true picks texts unlike each other among its closest calls (What to label next) teach("name", "text", "label") A text the model answers wrongly with the label it should give, written labeled at the top of its queue (AMP/<name>-to-label.csv), as the chips under the Try line do; the next fine-tune on the queue learns it. The label in the model's spelling; a text the queue has gets the label instead. Returns the queue's path, null when it isn't written (a model that keeps no texts has no queue; the console says why, never with the text) queue("name") The rows of its queue in order, labeled or not: .text, .label (empty while unlabeled), .labeled, .guess, .score, .runnerUp; printed as a table (an internal line). None for a model that keeps no texts planFineTune("name", data = null, fineTuneOptions(...)) What a fine-tune on the data would do, worked out without training, in the words of the plan strip: the rows, the labels they are and add, the earlier rows it replays, what it drops, what is worth a second look and what keeps it from starting (an internal line, and an error line when it would not start). Without data, on the labeled rows of its queue. .ok says whether fineTune would start; .rows, .known, .newLabels, .tooFew, .nearMisses, .replayRows, .problems regradeQueue("name") What the model answers now to every text of its queue, as the Models page grades it after a fine-tune, rollback or calibration: each row's guess, score and runner-up written again, the labels kept; returns the rows. The console says how many labeled texts it answers right embeddingCache.print(), embeddingCache.clear(), embeddingCache.sizeOnDisk() The sentence vectors kept in AMP/cache/embeddings, so a text is embedded once, and the bytes they take checkData(data) The preprocessor alone, without training: what it would clean, drop and refuse, and whether a build could start (returns true then) initMod("name") The session of an exported model: the one already open, else a new one (listed on the Models page, terminable there); .predict("text") returns the predicted label, .scores("text") every label with its score (best first), .inference("text") the raw label:probability lines sorted best first; .close(). initMod("dummy") works on a fresh checkout. An encoder and decoder pair (a T5 or BART export, encoder_model.onnx with decoder_model.onnx) opens as two sessions a script wires itself: .encoder.run(mapOf("input_ids" to t.ids, "attention_mask" to t.mask)) gives the hidden states, .decoder.run(...) the next token's logits for the ids so far (.decoder.inputs names its tensors), .decoderWithPast the decoder that takes the past state back when the export has one, .tokens(text) the ids and mask, .text(ids) the words, .startToken and .endToken the ids the decoding starts from and stops at (from the config files). See Encoder and decoder pairs. A model that lacks something it needs is refused before anything opens, with all of it in the message. How sessions live and die: Running sessions sessionMod("name") A model to ask and nothing more: a snapshot of the head it has now, in memory. .predict, .scores, .predictions, .run, .answer, .inference, and .version, .labels, .name. It can't train or change the model, writes nothing to its sessions.log, needs nothing else open and stays on that head through a fine-tune or a rollback. Everything that asks for the same head shares one snapshot. It goes when the run ends, or with .close(); val m by sessionMod("name") works too. A jar is refused. See Running sessions sessionMod("name") { ... } The same for one block, the model's functions at hand: sessionMod("name") { predict("text") }. It goes when the block ends and the call returns the block's value model.inBackground("text") Asks any model a script holds on a thread of its own and returns at once with a job: job.await() is every raw answer, job.await(millis) waits that long at most and gives null if it isn't done, job.done, job.state (queued, running, finished, cancelled or failed), job.cancel(). At most -Damie.model.jobs=N run at once, half the cores by default, the rest wait first in, first out; calls made directly never wait. A job ends with the script that started it, however it ends, with the ortClosable block it was started in, which waits for it, and with its model; await throws when it was cancelled or failed. It is on the Sessions tab, queued or running, with Terminate; the tab lists the first 100 initMod() The bundled BERT NER model, kept open: .inference("text") is one tag per token group("name") The swarm of a model group of the env: the models asked together as one session (the one already open on the group, else a new one, listed on the Models page as a model group session). .predict("text") is the label with the best score across the models, .scores("text") each label's best score, .vote("text") the label most models give, .each("text") every model's own label, .ask("text") every model's raw lines, .combined("text") all of it from one asking (.each every model's labels and scores, .merged the labels with their best scores, .vote, as the page's Try line shows them); .close() closes the sessions it opened. When one of its models was terminated meanwhile (on the page, or a script's .close()), group("name") opens a new swarm in its place rather than handing out one that lacks that model. Groups are made on the Models page (a model's ⋯ menu) or with groups huggingFace("owner/name") A model of the Hugging Face Hub as AMP/models/imported/<name>, by its repo id or its huggingface.co address. It returns the local name, so initMod(huggingFace("onnx-community/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")) opens it. The first call downloads what the Models page would pick, a plain model.onnx when there is one, with the config and tokenizer files beside it (amie hf import at a terminal offers every file that runs here as a list picked with the arrow keys, that one under the cursor; --take 3 picks for a pipe); an encoder and decoder pair takes its marked encoder and decoders, the menu amie hf import offers at a terminal said first. Once the folder is there, a call asks nothing of the network. huggingFace("owner/name", "my-name") picks the folder's name, which is the repo's last part by default. A private or gated repo needs HF_TOKEN in the app's environment. A repo that can't be read, has nothing that runs here or doesn't fit on the disk is refused with the reason. See From Hugging Face huggingFace.search("bert", format = "onnx", task = "any") Searches the Hub for models in a format initMod opens and returns their repo ids, the most downloaded first, printing each with its task, downloads and formats. format is onnx, torchscript, tensorflow, tflite or all (the default), task a Hugging Face task (text-to-speech, automatic-speech-recognition, text-classification, token-classification, feature-extraction, text-generation, audio-classification, image-classification, or a word for one: tts, asr, ner, embeddings, labels) or any (the default), and limit sets how many (20). Blank text with a task lists the most downloaded of that task. Formats are read off each repo's files, so weights-only repos are left out. Pass an id to huggingFace("…") groups The model groups of the envs: groups.print(), groups.names(), groups.create("name", listOf("a", "b")) (in the env the script is sourced in), groups.add("name", "model"), groups.remove("name", "model"), groups.delete("name"), groups.closeAll(). A group belongs to an env: it is kept in AMP/env/<env>/groups.json, group("name") looks in the script's env first, and internalEnv() lists them with the packages initAmie("text") Named entities in one text with the same NER model, opened and closed for the call: the tags are printed and returned. For many texts use initMod() initMod("whisper"), initMod("voice") The speech models speech.properties names, or initMod("whisper-base.en") for one by its folder. Whisper's .answer(wav) is what was said, a voice's .answer(text) is the file it spoke into. One session each, held by a block around it, on the Sessions tab, ended by Terminate model.can("chat") Whether a model can do something before you call it: chat and generate for a text model, classify and fineTune for a built one, tag for initMod(), hear and speak for speech, run for all initMod("name.jar") A new instance of a package jar: .run("text") calls its run(text) and returns every answer, .answer("text") the first (null when none), .close() its close(). predict, scores and predictions throw on a package: it has no labels. Looked up in the env, AMP/pluginDir, as a path, then fetched from the repositories in AMP/github.json; initMod("github:owner/repo/x.jar@ref") takes it from that repository (below) validateMetrics("name", labels = listOf(...)) Prints the stored validation table of a model, with the range of its accuracy and macro F1 when the run kept them, and returns it: .accuracy, .macroF1, .accuracyRange and .macroF1Range (low, high; null for a run from before) metricsChart("name", labels = listOf(...)) ASCII bars: accuracy, macro F1 and the F1 of each label with precision, recall and support metricsHistory("name") ASCII line chart of accuracy and macro F1 across every build confusionMatrix("name") The last validation's confusion matrix as a shaded ASCII grid mistakes("name"), suspects("name") The validation rows the last run got wrong, the surest first; the training rows a cross-validated build doubts. Texts only when the model keeps texts calibrationChart("name"), trainingCurves("name") How often each score bin is right and what a score gate keeps; loss and accuracy by epoch forwardContext("text") { ids -> } Runs the encoder and returns the hidden state [batch][token][hidden] importModelOnnx("path.onnx") Any ONNX model behind the inference / getStatus / close interface importModel("path") Any model by its path: an .onnx file, a TorchScript file (.pt, .pth, .torchscript), a TensorFlow SavedModel folder, or a folder holding one such as a Hugging Face repo. Text in with its tokenizer.json, labels from its config.json, tensors through .inputs, .outputs and .run(...). Never throws: what can't be opened is one error line with what would work, and null. See Models from outside initMod("bert-onnx"), initMod("/path/model.pt") A model of AMP/models/imported/<name> (a Hugging Face repo or a folder copied in), or a model by its path, after every kind above: opened as importModel opens it, held by the block around it, on the Sessions tab with Terminate. A refusal throws, with all it lacks in the message sessions.print(), sessions.cancel("name"), sessions.cancelAll(), ortSessions() The open ORT sessions; ortSessions() returns them as the lines sessions.print() prints ortClosable(name) { } What the block opens is for that block alone: closed when it ends, however it ends, the last opened first, so a handle kept past it fails as closed. A session open before the block is used and left open. A template started in the block works inside it and ends with it. Returns the block's value. See Scope functions ortAsync(name) { } ortClosable run in the background: the block runs on a thread of its own and the call returns a job at once. What the block opens is closed when it ends, however it ends, and a template started in it ends with it. Its log lines go to the script's console. The job ends with the script, however it ends (done, stopped or terminated), and with an ortClosable block around the call, which waits for it: it is cancelled and what it opened is closed. job.await() is the block's value and rethrows its failure, job.await(millis) waits that long at most and gives null if it hasn't ended, job.done, job.state (running, finished, cancelled or failed), job.cancel(), which interrupts the block as Stop does a script. The name is async unless given. val job = ortAsync("warm") { initMod("dummy").predict("turn the lights on") }, then log(job.await()) ortStatic(name) { } What the block opens stays open across runs until it is terminated or freed, and a session open before the block is kept too. Returns the block's value. See Scope functions. ortForever is its old name: a saved script that calls it still runs, and the console says the new name ortRequired(name) { } Kept like ortStatic while anything else is in session: a model, package, group, template or background job that no required scope holds. The encoders models share, and an intent model's BERT encoder, don't count. Once nothing else is open it is freed within a couple of seconds, unless its block is still going or what it holds is running, and the block opens it again when next run. For what other models need beside them, an encoder they share, say. Returns the block's value ortLimited(name, max) { } Kept like ortStatic, at most max sessions under the name: when one more is opened the oldest is closed first. Returns the block's value Memory running short Below 32 MB of free heap or 512 MB of free RAM, the app closes the idle sessions of ortLimited scopes and the model handleBy opened, oldest first, one at a time, with a console line for each. It never closes what is running, what a block still going holds, what has a model.inBackground job on it, or anything in ortStatic. A script that keeps such a session gets an error on its next call, as after ortScopes.free ortScopes.print(), ortScopes.free("name"), ortScopes.freeAll() What each static, required and limited scope holds; closing what one holds, or what all of them hold, which return how many were closed handleBy(handler) { } Runs the block and returns its value; when it throws, the handler's value for what it threw instead, and the run goes on: val text = handleBy({ e -> log("failed: ${e.message}"); "" }) { initMod("dummy").predict("hi") }. A stop, a cancel (Stop, Terminate, a template's or a job's cancel) and an Error such as OutOfMemoryError are never handled: they go on as they would handleBy("message") / handleBy(e) What the local text model (AMP/models/text, the one assistantModel in settings.json names, else the first) makes of an error: what is wrong and how to fix it, from the message, main.kts and the env, printed and returned. It only answers; the script stays as it is. handleBy({ e -> handleBy(e) }) { source(Path("intents.csv")) } asks about what the block threw. Without a text model, or short of RAM to open one, an error line says why and the answer is "". The model stays open five idle minutes, as handleBy under Still open errorLog(last = 20), handleBy(), handleBy(lines) The error terminal's log: the last error lines the console showed, oldest first, as it has them: a run's failures, what a command printed on stderr and why it failed, the app's own error lines. Emptied with the console, which a run does when it starts, so they are the run's. handleBy() hands the last ten of them to the local text model with main.kts and the env, so one call after a failed command or run asks about what the console showed in red; handleBy(lines) takes any list of lines. With nothing there it says so and asks nothing importModelTensorflow(Path.of("…")) importModel under its old name: a saved script still runs, and the console says the new name packages.available(), packages.fetch("x.jar"), packages.print(), packages.closeAll(), packages.github(), packages.check("x.jar"), packages.meta("x.jar"), packages.config("x.jar"), packages.setConfig("x.jar", "key" to "value"), packages.test("x.jar") The package jars the GitHub repositories offer, a download into AMP/pluginDir, the open package sessions; the jars of the GitHub repositories in AMP/github.json; the check initMod and a fetch make, a jar's metadata, the keys and values of its config files and setting them, and its tests run (below) saveState("name", json), loadState("name"), listStates() A JSON text kept per user on the Amie backend (signed in): store it under a name, read it back (null when absent), list the names. The sandbox has no state that outlives a run; this is how a script remembers a choice across runs and machines database(name = "main") A Postgres database from AMP/databases.json: .query(sql, params…) rows as maps, .scalar, .execute for changes, .print(sql) a table in the console, .tables(), .close(). Failures are one Error line and a DatabaseException databases.print(), databases.names(), databases.closeAll() The configured databases shell("du -sh ~/Documents") Runs a command in your login shell and returns what it printed: .ok, .exit, .out, .err, .lines. dir, timeoutSeconds and env are optional (Shell commands) shellScript("~/bin/lookup.sh", listOf("arg one", "arg two")) Runs a script file with its arguments passed one by one; returns what shell returns exportJvm("main.kts", to = "~/bundles/talk") Exports a script as a bundle that runs without the app, as Export… does (Exporting a script): main.kts, a template's name or id, or a file, into a new or empty folder, the first free one under ~/amie-bundles when to is empty. What can't be included stops it unless anyway = true; planOnly = true only says what would go in; compiled = false carries the text and the compiler. The console says what goes in and where it went; returns the bundle's folder, null when nothing was written serve("name", port = 8765) Serves the model over HTTP like the Models page's Listen; returns the predict URL or null. minScore = 0.75 makes it abstain under that score, answering fallbackLabel or no label (Serving a model); minScore = 0.0 and fallbackLabel = "" take saved ones away, and a min score outside 0 to 1 doesn't start it. stopServing("name"), servingUrl("name"), accessLog("name", last = 20) (the last requests of its access log, printed and returned) importPlugin("plugin.jar") Runs a static run() or main of a plugin jar once (not a package session; open packages with initMod("x.jar")), found in the env, AMP/pluginDir, as a path or in the GitHub repositories; never throws: a missing jar, a jar without an entry point or a plugin that fails is one Error line and the script goes on implementation("group:module:version"), dependency("…"), amie.import("...") Add a package to the script's environment (dependency is another name for implementation) (the Models page's Add → From Maven Central… does the same with a search) implementation("my.jar"), amie.import("my.jar") Add a jar file to the environment environment(SettingsEnv("name", "profile")), amie.import(SettingsEnv(...)) Select the script environment (must be written literally) internalEnv() Print what the environment contains implementation(BuildSettings(...)) Evaluates Gradle build settings in the background coroutineTemplate("name", input = listOf(...)) Starts a saved template in the background and the script goes on; the run it returns answers to .send(text), .receive(), .closeInput(), .await(), .cancel() and .state. See Templates in the background input(), output("text") The next line of input, waiting for one, null once input is closed; and an answer for receive(). In a template the line comes from .send; in main.kts it is typed in the console, or read from standard input in an exported bundle, and output logs templateRuns.print(), templateRuns.cancelAll() What runs in the background, and cancelling all of it

docs.title: Models from outside
docs.text:
initMod("<name>") opens the folder AMP/models/imported/<name>, and initMod("/path/to/model") or importModel("/path/to/model") a model file or folder anywhere. The kinds initMod knew before come first: an intent model, a text model or a speech model of that name is opened as ever, then an imported name, then a path.

Format Files Runs on ONNX *.onnx, also a repo's onnx/model.onnx The ONNX Runtime the app ships TorchScript *.pt, *.pth, *.torchscript saved with torch.jit.trace or torch.jit.script PyTorch 2.5.1 through DJL 0.31 TensorFlow A SavedModel folder: saved_model.pb and variables/ TensorFlow 2.16.1 through DJL 0.31, in the lightweight build TFLite *.tflite Refused: DJL dropped TFLite after 0.27. Convert it with python -m tf2onnx.convert --tflite model.tflite --output model.onnx

Refused with what would work: a frozen TensorFlow graph (any .pb but saved_model.pb), PyTorch weights saved with torch.save (a .pt or .pth with no code in it), and weights alone: *.safetensors, pytorch_model.bin, *.gguf, *.h5, *.keras. No engine runs those without the model's Python code, so export the model to ONNX (optimum-cli export onnx --model <repo> <folder>) or TorchScript, or take the repo's onnx/ folder when it has one.

A folder with several formats opens its ONNX first, since it runs on the bundled runtime; otherwise the format its source.json names ("format": "onnx|torchscript|tensorflow|tflite", which a Hugging Face import writes); otherwise the first that runs on this machine. Whenever there was a choice, the console says which was taken. Of several files of one format, model.onnx comes before onnx/model.onnx, and a full model before a quantized or fp16 one.

val bert = initMod("distilbert-sst2")                 // AMP/models/imported/distilbert-sst2, its onnx/model.onnx
log(bert.predict("what a lovely day"))                // POSITIVE, from its config.json id2label
log(bert.inputs)                                      // [input_ids int64 [-1, -1], attention_mask int64 [-1, -1]]

val resnet = importModel("~/models/resnet18.pt")      // TorchScript on PyTorch, which declares no shapes: give one
val image = Tensor.of(FloatArray(3 * 224 * 224), 1, 3, 224, 224)
log(resnet?.run(mapOf("image" to image))?.values?.first())   // output0 float32 [1, 1000]: …

val tf = initMod("/models/classifier/saved_model")    // a SavedModel folder, lightweight build
log(tf.run(mapOf("input_1" to floatArrayOf(0.1f, 0.2f, 0.3f, 0.4f))))
  • Text goes in when a tokenizer.json is next to the model or in a folder above it, up to the imported folder: the token ids, the attention mask and the token type ids fill the inputs of those names (a TorchScript model, which names none, gets the ids and the mask in that order). Without one, predict("0.1, 0.2, 0.3") reads the text as numbers. The labels come from config.json's id2label.
  • A language model (GPT-2, Llama, BERT for masks: logits [1, tokens, vocab], such as [1, 1, 50257], which is a score for every token of the vocabulary at every place, not a hidden state) answers in text. One that continues text (…LMHeadModel, …ForCausalLM in its config.json) goes on greedily, a run a token, up to 24 tokens or its end token: answer(text) and predict(text) are that text, the rest of run(text) its 5 likeliest next tokens as token:probability (scores(text)). One that fills a mask (…ForMaskedLM) gives the likeliest tokens at [MASK]. An export that wants its key and value cache (past_key_values inputs) gives its first token only
  • Tensors: .inputs and .outputs are each tensor's name, shape (-1 for a size left open) and type. TensorFlow and ONNX say them as soon as the model is open, TorchScript after its first run. .run(floatArrayOf(…)) and .run(longArrayOf(…)) feed the one input, in its shape with a batch of one (one row when the model says no shape); .run(mapOf("name" to values)) feeds each by name, a value being an array or Tensor.of(values, 2, 3) for a shape of your own. TorchScript takes its inputs in the map's order, whatever their names. Every output comes back by name as a Tensor: .shape, .type, .floats(), .longs().
  • Natives: PyTorch's and TensorFlow's native libraries are downloaded from publish.djl.ai into ~/.djl.ai (DJL_CACHE_DIR moves it) the first time a model of theirs is opened on a machine, which the console says once with the size: PyTorch about 40 MB on an Apple Silicon Mac, 65 MB on a Raspberry Pi 5, 110 MB on Linux x86-64; TensorFlow 130 to 150 MB. The CPU build is taken unless PYTORCH_FLAVOR says otherwise. Offline, the first open fails saying what it wanted; after that they are read from the cache. DJL's telemetry is turned off as it is for the tokenizers.
  • Where each runs: PyTorch on macOS arm64, Linux arm64 and x86-64 and Windows x86-64, not on an Intel Mac. TensorFlow everywhere, but only in the lightweight build (-Pamie.lightweight=true, the default on an Apple Silicon Mac and arm64 Linux): the full build carries TensorFlow 1.15 for KotlinDL, whose classes clash with TensorFlow 2's. A model that can't run on the machine or in the build is refused naming what is missing.
  • Lifetime: every call opens a new model. It is held like importModelOnnx's: closed with the ortClosable block around the call, kept by a static, timed or limited one, listed on the Sessions tab (an Imported model row for PyTorch and TensorFlow, an ONNX session row for ONNX) with Terminate, and .close() gives its natives back once the runs in flight are done. importModelTensorflow(path) is importModel under its old name.

docs.title: Encoder and decoder pairs
docs.text:
A sequence-to-sequence export (T5, BART, Marian translation, Whisper) is two ONNX files in one folder, encoder_model.onnx with decoder_model.onnx and often decoder_with_past_model.onnx. Neither answers a text alone: the encoder turns the input into hidden states, the decoder takes those with the ids written so far and gives the next token's scores, one step at a time. amie hf import offers every encoder and decoder of the folder at the terminal, picked with the arrow keys, the default marked (the full variant, the merged decoder left out when the plain and the with-past ones are there): space takes or leaves the file under the cursor (the quantized ones, say), Enter imports, n leaves; --take "2 6 8" picks for a pipe. huggingFace("…") in a script takes the marked files. initMod("<name>") then opens both sessions, and a script wires them. .inference(text), .predict and .answer refuse on a pair, saying how.

Member What it is Comes from m.encoder The encoder session, run with tensors: .inputs, .outputs, .run(mapOf(…)) encoder_model.onnx m.decoder The decoder session, the same way decoder_model.onnx m.decoderWithPast The decoder that takes the past attention state back, or null when the export has none decoder_with_past_model.onnx m.tokens(text) The token ids and the attention mask of a text, as .ids and .mask tokenizer.json beside the models m.text(ids) The words of a list of ids The same tokenizer m.startToken The id the decoder starts from, or null when no config names one decoder_start_token_id, else bos_token_id, of generation_config.json, then config.json m.endToken The id that ends the decoding, or null eos_token_id of the same files m.encode(text), m.encode(file) The encoder run: a text through the tokenizer, or an audio or image file through the preprocessor; .hidden the states, .mask the text's mask tokenizer.json, or preprocessor_config.json m.decoderFeeds(encoded, ids) The decoder's inputs for one step: the ids so far, the hidden states, and the encoder's mask when the decoder names one m.decoder.inputs m.startTokens(encoded?, vararg tokens) The ids the decoder starts from: the start id and the forced ones after it, each replaceable by a name the config knows: a language ("de"), a task ("translate", "transcribe"), "timestamps" or "notimestamps". A language left open and not named is detected from the encoding, else English forced_decoder_ids, lang_to_id, task_to_id, no_timestamps_token_id of the config files m.preprocessor The preprocessor_config.json as JSON: sampling rate, mel bins, image size, mean and std That file m.abilities encoder, decoder, and decoderWithPast, tokens, startToken when the folder has them; text, audio or image for what the encoder takes The folder m.getStatus() Each session's status, by name Both sessions m.close() Closes every session of the pair

What the encoder takes is read off the folder: a text pair has no preprocessor_config.json and takes text through its tokenizer; one whose file names a feature extractor (Whisper) takes an audio file, wav or aiff at any rate, turned into the log-mel spectrogram that file describes (80 bins, 16 kHz, 30 seconds, padded with silence or cut); one naming an image processor (TrOCR, Donut, Nougat) takes an image file, resized to size, rescaled and normalized by image_mean and image_std. encode does whichever applies, and decoderFeeds fills the decoder's inputs by their names, Marian's encoder_attention_mask among them. The same greedy loop then translates or transcribes:

val m = initMod("t5-small")                                   // or "whisper-tiny", with a wav in place of the text
val e = m.encode("translate English to German: The house is wonderful.")
val starts = m.startTokens(e)                                 // Whisper: start, language (detected, or startTokens(e, "de")), transcribe, no timestamps
val ids = starts.toMutableList()
for (i in 1..40) {
    val logits = m.decoder.run(m.decoderFeeds(e, ids.toLongArray())).getValue("logits")   // [1, ids so far, vocabulary]
    val vocab = logits.shape.last().toInt()
    val last = logits.floats().takeLast(vocab)                 // the scores at the last place
    val best = last.indices.maxBy { last[it] }
    if (best.toLong() == m.endToken) break
    ids.add(best.toLong())
}
log(m.text(ids.drop(starts.size).toLongArray()))              // Das Haus ist wunderbar.
m.close()

Under encode, the sessions are still there for a script that wants them raw: m.tokens(text) and m.encoder.run(mapOf("input_ids" to t.ids, "attention_mask" to t.mask)) are what encode(text) does, and m.encoder.inputs names what a file becomes (input_ids, input_features, pixel_values).

Running the whole id list each step is simple, not fast. A faster loop runs m.decoder once, then m.decoderWithPast with each step's present.* outputs fed back as its past_key_values.* inputs, which its .inputs name.

docs.title: Reading a prediction
docs.text:
Every model session, whatever opened it (initMod("name"), importModelOnnx(...), group("name")), answers through the same three calls on top of inference. A package (initMod("x.jar")) has no labels and refuses them: call it with run(text) / answer(text) instead. A sessionMod("name") answers through the same calls.

Call Returns Example predict("text") The predicted label: the best answer of inference without its score (the argmax of a classifier). Throws when the model answers nothing "lights" scores("text") Every label with its score, best first, as a Map<String, Float>. Answers without a score are left out {lights=0.67, weather=0.50, greeting=0.33} predictions("text") The raw answers parsed into Prediction(label, score), in the model's order; score is null when the answer had none [lights:0.67, weather:0.50, …] inference("text") The raw lines a model answers: label:score for a classifier, one tag per token for the NER model, whatever run(text) returned for a package ["lights:0.67", "weather:0.50", …] run("text") The same raw answers, the name to use for a package ["lights:0.67", "weather:0.50", …] answer("text") The first raw answer as it came, scores and all; null when there was none "lights:0.67" 
val m = initMod("intents")
log(m.predict("turn the lights on"))                        // lights
val scores = m.scores("turn the lights on")                 // {lights=0.97, weather=0.02, greeting=0.01}
log("confidence ${scores.values.first()}")                  // 0.97
if (scores.values.first() < 0.5f) log("not sure", LogLevel.ERROR)
m.predictions("turn the lights on").forEach { p -> log("${p.label} ${p.score}") }

Each call is logged as a Data line in the console in the shape it was asked: predict logs the text and the one label with its score (intents "turn the lights on" -> lights 0.970), scores and inference the text and every label with its score. Each of the three calls runs the model once, so ask once and keep the result instead of calling predict and scores on the same text. A package (initMod("x.jar")) has no labels: predict, scores and predictions throw on it, so ask it with run or answer.

docs.title: Building a model
docs.text:
val train = source("intents.csv")          // columns: text,label
relate(train, "intents-test.csv")          // optional test file
val model = modelBuilder("intents", train)
model.modelStatus()                        // the stored validation table
model.modelChart()                         // bars, build history and confusion matrix

val m = initMod("intents")
log(m.predict("turn the lights on"))                 // lights
log(m.scores("turn the lights on").toString())       // {lights=0.97, weather=0.02, greeting=0.01}
m.close()

intents.csv stands for your own file. source() finds it as given, relative to the folder amie was started in, then in AMP/, then in AMP/pluginDir/; an absolute path is taken as it is. A new AMP folder has sample-intents.csv (45 rows) to try, and a name that is not found is reported with the folders looked in and the csv files of AMP whose names come closest.

The charts are described with examples in Models and metrics.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
A package is a jar with one public class that fulfils the backend's AmiePackage interface: a public no-arg constructor, run(input: String): List<String> and close(), both required. That is the contract the website checks on upload and the samging/jar-jar workflow checks on every jar; implementing the interface is the easiest way to get there, and any class with the same methods qualifies. amie's own loader is more lenient (any non-void run, close() optional), so such a jar opens locally but cannot be uploaded. The amie guide has the whole contract with an example. Packages are bottles: every initMod("name.jar") makes a fresh instance in its own class loader, so two sessions on the same jar never share state, and close() releases that instance and its loader. The jar is looked up in the active env, then AMP/pluginDir, then as a path; when it is nowhere local it is fetched from the GitHub repositories of AMP/github.json (below) and stored in AMP/pluginDir, so the next open is local. The Amie server (the website's /api/jar-download, else the S3 service's /api/aws/jars/<name>) is off, like accounts and Keycloak, until AMIE_ACCOUNTS=1 turns them on. Next to it, AMP/pluginDir/<name>.source.json records where it came from: the exact download URL, the website page that lists and describes it (<site>/downloads), version, size, publish date and fetch time. getStatus() of a package session carries the url and page, and the Models page shows them behind the i toggle of the package.

val echo = initMod("echo-1.0.jar")        // fetched from GitHub when it is not local
echo.run("hello there").forEach { log(it) }   // every answer of its run(text); echo.answer(...) the first
log(echo.getStatus().toString())          // jar, class, source, runs
echo.close()

packages.available().forEach { log("${it.name} ${it.size}") }   // what the repositories list
packages.print()                                                   // open package sessions

docs.title: Jars from GitHub
docs.text:
A jar can come from a GitHub repository. initMod("github:owner/repo/x.jar") takes it from that repository's default branch; github:owner/repo/libs/x.jar@v1.2 names a folder and a branch, tag or commit, and a github.com file address (https://github.com/owner/repo/blob/main/x.jar) works too. A name that is not a file of the repository is looked for among the assets of its latest release (or of the release tagged with the ref). A plain initMod("x.jar") that is nowhere local is looked for in the repositories listed in AMP/github.json ({"repos": ["samging/jar-jar"], "token": null}, written on first use).

packages.github()                                       // the jars of the repositories in AMP/github.json
packages.github("samging/jar-jar")                      // one repository's
val tr = initMod("github:samging/jar-jar/google-translate.jar")
log(tr.answer("to de: good morning"))                   // Guten Morgen
packages.check("google-translate.jar")                  // package class com.amie.translate.GoogleTranslate (run(String) and close() by shape)

Every downloaded jar is checked before it is kept (from GitHub, and from the Amie server when accounts are on): it must read as a jar, its classes must load on this app's Java, its metadata's java must hold, and a class must satisfy the package contract (public, a no-arg constructor, run(String) returning the answer, close(); implementing AmiePackage is the easiest way), and when the metadata names the entry class, that class must be it. The check loads classes without initializing them, so no code of the jar runs. A jar that fails is not kept (a copy already in AMP/pluginDir stays) and the reason is the error. The check is about the contract, not about trust: only open jars from repositories you trust.

A jar from GitHub lands in AMP/pluginDir with its origin beside it (repo, sha, page). A github: open asks GitHub for the file's current version and downloads it only when it changed; when GitHub cannot be reached, the copy already there is used. A jar of the same name that came from elsewhere is replaced only when its bytes are the repository's (same git blob sha); otherwise the open fails and says so. Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests an hour; token in AMP/github.json or GITHUB_TOKEN raises that and opens private repositories. Without a token a private repository answers as if it were empty, so its jars are reported as not found. On the Models page the repositories' jars are listed under On GitHub, with Fetch from GitHub in their menu.

A jar reaches samging/jar-jar through a pull request that adds it at the top of the repository. The repository's Check jars workflow checks every jar the way amie checks a download, with the same rules as above and without running any code of the jar. A second step then opens each jar as packages.test does: it calls run() with every declared test and then close(), each jar in a JVM of its own. A class without List<String> run(String) and close() fails; missing metadata is a note. Once merged, a plain initMod("x.jar") finds it; a machine that already has an older copy in AMP/pluginDir takes the new one through a github: open. The amie guide has the steps.

The package class is the one the jar's metadata names (below) when it satisfies the contract, else the manifest's Main-Class when it does, else a class implementing an interface named AmiePackage, else the first class in the jar that does. run executes on amie's amie-package-call thread with the jar's class loader as context loader while the caller waits; stopping the script interrupts that thread. What it returns is shown one line per element. Open package sessions also appear under Sessions on the Models page.

docs.title: What a jar needs: metadata, configuration and test runs
docs.text:
A jar can say what it requires in META-INF/amie/package.json (or amie-package.json at its root). For a jar that ships none, AMP/pluginDir/<jar>.package.json beside it says the same (⋯ > Write metadata template on the Models page writes one to fill in); when both exist, the sidecar's fields override the jar's. The shape:

{
  "name": "weather", "version": "1.2", "description": "answers with the forecast for a place",
  "java": 21,
  "entry": "com.example.Weather",
  "config": [
    {"file": "weather.properties", "required": true, "description": "the API key", "template": "apiKey=\n"}
  ],
  "env": [{"name": "WEATHER_PROXY", "required": false, "description": "an HTTP proxy, if one is needed"}],
  "tests": [
    {"name": "a known place", "input": "Paris", "contains": "Paris"},
    {"name": "answers in one line", "input": "Berlin", "lines": 1},
    {"name": "exact", "input": "ping", "expect": "pong"}
  ],
  "notes": "free text for whoever runs it",
  "flags": [{"text": "stable", "color": "green"}, {"text": "v2 api", "color": "blue"}]
}

flags are coloured tags the Models page shows on the jar's row and panel beside its version, Java, language and test flags; the colour is one of slate, green, amber, red, violet, blue. Flags added on the page go to the sidecar and add to the jar's own.

The runtime reads it before the jar is opened (pluginEngine/PackageMeta.kt, JarPackages.open):

  • Configuration lives in AMP/pluginDir/config/<jar without .jar>/. The folder is made on the first open, and every declared config file that is missing is written from its template, so the person finds a file to fill in instead of a stack trace. The package finds the folder three ways: it is the first root of the jar's class loader, so getClass().getClassLoader().getResource("weather.properties") (or getResourceAsStream) resolves there, ahead of a default copy inside the jar; the system properties amie.package.config (the folder) and amie.package.name (the jar) are set while it is opened, with amie.package.config.<jar> kept for the jar; and a public configure(File), configure(Path), configure(String) or configure(Map<String, String>) method of the package class, when it has one, is called with the folder right after the constructor (the map holds dir and each file in the folder by name). importPlugin("x.jar") loads a jar the same way, but it isn't refused as below. amie packages setup <x.jar> asks for each key at the terminal, and amie packages config <x.jar> key=value sets one, so the files need no editor. In a script, packages.config("x.jar") reads the keys and packages.setConfig("x.jar", "key" to "value") sets them; at the prompt, :config and :setup do the same.
  • initMod refuses a jar that lacks what it says it needs, before any instance is made: a required config file that is missing, a required one that still equals its template (the template is for the person to fill in, so mark a config whose template works as it stands "required": false), or a required env variable that is not set. The message names every problem and the config folder, and the template is written first, so there is something to fill in. A jar that declares nothing runs as before.
  • java is checked against the Java this app runs: a jar that needs a newer one is refused with the reason.
  • entry picks the package class when the jar has more than one candidate.
  • tests are the jar's own test runs: packages.test("x.jar") in a script, or Test run on the Models page, opens a fresh session as initMod would (configuration included), sends each input through run, checks the answer against expect (the whole answer), contains (some line) and lines (how many), closes the session, prints the report and keeps it as AMP/pluginDir/<jar>.tests.json. A test with none of the three passes when run does not throw. With no tests declared the run is one call with "hello" that must answer.
packages.meta("weather.jar")?.let { log("needs Java ${it.java}, files ${it.config.map { c -> c.file }}") }
val report = packages.test("weather.jar")          // the console gets one line per test
log(if (report.ok) "all ${report.passed} passed" else "${report.failed} failed")

The Models page shows all of it on the jar's panel: Requirements (Java, package class, metadata, config folder, every config file and variable, the last test run, each marked met or not, with the verdict initMod gives), Config (the folder with Reveal folder, the files and their state) and Tests (what is declared, and the last run's answers).

docs.title: Session logs
docs.text:
(How to work with sessions day to day, keep them warm between runs and close them is in Running sessions.)

Every session of a model or a package keeps a log of what it was asked and answered: an open line, one run line per inference call with the text, the first answers and the time it took, an error line when the call threw, and a close line with the number of runs. The Models page shows it behind Log on the session, and the same lines are appended to AMP/models/intents/<name>/sessions.log for a model and AMP/pluginDir/<jar>.sessions.log for a package (runtime/SessionLog.kt), so a terminated session's history stays readable:

2026-10-14T17:40:02.118Z dummy #3 open  opened as session #3
2026-10-14T17:40:05.402Z dummy #3 run   "turn the lights on" -> lights:0.61, weather:0.22, greeting:0.17 (14 ms)
2026-10-14T17:41:10.009Z dummy #3 close closed after 1 runs

docs.title: Building a package
docs.text:
The Packages tab of the Models page reads a jar's classes and resources, the Java it needs (from the class file version) and what built it (the manifest), so a jar can be checked before a script opens it. The shape of a build that produces one:

plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.1.0" }
repositories { mavenCentral() }
kotlin { jvmToolchain(17) }
tasks.jar {
    archiveFileName = "echo-1.0.jar"
    manifest { attributes("Main-Class" to "org.example.Echo") }
}

package org.example

class Echo {
    fun run(text: String): List<String> = listOf("echo: $text")
    fun close() {}
}

The app runs on Java 21, so a jar compiled for Java 21 or older loads; the page says so next to the class file version.

Accepted data shapes: a DataSource from source, List<Pair<text, label>>, Map<label, List<text>>, or rows of [text, ..., label].

docs.title: What modelBuilder does
docs.text:
buildClassifier in jetbrainDLBuilder/JetBuilder.kt:

  1. checking data: the preprocessor (jetbrainDLBuilder/Preprocessor.kt) cleans the rows, unifies label spellings, drops empty, junk, repeated and conflicting rows with a reason each, measures the set and refuses one a classifier cannot come out of; every line goes to the console and metrics.json. The reasons are listed in Models and metrics.
  2. embedding: every text goes through the BERT encoder once; the hidden states are mean-pooled into one vector each. A text embedded before comes from AMP/cache/embeddings (EmbeddingCache.kt).
  3. training: every candidate head (Architecture.kt; by default linear, dense[16], dense[32], dense[64, 16], or what buildOptions names) is trained with Adam on plain Kotlin arrays (DenseNet.kt, any number of hidden layers, relu or tanh; weight decay, dropout, label smoothing, rate schedules and early stopping when a head asks for them) on the same rows, scored on the same validation rows, and the best by macro F1 (or accuracy) is kept; with folds the heads are compared over the folds instead (TrainingKit.kt, Search.kt). The comparison and every head's learning curve are stored with the build.
  4. validating: the chosen head on the related test file, or on a stratified 20% split; precision, recall, F1 per label, then the calibration error and its gates, the rows it got wrong, and with calibrate a temperature folded into the last layer (Calibration.kt).
  5. exporting: the layers are written by hand as ONNX (opset 13) to AMP/models/intents/<name>/model.onnx with module.json (encoder, dims, labels, version) and metrics.json (one entry per build); the head it replaces is kept under versions/ (modules/ModelVersions.kt). fineTune (FineTune.kt) and calibrate (ModelCalibration.kt) end the same way.

docs.title: Build progress
docs.text:
ModelBuildProgress (jetbrainDLBuilder/BuildProgress.kt) is a StateFlow the builder updates at every phase and step: text n of N while embedding, epoch n of 150 while training, each validation sample, then export. Phases are weighted (embedding 60%, training 30%, ...) into one fraction that drives:

  • the console strip (running 12s · modelBuilder 'intents' training 72/150 · epoch 72 loss 0.3102 accuracy 0.912 · 48%, with a thin bar under it),
  • the build line at the top of the Models page's list, with its thin bar.

Every 25 epochs the loss and accuracy are also logged to the console. Finished builds (with their duration and outcome) stay in ModelBuildProgress.history; the console strip's tooltip names the last one while idle.

docs.title: Saved states
docs.text:
Not available yet: accounts, Keycloak and the Amie backend are off, so these calls print one Error line and do nothing until AMIE_ACCOUNTS=1 turns them on. Signed in then, a script can keep small JSON documents on the Amie backend, which stores them as uploads/<user>/state/<name>.json next to your packages (your devices live there as devices). The calls block like a package fetch and print one line each; a failure (a guest, an unreachable backend, a bad name) is one Error line and loadState then returns null. A name matches [A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}, a document is at most 1 MiB.

saveState("labels", """{"intents": ["greet", "bye"]}""")   // PUT /state/labels
listStates().forEach { log(it) }                                 // devices, labels, ...
val labels = loadState("labels")                                 // the JSON text, null when there is none

docs.title: Shell commands
docs.text:
A script can run commands and script files on the computer and use what they print.

val r = shell("ls -la ~/Documents | head")      // runs it, the console shows it as it runs, then returns
log("exit ${r.exit}, ${r.lines.size} lines")
if (r.ok) log(r.out) else error(r.err)

shell("du -sh .", dir = "~/Documents", timeoutSeconds = 60, env = mapOf("A" to "1"))
shellScript("~/bin/lookup.sh", listOf("arg one", "arg two"))

shell runs the command through your login shell ($SHELL -lc, so your PATH and tools work; /bin/sh -c when SHELL is not set and cmd /c on Windows). A login shell reads .zprofile or .profile, not .zshrc, so a tool set up only in .zshrc is not found. shellScript runs a file: directly when it is executable, through the shell otherwise. Its arguments go to it one by one and are never joined into a command line, so spaces and quotes arrive as they are. A relative path starts from dir.

On the result .ok The exit was 0 and it was neither timed out nor cancelled .exit Its exit code, -1 when it could not start .out, .err What it printed, without the line breaks at the end. As text the result is .out: "${shell("whoami")}" .lines .out as a list of lines .timedOut, .cancelled How it was stopped .command What ran, as the console showed it
  • A command that fails is not an exception. A non-zero exit gives ok = false and an error line with the exit code, so the script decides. A command that can't start, a missing script file and a missing dir are the same, with exit -1 and the reason in .err.
  • .patchBy { error -> ... } runs when the command failed, with what it said, and gives the result back. The function can send it anywhere: .patchBy(::log), a voice, llama.answer(error), a template, or .patchBy(::handleBy) for the local text model. A command stopped with its script doesn't count.
  • What a command printed on stderr, and why it failed, are the error terminal's lines too: errorLog() pulls the last ones and handleBy() hands them to the local text model, with main.kts and the env, as .patchBy(::handleBy) hands what the one command said the moment it fails.
  • A relative path for shellScript that isn't there is looked for under AMP/ and AMP/pluginDir, so shellScript("voice/weather.sh") finds a script of AMP and an export carries it.
  • Each command is printed to the console before it runs, and what it prints follows as it arrives, both at the internal level: turn Internal on in the console strip to see them, so a script that runs commands keeps the console for what it logs itself. stderr comes as error lines. A command that fails turns the error level on, as a failed run does, so its reason is in view. All of it also goes to AMP/logs.txt. None of this goes to the error log on the backend, unlike other error lines.
  • dir is where it runs; without it, your home folder, where a new terminal starts. ~/ works in dir and in a script's path.
  • timeoutSeconds is 120 unless given, and 0 means no limit. After it the command and everything it started are stopped and .timedOut is true. Interrupting the script's thread does the same, with .cancelled, and the thread stays interrupted. Commands still running when the app exits are stopped too. A command that puts something in the background and ends (server &) has ended, so what it left running stays, as from a terminal.
  • Standard input is closed, so a command waiting for input fails instead of hanging.
  • .out and .err keep the last 1 MB of each stream; past that the first line says how much was cut. The console shows the first 1000 lines of a command, each cut at 4 KB, and says how many it left out.

A script could already run any JVM code, so this adds convenience, not power. There is no confirmation and no list of allowed commands, and a template loaded from someone else runs its commands with your rights: read it before you press Run. Only script code reaches shell; no route of a served model does. Text that came from outside, such as what was sent to /teach, goes to shellScript as an argument, never into the command line of shell, where the shell would read it as a command.

docs.title: Templates in the background
docs.text:
A saved template (see Templates) can run beside the script that starts it, and the two can talk: coroutineTemplate starts it and the script goes on, the template reads with input() and answers with output(text). The two halves are starters in the Templates pane: Background templates: coroutineTemplate, the caller, which you load and Run, and Background template: a reader, the template it starts.

// Starts the saved template "Background template: a reader" beside this script and talks to it: send gives it a
// line for its input(), receive waits for what its output(...) answers. Meanwhile Models > Sessions lists the run
// under Scripts with what it holds, and the Templates pane's fold says it is running.
val job = coroutineTemplate("Background template: a reader")
job.send("turn the lights on")
log("the reader answered ${job.receive()}")
job.send("what is the weather")
log("the reader answered ${job.receive()}")
templateRuns.print()                                 // every run in the background, this one among them

// No more input is coming: the reader's input() turns null, its loop ends and the run ends with it.
job.closeInput()
log("the reader ended: ${job.await()}")              // finished, or failed: and the reason

// When the run ends it prints its own resources line, as a run of main.kts does: memory, cpu, sessions. The dummy
// session it opened stays open, as with any script; Models > Sessions shows it until it is closed or terminated.

// The template half of a pair. The starter "Background templates: coroutineTemplate" starts this one in the
// background, feeds it lines with send and reads its answers with receive. Run by itself it reads the console:
// each line typed there is one input(), and eof ends it.
val model = initMod("dummy")
while (true) {
    val text = input() ?: break          // waits for the caller's next line; null once its input is closed
    output(model.predict(text))          // the label goes to the caller's receive(), and to the console
}
log("input is closed, the reader ends")

coroutineTemplate("name", input = listOf("a", "b")) starts one with those lines already waiting for its input().

docs.title: A script that waits to be called
docs.text:
In main.kts input() waits for a line typed in the console, so a script can load nothing until it is asked. Give it a main entry point:

fun work() = ortClosable("work") {
    val model = initMod("dummy")
    log(model.predict("hello"))
}

fun main() {
    log("Type go in the console to start")
    while (true) {
        when (input()?.trim() ?: break) {
            "go" -> work()
            else -> log("go starts it")
        }
    }
}

main()

It works as a Run window does: while the script waits, every line typed is its input, and the console's commands wait until it reads no more. eof gives it the null of a closed input, and Stop ends it where it waits. A line typed while it isn't waiting isn't kept: it counts as a console command or, like log("hi"), as a line of script that runs in the background, and the console says when it is neither.

An exported bundle has no console, so there input() reads standard input: type at ./run.sh, or pipe lines in with echo go | ./run.sh. When standard input ends, input() is null. It works the same with --template.

Call What it does coroutineTemplate("name") Starts the template and returns at once. The name is matched in any case, or give its id; a name no template has is an error that lists the templates coroutineTemplate("name", input = listOf("a", "b")) The same, with those lines waiting for its input() job.send("text") Gives the template a line of input. It never waits: what is sent stays until the template reads it. False when the line can't reach it, input being closed or the run ended job.receive() The template's next output, waiting for it; null once it has ended and everything it said was read job.receive(5000) The same, waiting five seconds at most; null then too, and job.state tells the two apart job.closeInput() No more input is coming: the template's input() is null once it has read what was sent job.await() Waits for the end and returns how it ended job.cancel() Ends the run (below) job.state How it stands: running, finished, cancelled, or failed: and the reason. .running and .failed say so as true or false, .reason is the reason job.name, job.id, job.startedAt, job.endedAt Which run it is, and when it began and ended (endedAt is null while it runs) template("name") A template to call like a function: see Delegating to a template templateRuns.print() An internal line for each run and for the last three that ended (#3 Reader running 4s); the lines are returned too templateRuns.cancelAll() Cancels every run and returns how many there were

A template is an ordinary script with the whole API, and what it opens stays open as with any script. Its console lines start with its name, and output(text) logs the text as well as handing it over. Run in the foreground (loaded into the editor, say) input() returns null at once, with one line saying nothing feeds it, and output only logs, so a template can be tried with Run.

How long a run lives. A run of coroutineTemplate outlives a script that ends by itself, until it ends, is cancelled, or the app closes. Stop on the script ends it too, with whatever it started in turn. At most eight run at once, fewer on a small heap; a ninth is an error that says so. A start also needs the memory for it, or it is refused with what is short and what to close (The sandbox). The fold in the Templates pane and the Sessions tab of the Models page list them (The sandbox).

Output nobody reads. A run never waits at output. The newest 1024 answers are kept for receive(), and the console says it once when older ones are dropped, so a run started with Run in background neither stops nor fills the memory.

Cancelling. job.cancel(), Stop in the Templates pane and Terminate on the Sessions tab are the same, and each reaches what the run started, however deep, also through a run that has ended. A blocked input() or a sleep ends at once. A busy script ends at its next log, info, error, data, input or output, each of which throws CancellationException once the run is cancelled; until then the pane reads Stopping and the run still counts as one of the eight. A cancel during its compile takes effect when the compile ends: every compile in the app reads the classpath through one shared file system, and interrupting one breaks the compiles beside it, main.kts included.

When it fails. The run ends failed, and the script that started it goes on. The reason names the template's own file and line (failed: reader.kts:3: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom), and the console has a line for each problem. job.await() returns that state rather than throwing.

The env. A run stays in the env that is current when it starts, and changes nothing of it. A template with environment(SettingsEnv("other")), or with an implementation("...") this env doesn't have, is refused: coroutineTemplate throws an error that says what to do instead. Another env's class loader could be had, but the API a script calls looks up the current env (group(), jars), so the template would run half in one env and half in the other. A template that names no env runs in the current one, and an import that only happens as the template runs is an error line, the env left as it is.

Each run has an engine of its own, made for the run and dropped when it ends, so a run begins with a compile of a few hundred milliseconds. This is what lets main.kts wait in receive() while the template runs: an eval holds the lock of the engine state in its bindings to its end, so a template evaluated on the bindings of main.kts would wait for main.kts, and main.kts for it.

docs.title: Delegating to a template
docs.text:
template("name") gives you a saved template to call like a function, for when all you want from it is an answer:

// Delegation: a saved template called like a function. The first call starts "Background template: a reader", gives
// it the line and returns what its output(...) answers; the next calls go to the same run.
val reader by template("Background template: a reader")
log("the reader answered ${reader("turn the lights on")}")
log("the reader answered ${reader("what is the weather")}")
log("run #${reader.run.id} is ${reader.run.state}")      // reader.run is the run behind it

// A template that fails makes the call throw, with its name and its error, so a failure never passes for an answer.
// close ends its input and waits. A script that doesn't is closed for when it ends, and Stop ends the reader with it.
reader.close()
log("the reader ended: ${reader.run.state}")
Call What it does val reader by template("name") Nothing starts yet. val reader = template("name") is the same reader("text") The first call starts the template. Each call gives it the line and returns its next output(...), on the same run reader.close() No more input is coming, and it waits for the end reader.run The run behind it, a TemplateRun as coroutineTemplate returns; asking for it starts the template

When it fails. A template that failed makes the call throw, with its name and its error (Template 'reader' failed: reader.kts:3: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom). One that ended without answering, or was cancelled, throws as well, so the call never returns null. A start that was refused, for memory say, throws the reason, and the next call tries again.

When the script ends. A script that ends, however it ends, has its template values closed for it: their input closes, and a run still going ten seconds later is cancelled. A template's own template values are closed when it ends in the same way. coroutineTemplate is the one that carries on.

Nesting. A template can start templates. One that would start itself, directly or through another, is refused with a line naming the way round (Not started: template 'a' would be calling itself: a > b > a), and they nest four deep at most. Stop on a script cancels everything below it.

docs.title: Serving a model
docs.text:
Open the Models page, expand a model, set host, port, path and methods, save, and switch Listen for incoming data on. Then:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict -d '{"text":"turn the lights on"}'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict?text=turn+the+lights+on'

Every request is appended to AMP/models/intents/<name>/incoming.jsonl and counted on the Models page. Models that were listening when the app closed start again on the next launch.

docs.title: The sandbox
docs.text:
The sandbox is the screen the app opens on, laid out as a JetBrains IDE: a rail of icons at the far left, the Kotlin script editor in the middle, and tool windows round it. It uses the IDE's fonts (JetBrains Mono for code, Inter for everything else) and its dark colours, and the Kotlin colours in the editor.

The rail holds the pages (Sandbox, Models, Settings) and the tool windows (Templates, ⌘1, and Console, ⌘4; Ctrl elsewhere). Each opens and closes on its own, and they stand side by side: nothing closes one to show the other, and a run leaves the templates open. A closed console keeps its output and the templates keep what was typed in them.

Docking. Templates start at the left and the console at the bottom. Drag a window's header to the left, right or bottom edge to move it there, a blue area shows where it lands, or right-click the header and choose a side. Two windows on one side share it. Drag the line at a dock's edge to size it. Sides and sizes are kept in AMP/settings.json.

The console starts hidden, since there is nothing to show, and opens by itself at the first line a run logs (one the level toggles let through). It holds what the script logs and nothing else: the run's own lines (Running pluginDir/main.kts, Finished in 0s and the Resources: line) are at the internal level, off at start, since the strip over the console can say the same; a script that logs nothing leaves the console closed. It can be hidden at any time, output or not; it stays hidden for the rest of that run, and the first line of the next run (which empties it first) brings it back.
