It has three tabs: Console with the output and a line for commands, Recent runs, and Still open. The Console tab starts with two muted lines, as Python's interpreter greets: Amie pilot 1.0.0 (default, Nov 06 2026, 02:23:55) [Kotlin 2.1.0, JDK 21.0.11] on darwin, then what to type there; the >>> prompt follows on the line after the output, as in a terminal: the console reads from the top down, the prompt going down with each line until the pane is full, and the pane scrolls from there. A click under the prompt puts the cursor in it, and typing while scrolled up goes back down to it. The prompt shows no words, only a block cursor that blinks while it has the keyboard (an outline while it hasn't); what it is for is in the tooltip of >>>, and Enter sends the line. The two greeting lines are no log line, so Clear and a run leave them. The run's status and figures in the strips are Run details on the Settings page, off by default: off, the strip over the console has only its level toggles, Find, Details and Clear, and the steps under Running that name the status are what it shows when on. With the console hidden the run's status (running 12s, Finished in 41s, Failed after 3s with the error in its tooltip, and the last modelBuilder build's phase and time) moves up into the bar over the editor. Before the first run there is no status at all, unless a build has ended, whose outcome stands in its place; the other controls keep their places either way.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
Indentation is drawn: a thin vertical line stands at every four leading spaces, so the lines of a block are joined down its left edge, across its empty lines too; the guide of the block the caret is in is lit. The editor keeps the indentation for you: Enter starts the new line at the current line's depth, one level deeper after {, ( or [, and between { and } it puts the closing brace on its own line below the caret. Enter also re-indents the whole script as it goes: every line to its depth in braces and parentheses, continuing lines (.map, ?.let, ?:, &&, ||) one level in, the inside of strings and comments left alone, and the caret on the new line at its depth. re-indent on Enter in Settings (Editor) turns that off; Enter then only starts the line. ⌘⇧F (Ctrl+Shift+F elsewhere) re-indents the whole script at any time, the caret staying where it was in its line. Tab inserts four spaces, or indents every line of a selection; Shift+Tab moves them back.

  • There is one script and it is always AMP/pluginDir/main.kts, named at the left of the window's top bar, which is the sandbox's toolbar; it is saved as you type, so nothing says it was. The right end reads as IntelliJ's run toolbar, every button flat and of one size. First the env, where the IDE has its run configuration: a small box, the env the script is sourced in and a chevron (default unless the text says environment(SettingsEnv("name"))); choosing another from its list writes that line into the script (or rewrites the one there, keeping its profile) so the choice is in the text. Then Run, an outlined green triangle (an outlined red square while the script runs, which stops it); and export, an outlined arrow out of a tray: the script as a folder that runs with plain java, ⌘E, Ctrl+E elsewhere; it opens the Templates window on the export, see Exporting a script.
  • The file is saved as you type (a third of a second after the last keystroke). You can edit AMP/pluginDir/main.kts with anything else too; the editor loads it at start.
  • Highlighting in a calm palette: keywords a steel blue, strings sand, numbers gray-blue, comments gray, and the sandbox API functions (source, modelBuilder, metricsChart, …) in the one accent, a muted teal, so you can see at a glance what talks to the app. The editor reads the strings and comments itself, so a // or a # inside a string (source("https://…")), an apostrophe ("don't"), an escaped quote, a ${…} template or a raw """…""" string ends where it ends in Kotlin, and the lines after it keep their own colours.
  • Current line: the line the caret is on sits in a faint box that runs across the gutter and the text, and its number in the gutter is bright. Every number in the gutter stands on the baseline of its line.
  • Long lines don't wrap: the editor scrolls sideways, as wide as its longest line, and is as wide as its pane again once that line is gone or the pane is wider. The text keeps its margin from the gutter and from the top edge when the editor takes the keyboard, however long the script or its lines: the first letter of every line and the first line stay in sight.
  • Folding: every fun, class, object or interface whose line ends with { has a small arrow in the gutter. Click it, or press ⌘- (Ctrl+- elsewhere) with the caret anywhere in the block, and the block folds down to its first line: fun greet(name: String) { … }. Click the arrow or the …, or press ⌘= (Ctrl+=), to open it again; with Shift the two shortcuts fold or open every block. Typing into a folded block, or moving the caret into it, opens it, so nothing ever happens out of sight. Folding changes nothing in the file: saving and Run always see the whole script, and a fold stays in place while you edit other lines.
  • Completion dropdown: start typing a name and a list of matching API functions opens under the caret with the signature and a one-line description. Up / Down move, Enter or Tab insert the call and put the caret between the parentheses, Esc closes it, Ctrl+Space opens it on demand. A function that needs a block goes in with its braces (sessionMod("") { }, modelBuilder("") { }), the caret in the name, or in the braces when the block is all it needs. After m. for an m that sessionMod or initMod gave, the list is what that model can be asked (predict, scores, and version, labels on a sessionMod); inside a sessionMod("name") { } block, also in a lambda in it, those come first.
  • Marks as you type: a moment after you stop typing (a third of a second), the editor checks the calls to the script API, without running or compiling anything. A mistake gets a red wavy line, and its line number a red dot; rest the pointer on either and a short message says what is wrong. It marks a call with too few arguments (ortLimited("x") { }: ortLimited needs max) or too many, a named argument the function hasn't (log("x", levle = …): log has no parameter levle. Did you mean level?), a literal of the wrong type (initMod(12): initMod takes a String, not a number; learningRate = 1: write 1.0, not 1), and a member that amie, or a model taken with val m = initMod(…) or sessionMod(…), doesn't have (amie.lgo(…)). A call that fits any of a function's overloads is right, and a block after the call counts as its last argument. Only what is certain is marked: a variable or an expression passed is never judged, nothing inside a string or a comment is looked at, and a name the script declares or imports itself is left alone, as is a call inside a block whose receiver may have a function of that name (apply, with, a class with a supertype). The marks follow your edits until the next check; one you type into goes until then.
  • The API is available without a prefix. log("hi"), source("x.csv") and modelBuilder("name", data) are the same as amie.log(...), amie.source(...) and amie.modelBuilder(...); both spellings work in the same script. Only amie.import has distinct names without the prefix: implementation("group:module:version") (or dependency(...)) for a package and environment(SettingsEnv("name", "profile")) for an environment, because import(...) without amie. reads as a Kotlin import statement. Tab in the editor inserts four spaces.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
The bookmark on the rail (⌘1) opens the Templates window, which says how many templates run in the background, if any. Keep as a template folds the save form away so the list comes first. New template at the top, or the + beside the main.kts tab over the editor, which opens the window too, starts a new script: the editor is emptied (what it held is kept under Previous scripts, as a load keeps it) and the save form opens with the cursor in Name; write the script, then Save. A second Load within a second of another is ignored: a double click, or a click on the row the first load moved under the pointer, would put back the script just replaced. Saving the script already in the editor is Keep as a template itself. Closing the window keeps what it held, a half-typed name included. It is where scripts are kept to start from again, in AMP/templates/ (<id>.kts the code, <id>.json what is known of it):

  • Save keeps the script in the editor under a Name (the form says so when that script is already a template's, unchanged, since saving it would only make a copy), with an About line and Tags (commas between them; tags are kept in lower case, each once). The metadata kept with it: where it came from (main.kts, a previous script, or starter), its line count, the env it sources itself in, what it opens (model x, group x, package x.jar, read from its initMod/sessionMod/group calls, comments aside), when it was made and saved, and how often and when last it was loaded. A name already kept is Replaced: the same template, made again, its creation time and loads kept.
  • Templates lists them, the last saved first, one line each: the name, then Load, Run in background and ⋯ as icons. The name's tooltip has its about line, its tags and those facts. Load (the open-file icon) puts one in the editor, ready for Run; the script that was there is kept under AMP/pluginDir/backup/ first. Run in background, the play icon, runs it beside what you are doing, the editor staying as it is (below). Its ⋯ has Load, Export… (Exporting a script) and Delete… (then the red Delete). A search field filters by name, tag, about or what it opens once there are more than six. A load says nothing in the console, the editor shows it; only a script that could not be kept says so. Its files are written off the window's thread.
  • Previous scripts are those backups, the newest twenty first: Load brings one back (what was in the editor is kept in turn) and Keep as template fills the save form with it under the name Script of <time>, to rename and save; Not this one goes back to saving the editor's script.

The first time the pane's folder is made it is seeded: every starter script (log at every level, ask the dummy model, a confidence gate; train a model from a csv, train with your own heads, fine-tune it on a new label, search heads cross-validated, which texts to label next, read a model's metrics, named entities, embeddings, a group of models asked together, a model to ask and nothing more, sessionMod as a block; Postgres; serve a model and call it; the sessions that are open, the scope functions, what a script uses, a template in the background and the reader it talks to, templates you call like functions, what to do when something goes wrong), tagged starter and its group, and the script main.kts held then, as My script. That happens once (AMP/templates/.seeded says so). A starter the app gains later comes once to a folder seeded before it (.seeded-level says how far it got), unless a template already has its name; a starter deleted stays deleted. A starter that gained a new title comes the same way: the template under its old title is renamed and brought up to date, keeping its id, times and loads, as long as it is still the starter (never saved over); one you saved over is yours and is left alone, and the starter comes beside it under its new title. None of the starters needs an account or a server; the longer versions, with the explanations, are in the Cookbook.

docs.title: Cloud save
docs.text:
Saving here is always the first thing that happens, and it works the same logged in, logged out and with the server down. Under the save form the pane says what the cloud does with it:

  • Logged out it says Saved here only and offers Log in to save to the cloud. That opens the log in page (or Create account) and comes back to the sandbox with the pane as you left it. Nothing is sent anywhere while you are logged out.
  • Logged in it says Logged in as …, and after each save one of three plain lines: Saved here. Saving to the cloud…, Saved here and to the cloud., or Saved here. Not saved to the cloud: followed by why (the server can't be reached, the login was not accepted, the cloud takes 20 saves a minute, a file is too large). A failed send loses nothing and blocks nothing: the file stays saved here and goes up on your next save, or at your next login.

What goes up is exactly your templates (AMP/templates/<id>.kts and <id>.json), AMP/settings.json and AMP/pluginDir/main.kts, the same allowlist as the backup. session.json, keycloak.json, databases.json, github.json, tokens, models and logs are never sent, nor is anything else in AMP. Saves are gathered for two seconds and sent from a background coroutine, so typing in the editor is never waiting for the network. The starter templates the app ships are the same on every Mac and are not sent until you save over them.

At login (and when the app starts with you still logged in) what your account has and this Mac doesn't comes down: templates and main.kts are written, settings.json applies at once, and a main.kts already open in the editor is replaced by the one from the account. Each file is compared with the version both sides had at the last sync (AMP/cloud-sync.json, hashes only, kept here):

  • only the account changed it: it comes down in place, and the script it replaces is kept under AMP/pluginDir/backup;
  • only this Mac changed it: it goes up;
  • both changed it, or this Mac never synced it and the two differ: both are kept. The newer stays in place, the other is saved as <name>-cloud-<time>.<ext> or <name>-this-mac-<time>.<ext> under AMP/pluginDir/backup, where a script shows among Previous scripts and Keep as template turns it back into a template. The pane's line names the file. Nothing is overwritten without a copy.

Deleting a template here does not delete it in the cloud, and it does not come back at the next login. AMIE_CLOUD_SAVE=off turns cloud save off for a run. The cloud's side is described in Amie backend.

The editor's text size is in Settings (Editor), and ⌥⌘+ / ⌥⌘− / ⌘0 (Ctrl+Alt and Ctrl elsewhere) inside the editor make it a point larger, smaller, or the default 14pt. ⌘+ and ⌘− without ⌥ fold and unfold (see the keyboard summary).

docs.title: Templates in the background
docs.text:
Several saved templates can run at once, beside the script in the editor. Run in background, the play icon on a template's row, starts it now, without input; the editor stays as it is and you can go on working. The pane's strip counts what runs (AMP/templates · 17 kept · 2 running). A script starts one with coroutineTemplate("name"), and can then give it input and read what it answers: the calls are in Templates in the background. Run is not involved: a run in the background doesn't dim it, and the strip's Running 12s stays that of main.kts. At most eight run at once, fewer on a small heap.

Before a template starts, memory is checked, whether the play icon, coroutineTemplate or template starts it:

  • The heap has to have 64 MB free, what a run's engine and a small script hold.
  • The machine has to have that free as well, plus the size of the encoder when the template opens a model and that encoder isn't loaded yet. An encoder loads outside the heap, so it counts against the RAM and not the heap.
  • Before refusing, the app collects the heap's garbage and asks the system what it could give back, so a figure that only looks short doesn't stop a run.

What falls short is refused with a console line and, on the pane, in red under the row:

Not started: 40.0 MB of heap free, a run needs 64.0 MB; stop a template or free a scope
Not started: 300.0 MB of RAM free, a run needs 464.0 MB with the encoder; close a session or another program

The check looks at the moment of the start, so several started within the same second don't see what each other is about to take.

While they run, a light watch keeps to it. It is a thread that exists only while a template runs in the background, and looks once a second at the free heap, a few calls on the runtime. When it has been under 32 MB (half of what a run needs to start) three readings in a row, the heap is collected and read once more, since garbage makes it look fuller than it is; if it is still short, the newest template is cancelled, with a console line in red that says which and why:

Reader: stopped, because only 24.0 MB of heap is free, under the 32.0 MB the templates in the background need to go on. It is the newest of 3; if memory stays short the next newest is stopped too

One at a time: the next waits until that one has ended and memory has stayed short again for three readings, so what a stopped run gives back is seen first. main.kts is never cancelled for this; while it runs it gets a warning line, once each time memory runs short (Memory is short: only 24.0 MB of heap is free ... main.kts is not stopped for it). A run that grows past the heap's limit outright is the JVM's to stop: its console line at the end says the peak.

Running in the background, the fold over TEMPLATES while there is a run to show, lists them: what runs first, the oldest on top, then the last three that ended. Each row has the template's name, how it stands (Running, Finished, Failed with the reason in its tooltip, Cancelled), how long it has run and, while it runs, Stop and a line of its own figures: what its sessions hold, what its thread allocated and its cpu time (holds no sessions · allocated 878.3 MB · cpu 1.39 s), so rows side by side differ with what each does. Stop also ends what that run started. A blocked input() or a sleep ends at once. A busy script ends at its next log, input or output; until then its row reads Stopping.

In the strip at the foot of the window. While anything runs, the strip's left end says how many (2 running, main.kts counted when it goes). Click it for a small panel over the strip: one line for each, with its name, its own figures and how long it has gone, and Stop for that one alone (Stop on the main.kts line also ends the templates it started): holds 416.5 MB · allocated 878.3 MB · cpu 1.39 s · 5s. The figures are the run's own, not the app's:

  • cpu is the CPU time of the thread its script runs on, and allocated the bytes that thread allocated, which is what it churned through, not what it keeps. Both are kept after the thread ends, so nothing is lost when a run moves to another thread. A thread the script starts itself is not counted. For main.kts they include its compile; a template's count from the moment its script runs.
  • holds is the weight of the sessions the run opened that are still open, as the files they loaded (the app's own estimate, since ONNX Runtime doesn't say what it keeps): a model's head, a package's jar, an ONNX file, and the encoder they run on. An encoder shared with another row is counted once, in the first, and the other row says + shared encoder. A run with none open says holds no sessions.

The Templates pane's rows under Running in the background show the same figures. They are read off the UI thread, every second while something runs and every two otherwise, from two calls on the thread bean and the sessions the run opened. The strip's ✕ hides it, the panel with it, and Memory in the sidebar brings it back.

A run's console lines start with the template's name (Reader: started in the background, Reader: finished in 3s). A failed one's name the template's own file and line, reader.kts:3: java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom, without the underline of a failed main.kts, since that file isn't in the editor.

Every run has a row on the Models page's Sessions tab too, of the kind background template: Terminate cancels it and what it started, and Terminate all cancels them all. A run started by coroutineTemplate outlives a script that ends by itself; Stop on the script ends everything it started, nested runs included. A value of template is closed when its script ends. Runs end with the app, which closes as it always does with a run in progress.

A run stays in the env that is current when it starts and changes nothing of it. A template that names another env, or imports what this env doesn't have, is refused, and Run in background says why in red under its row: load it and Run it, or run main.kts in that env first. A template that names no env runs in the current one.

docs.title: Exporting a script
docs.text:
The export button in the window's top bar (⌘E, Ctrl+E elsewhere), Export… on the Templates pane's strip, and Export… in a template's ⋯ for that template, make a folder that runs the script with plain java: no amie pilot, no Gradle, no window. A script does the same with exportJvm("main.kts") (Scripting API). So does the command line, without opening the app:

./gradlew :desktopApp:exportScript --args="main.kts --out /some/new/folder"
./gradlew :desktopApp:exportScript --args="main.kts --out /some/new/folder --template reader --script"

main.kts can also be a template's id or a file. --template carries a saved template besides those the script starts (as often as needed), --script chooses the script mode below, --plan only says what would go in, and --allow-missing writes the bundle although something could not be included, and --no-jars leaves out the env's Maven jars and the package jars: require.txt in the bundle lists each with the path to put it at, run.jar --check says which are still missing, and a run fetches a missing Maven jar from Maven Central when it can reach it, while a missing package jar stops it. A packaged app takes the same arguments after --export-script.

The pane shows what the script reaches before anything is written: the env, models, encoder, groups, packages, databases, data, the Java it needs and the size, what a deployer has to supply (To supply), and what could not be included (Can't include), which stops the export until it is dealt with. Export anyway writes it regardless and says so in its README and bundle.json. Once written, the pane says where the bundle is, how big it came out, and the exact java -jar line that starts it, with Copy beside it; Show it opens the folder.

Two modes. Compiled, the default, compiles main.kts and every template going in to classes with the same compiler Run uses, and puts them in lib/scripts.jar: the bundle carries no compiler, starts without compiling, and runs on Java 21 or newer. Script carries the text and the Kotlin compiler instead; AMP/pluginDir/main.kts can then be edited in the bundle and compiles when it starts, which takes some seconds, and the compiler stops on Java 25, so that bundle needs Java 21 to 24. A compiled bundle keeps the script's text too, for reading; editing it changes nothing until the script is exported again. A script that doesn't compile is refused with its lines, and nothing is written.

Templates. The pane lists every saved template. Those the script calls, with template("name") or coroutineTemplate, are checked and stay so, since the script needs them; any other can be checked to go in too. Each template in the bundle is an entry point of its own: java -jar run.jar --template "name" runs it instead of the script, --list says what the bundle can run, and the templates call each other with template or coroutineTemplate through the bundle's own background runs, as in the app and without it. --template gives a template no input: its input() is null at once and the run says so. A template still waiting for input when the script has ended is told the same, its input is closed, and the bundle ends instead of waiting for good; send its lines before the script ends.

Why a folder and not one jar. The encoder is over 400 MB and its native libraries have to be real files. AMP/ has to stay writable, since a script retrains models and writes logs there. A deployer has to be able to fill in secrets and edit the database url. So a bundle is a folder, and run.jar is a thin jar naming everything in lib/:

Path What it is run.sh, run.bat, run.jar Start it. Both check the Java version first; java -jar run.jar is the same thing lib/scripts.jar Compiled mode: the script and its templates as classes (Main, Template_<id>), loaded over the env, so run.jar doesn't name it lib/ Compiled: the Kotlin runtime, coroutines, serialization, ONNX Runtime and the tokenizers for this platform only, the amie runtime's own classes cut down to what a run reaches, the package jars, the Postgres driver when the script opens a database and the Ktor client when it saves state on the server. Script: the app's jars less the UI, TensorFlow and the Gradle API, the script engine among them, with the native libraries of every platform AMP/ What the script works on, laid out as here, with pluginDir/main.kts and templates/. In script mode, edit the script there and run again models/bert/ The encoder a model uses, and the named-entity model if the script opens it secrets.env What the deployer fills in, blank; an environment variable of the same name wins bundle.json The manifest: where it came from, the mode, the classes, what went in, each file's size and SHA-256 README.md How to run and deploy it and what to supply, written for this script

Size. Measured on an Apple Silicon Mac with Java 21, the same script exported both ways:

Script Mode Bundle lib/ java -jar, start to exit Peak memory Calls two templates, no model Compiled 20 MB 20 MB 0.3 s 87 MB Script 189 MB 189 MB 4.3 s 430 MB Scope functions starter, dummy model and bge Compiled 436 MB 20 MB 2.9 s 1.1 GB Script 606 MB 189 MB 6 to 10 s 1.3 GB

The encoder is about 420 MB in both modes. In a compiled bundle's lib/ ONNX Runtime and the tokenizers, with this platform's natives, are most of it; a script bundle's also holds the compiler, its scripting jars, Ktor and the natives of four platforms. run.jar itself is a few KB: it names what is in lib/, so keep the folder together.

A run ends with the same Resources: line as in the app, on standard error so that standard output stays the script's own; each template's run says its own among the script's lines.

./run.sh --check says whether it can run, without running it: Java, the jars and models, native libraries, each secret, and that the classes load (compiled) or the script compiles (script). What the script prints goes to standard output and its errors to standard error, every level goes to AMP/logs.txt, and the exit code is 0 when it finished, 1 when it failed and 2 when it could not start. --levels info,data,error,internal chooses what is printed. A script that leaves a model serving keeps the process up until it gets Ctrl-C or SIGTERM. With AMIE_AMP_DIR set the bundle works in that folder, filling in what it lacks from its own AMP/ and always taking the script, so a read-only image can keep its data on a volume.

What goes in is read from the script's text. Names come from the calls of the script API, and from a val holding the name. A name known only when the script runs stops the export, with its line, until a comment says what it will be:

// export: model intents
// export: file data/extra.csv
initMod(pick())

The kinds are model, group, package, database and file. A model takes its folder without what it was asked: sessions.log, incoming.jsonl, the access logs, dropped.csv, plots and icon stay here. An env goes whole, as a Run sees it, so nothing is downloaded. Any other string of the script that names a file is carried too; one under AMP/ keeps its place and one from elsewhere goes to AMP/files/, with the script pointed at it when it runs. A file a data call needs and that isn't there stops the export; a string that merely looks like a path doesn't.

What stays out. session.json, keycloak.json's client secret, github.json and anything named like a credential are never copied, even when a script names one, and neither is a package's configuration file that holds something like a key. A password in databases.json or in its url, and a model's serving key, become $ENV:NAME, listed in the README and in secrets.env: AMIE_DB_<NAME>_PASSWORD, AMIE_SERVE_<MODEL>_KEY, or the name the setting already had. Only the connections the script names go in; a script that names none and lists them takes them all. A script with what looks like a password in its text stops the export, since the script goes in as it is. saveState, loadState and listStates need a signed-in user, and a bundle has no browser: it takes AMIE_REFRESH_TOKEN, an offline token, or AMIE_ACCESS_TOKEN, used until it expires, and writes no session.json.

What it runs on. Java 21, a JRE being enough. A compiled bundle runs on any later Java too, and on the platform it was exported from: ONNX Runtime and the tokenizers go in with that platform's native libraries only (macOS arm64, Linux x64 or arm64, Windows x64), which the README names; for another platform, export there, or put the whole onnxruntime and tokenizers jars from Maven Central in lib/, which hold every platform. A script bundle carries all four platforms; 22 to 24 are let through but untried, and 25 is refused, since Kotlin 2.1's script compiler stops on it. Native libraries unpack under AMP/cache/, so that folder can't be a noexec mount, as Docker's plain --tmpfs is; DJL_CACHE_DIR moves them. Linux means glibc, so not Alpine: ONNX Runtime ships no musl build. An Intel Mac has ONNX Runtime but no tokenizers library in the jar. importModelTensorflow doesn't work in a bundle, and a script importing Compose, TensorFlow, KotlinDL, Groovy or the Gradle API is refused by name, since those jars stay behind. A database other than Postgres fails as it does here, for want of a driver on the app's class path.

Templates and shell commands. A template the script calls with template or coroutineTemplate goes with it, with whatever that template reaches, and the process stays until it has ended; one that fails after the script ended makes the exit code 1. It has to run in the script's env, as it does in the app, so one that names another env or imports what the env lacks stops the export; a template checked in the pane to go in besides is held to the same. In a compiled bundle a path the export moved to AMP/files/ is compiled in as that place under AMP/, which a data call finds; in a script bundle the text is pointed at the real path when it starts. Other work a script leaves on a thread of its own stops with the process, unless a model is being served. shell and shellScript run on the machine the bundle is on: a file named to shellScript is copied, but what a command calls can't be, so the commands are listed in the README's notes for the deployer. Nothing feeds a bundle's own main.kts, so input() there is null, as on Run.

The lines the app writes for itself stay in AMP/logs.txt, as they stay hidden in the console until Internal is on: metrics tables, charts, sessions.print(). --levels prints them.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
1. Press Run (the green square with the play icon over the editor) or ⌘↵ (Ctrl+Enter elsewhere) inside it; they are the same. While it runs the square is red and stops the run (⌘. does too, Ctrl+. elsewhere); ⌘↵ pressed again only logs "Script is already running".
  2. The console strip reads Running 12s with a moving bar under it, and under the status a line of figures, memory 1.20 GB, peak 1.40 GB · heap 340.0 MB of 4.00 GB · cpu 2.10 s · ort 12 runs, read every second from the same meter that writes the Resources: line at the end: the memory the process holds now and the most it held during the run, the heap in use of what it may grow to, the CPU since the start and the ONNX Runtime calls so far. So a script that grows is seen growing before it ends. When the run ends the line keeps its final figures, dimmed, until the next run starts; the whole reading is in its tooltip. While modelBuilder works the status shows the phase and step (modelBuilder 'x' embedding 40/120 · 43%). A run belongs to the app, not to the page. Go to Models, Settings or anywhere else while the script runs, to look at Packages or Sessions: it goes on, its lines keep arriving in the console, and the strip at the foot of the window says 1 running with the script's own Stop. Come back to the sandbox and it shows the run still going, with its live status, and Stop works as ever.
  3. The strip ends on Finished in 41s, Failed after 3s (the first error in its tooltip, and in the console) or Stopped after 12s when you stopped it; the console has the same line at the internal level.
  4. Right after that line, for a failed run too, the console's internal level has what the run used: memory, heap, CPU time, ONNX Runtime calls and sessions (see The output console). A session the script left open is named at the info level, in view.

When a run fails the console says where. Each thing the compiler got wrong is a line of its own that begins with its place in the script, main.kts:2:14: Type mismatch: inferred type is String but Int was expected, an import that doesn't resolve included (at its own line, wherever it stands). An exception names the line of the script it came through, main.kts:6: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: …: the innermost line of main.kts, so in a function of yours the line that threw, and in an API call that threw the line that made the call. An error a script throws is named the same way (java.lang.StackOverflowError, kotlin.NotImplementedError from a TODO()). The place is underlined. Click it and the caret goes there: a folded block over it opens, the line comes into view and the editor takes the keyboard. The error lines show even with error toggled off, since a failure turns it on. The warnings the compiler gives with an error (warning: Variable 'a' is never used) are info lines: they don't fail the run, and the run's status counts the errors only, main.kts:2:14: … (and 1 more). An error with no place in the script (an env that couldn't be sourced, say) reads Error: ….

What happens underneath: the script's dependency calls are read before it compiles and the packages are put on the classpath (configuration phase); then the script runs with the Kotlin JSR-223 engine on a background thread (execution phase). Details in Scripting API.

docs.title: Sessions: what stays open after a run
docs.text:
A script ends; what it opened does not. initMod("name") opens a session of a model (one per model, reused by the next run), initMod("name.jar") a session of a package (a fresh instance per call), and both stay open until they are closed in a script or terminated on the Models page, Sessions tab, where each one shows its runs and a log of what it was asked and answered. So the usual loop is: open the model at the top of the script, ask it, read the console, edit, Run again (instant, the model is already loaded), and close it when you are done. ortClosable { } closes what its block opened when the block ends; ortStatic("name") { } keeps it until it is freed, ortRequired("name") { } while anything else is in session, and ortLimited("name", 3) { } keeps the three newest. All of it, with the pitfalls, is in Running sessions.

sessionMod("name") is the other way to ask a model: a snapshot of its head, which can't train or change it, leaves nothing in its log and goes with the run or the block. The same tab lists Scripts over the sessions: the scripts running and those that left something open, with what each holds and has used (what the figures are).

docs.title: The output console
docs.text:
By default a line is just its message, in monospace so metric tables and ASCII charts keep their alignment, and coloured by its level: an error in the muted red, a line the app itself wrote in a dimmer gray, the script's own lines in the plain text colour. The console follows the newest line until you scroll up; scrolling back to the end re-attaches it. While it is empty it says how to run the script.

Level Shown as Used for internal dim gray text Lines the app itself writes: build phases, metrics tables, charts, session messages error muted red text Failures, Keycloak and backend errors, script exceptions data plain text Data your script logs with data(...), file dumps info plain text log(...) and info(...) from the script, run start and end

The strip over the console carries, at its right end, the four levels as toggles with their counts (Internal 12, Error 0, …; click one to hide or show its lines, All turns them all on again), the columns icon that adds the time, the level and the source (main.kts, sandbox, internal) in fixed columns before every line, as the log file has them, and Clear, which empties the view. Nothing is lost: everything the console ever showed is appended to AMP/logs.txt. When the console is narrow the toggles move under the status instead of squeezing it.

It works like an IDE's terminal. ⌘F (Ctrl+F elsewhere), or the magnifier on the strip, finds in the lines shown: it starts on the newest hit, Enter goes back to the one before, Shift+Enter on, and Esc closes it. ⌘K (Ctrl+L everywhere) clears. Up and Down in the input line bring back what you typed. A copy over several lines keeps them on lines of their own, and with the details on keeps the columns apart by a space. Right-click offers Find and Clear beside Copy. A main.kts:12 anywhere on a line goes to that line in the editor, a web address opens in the browser, and a script's ANSI colours (the 16, the 256 and true colour) are drawn. Scrolled up, the button at the corner goes back to the newest line. Every control on the strip says in its tooltip what it is for, which way it is right now and what a click does: a level's toggle reads On: its 12 lines show. Click to hide them or Off: its 3 lines are hidden, the count still moves. Click to show them; the columns icon says whether details are on; All says how many lines wait behind the levels that are off; Clear says how many lines it would empty, and that the next run empties the console anyway.

When the app starts only info is on, so the console shows the script's own log(...) lines and the start and end of each run. The counts on the other toggles still move: error 1 means one error line is waiting behind the toggle (a failed run turns error on), and the strip's status says Failed after 3s with the error in its tooltip either way.

Every run ends by saying what it used, for a failed run too. The Resources: line is at the internal level, out of view until internal is on (the strip's figures and their tooltip say the same); the Still open: line, a session the script left open, is at the info level, so it shows from the start:

Resources: memory 1.20 GB, peak 1.40 GB, 180.0 MB more than before · heap 340.0 MB of 4.00 GB · cpu 2.10 s · ort 12 runs in 640 ms · sessions 3 opened, 2 closed, 1 still open
Still open: web-ample #3
Figure What it says memory What the process holds at the end, heap and native together (ONNX Runtime's memory is native) peak The most it held during the run, read about once a second more or less than before How the end differs from the start heap The JVM heap in use at the end, of the most it may grow to cpu CPU time used during the run, on all cores together, so it can be more than the run took ort ONNX Runtime calls during the run and the time spent in them sessions ONNX Runtime sessions opened and closed during the run, then every session open when it ended, of any kind and from any run. So with a session left from an earlier run, or a package jar, the last number is not opened minus closed

The figures are for the whole app process, since the JVM can't split them per script: a served model answering during the run counts too. A figure the platform can't give is left out, such as the memory on Windows, where there is no ps. Still open is a second line only when sessions stay open, with their names and numbers as on the Models page, Sessions tab, the scope in brackets when one holds them, as in web-ample #3 (static search), and templates still running in the background as (background). The templates main.kts called with template(...) are closed for it as it ends, so they are given a moment to end and are not listed; one started with coroutineTemplate goes on by design and is. A run that stays up for more than five minutes, such as a gateway script, is read every 30 seconds from then on instead of every second. The words Still open: are a link: a click opens the Still open fold, below, where each of those sessions has a Terminate button.

Recent runs, folded under the console strip, keeps the last 20 runs: when each began (the time for today's, the date for an older one), how long it took, and Finished, Stopped, or Failed with the first error (all of it in the tooltip). They are kept in AMP/pluginDir/runs.jsonl, so they outlast the console, which each run empties, and the app.

Each of those rows also says what its run used, in short (1.20 GB memory · 2.10 s cpu · 12 ort runs), with the console's lines in the tooltip. A run kept from before this was added has nothing there.

docs.title: Still open: the sessions, right there
docs.text: Still open, folded under Recent runs with its count, lists every session open now, of any kind and whichever run opened it, with the same rows as the Models page's Sessions tab: owner and number, kind, the scope that holds it (forever search), its runs and age, and Terminate, which closes that one as the tab does. A row a kept scope holds has Free too, which frees the whole scope (ortScopes.free("search")), and Free all at the top does what Terminate all does on the tab: every session is closed and every background template cancelled. The list is read every two seconds while the console shows, so a session a running script opens appears as it does, and one the script closes goes. A long list scrolls inside the fold, so the console under it keeps its room, and in a narrow pane a row's name and details are cut short before its buttons are. With nothing open the fold says so. See Running sessions.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
The >>> prompt on the line after the output takes a line. A command runs on its own, without a script, and what it did follows at the info level. The line itself is echoed first (>>> free search), so what was typed shows:

Typed What it does help lists these commands sessions lists every open session, as the Still open fold does, with the scope that holds each scopes what the kept scopes hold, as ortScopes.print() says it free search closes what the kept scope search holds, as ortScopes.free("search") does; says how many were closed free all closes what every kept scope holds, as ortScopes.freeAll() does terminate #3, terminate web-ample closes that session (by number or by owner), as Terminate on its row does terminate all closes every session and cancels every background template, as Terminate all does clear empties the console, as the Clear button does reset forgets what the lines of script typed here defined eof tells the script waiting at input() that no more is coming log("hi"), any other line of script runs in the background, with or without a script running; terminate console ends one that goes on

Plain words that are no command are said to be none. While a script waits at input(), every other line typed is its input, as in a Run window: it shows in green and the prompt's tooltip says so.

The console remembers, as Python's interpreter does. The lines of script typed here share one interpreter, so what a line defines is there for the lines after it: val x = 12, then log(x) prints 12; a fun, a class or an import stays too, and val x = 5 later gives x a new value. A line that ends in a value prints it (twice(x) prints 24); a line that ends in nothing, or in a shell result whose output already showed, prints nothing more. reset forgets everything, and so does a change of env, since the lines were compiled against the old one's packages. A line waits for the ones typed before it, so they run in the order they were typed. A line of script needs no script around it, keeps going while you type on or close the sandbox, and reads input from the console as main.kts does.

A block over several lines. A line that isn't whole yet waits for the rest, and the prompt turns to ...:

>>> for (x in 0..3)
... {
...     log(x)
... }
0
1
2
3

It waits while a bracket, a """ string or a /* comment is open, while the line ends in an operator, a dot or a comma, and after a header with no body yet: for (…), while (…), if (…), else, try, catch (…), finally, when (…), fun f(…). It runs once it is whole. A blank line sends it as it is when no bracket is open (inside braces it is a blank line of the block), and Ctrl+C drops it. Ctrl+C with no block going stops the lines of script that are running, as terminate console does; with text selected it is the field's copy where Ctrl+C copies.

docs.title: Keyboard summary
docs.text: Keys Action ⌘↵ (Ctrl+Enter) Run main.kts Enter New line at the current indentation, deeper after {, ( or [; re-indents the script unless Settings turns that off ⌥⌘+ / ⌥⌘− / ⌘0 (Ctrl+Alt+= / Ctrl+Alt+− / Ctrl+0) Text a point larger, smaller, or back to 14pt Tab / Shift+Tab Indent or dedent the line, or every line of the selection; outside the editor, move between the strip's controls (the one with the keyboard shows a thin ring, Space or Enter presses it) ⌘⇧F (Ctrl+Shift+F) Re-indent the whole script (Enter does it too unless Settings turns it off) ⌘- (Ctrl+-) Fold the block the caret is in; with Shift, every block ⌘= (Ctrl+=) Open the folded block at the caret; with Shift, every block Typing a name Opens the completion dropdown Up / Down Move in the dropdown Enter / Tab Insert the selected function Esc Close the dropdown Ctrl+Space Open the dropdown

docs.title: Serving a model
docs.text:
Every exported model can answer HTTP requests from inside the app.

  1. Open Models and select the model.
  2. The gear (⚙) at the right of its header opens the serving settings: Host (default 127.0.0.1), Port, Path (default /models/<name>), the Methods (POST, GET), Min score and Fallback (below), and under Access who may ask and how much (below). Save writes AMP/models/intents/<name>/serving.json.
  3. Listen on :port starts the listener: the header says listening 127.0.0.1:8765, and Stop ends it. While the settings hold a value they can't take (a port, a min score, an origin, a limit), Listen and Save wait, and their tooltips say which to fix.
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict -d '{"text":"turn the lights on"}'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict?text=turn+the+lights+on'

The POST and GET URLs are listed under the settings with Copy and Copy curl.

  • Every request is appended to AMP/models/intents/<name>/incoming.jsonl (for a model that keeps no texts, the text's length instead of the text).
  • Every request, whatever came of it (answered, 400, 401, 403, 405, 413, 429, 500, a CORS preflight), is also one line of the model's access log, AMP/models/intents/<name>/access.log, tab-separated: time, request id, client address, method, path without the query (a GET's text is in it), status, milliseconds, the text's length, the answer's bytes and what came of it, in fixed forms: an 8-hex-digit id, 12ms, in 17 chars, out 96B, and the outcome (lights 0.912, abstained, refused: …, preflight, the error); status 0 means no answer was sent. It never holds a text, for any model. Each answer carries its id as the header X-Request-Id, so a client can name its line. Listening and stopping are lines of it too (with what the access settings require, and at the stop stopped after 8 requests (1 failed, 2 refused)). Past 2 MB it moves to access.1.log, the one before that going. The last twelve show under the settings in the Requests fold (closed until opened), newest first, errors in red, read again as the file grows. From a script, accessLog("name", last = 20) prints and returns them.
  • The header's status tooltip counts what the listener did since it started: 8 requests, 5 abstained, 1 error, 2 refused (refused: turned away by the access settings).
  • Changes to the settings apply after Stop and Listen; the settings say so while it listens. Save meanwhile keeps them for that next start, and Stop leaves what was saved as it is.
  • Models that were listening when the app closed start listening again on the next launch.
  • A new head of the model (a fine-tune, a build under the same name, a rollback, a /retrain from a client) never stops the listener: the new head is opened beside the one answering, put in its place once the answers in flight are done, and the old one is closed after. Every answer says which head gave it ("version": 3), the access log has a line for the swap, and the header's status tooltip counts the swaps.

docs.title: Teaching a model while it listens
docs.text:
A client that sees the model answer wrongly can correct it over the same port, without the Models page, and have the model retrained on its corrections while it goes on answering. Two routes stand beside /predict under the model's path:

Request What it does Answer POST <path>/teach with {"text": "lamp please", "label": "lights"} Writes the sentence with its label at the top of the model's queue of texts to label, AMP/<name>-to-label.csv, the same file Teach on the page and teach() in a script write to; a text the queue has already gets the new label instead. A label the model knows is taken in its own spelling (Lights is lights); any other label is a new one, which a retrain learns once it has three rows or more 200 {"model": "intents", "version": 2, "text": "lamp please", "label": "lights", "queue": "intents-to-label.csv", "labeled": 4} DELETE <path>/teach with {"text": "lamp please"} or ?text=lamp+please Takes the sentence out of the queue, whatever the case it was written in; a sentence that isn't there changes nothing 200 {"model": "intents", "text": "lamp please", "removed": true, "label": "lights", "queue": "…", "labeled": 3} ("removed": false and no label when it wasn't there) GET <path>/teach The queue as it is: every row with its label (empty while unlabeled), the model's guess, its score and the runner-up 200 {"model": "intents", "version": 2, "queue": "…", "labeled": 3, "unlabeled": 5, "rows": [{"text": "…", "label": "lights", "guess": "weather", "score": 0.41, "runnerUp": "lights"}, …]} POST <path>/retrain Starts a fine-tune on the labeled rows of the queue, in the background, and answers at once. The model keeps answering with the head it has until the new one is written; then the new head is opened, swapped in and the old one closed (above), the queue is graded again with it, and the head before is kept as a version for a rollback. ?wait=true or {"wait": true} holds the answer until it is over 202 {"model": "intents", "status": "running", "version": 2, "labeled": 3, "from": 2, "rows": 3, "startedAt": "…", "phase": "training 12/40 · …"}; with wait, 200 with "status": "done", "to": 3, "detail": "fine-tune v2 → v3 · accuracy 0.900 → 0.967 on …", or 500 with "status": "failed" and the reason in detail GET <path>/retrain How the last retrain went, or "status": "idle" with how many labeled rows wait 200 as above POST <path>/retrain while one runs, while the page builds or fine-tunes anything, or with no labeled row in the queue Refused; nothing changes 409 {"error": "nothing to learn: intents-to-label.csv has no labeled rows; POST a text and its label to /models/intents/teach first", "status": "idle", …} POST <path>/teach for a model that keeps no texts, or one renamed or destroyed meanwhile Refused: no text of another person's lands in a file 409 {"error": "…"} POST <path>/teach without a text or a label, DELETE without a text 400 {"error": "send {\"text\": \"...\", \"label\": \"...\"}"} 
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/teach -d '{"text": "lamp please", "label": "lights"}'
curl -X DELETE 'http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/teach?text=lamp+please'
curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/teach
curl -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/retrain?wait=true'
curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/retrain

What a retrain does is exactly a fine-tune on the queue with the default options, as Fine-tune on it under the queue on the page's Improve tab does: the rows it was trained on are replayed so it keeps what it knew, a label it doesn't know gets an output of its own, before and after are scored on the same held-out rows, and the console and the Metrics tab show the run. The rows stay in the queue after it (graded with the new head, so the Improve tab shows which it answers right now); take out of it what the model shouldn't learn again. A model that was fine-tuned on its queue names it under fine-tuned on, so the next retrain replays it.

Lessons go through the access settings as every request does: the key, the origins, the size and the minute all apply. Since a lesson changes the model, a request from another machine is answered 403 teaching from another machine needs a key unless a Key is set; this machine's own requests teach as they are. One retrain runs at a time, over every model, and none while the page is building, fine-tuning or calibrating something (409 busy fine-tuning weather); the lessons meanwhile land in the queue and the next retrain takes them. The access log has a line per lesson (taught: lights, forgot: weather, retrain: done v2 → v3), never the text.

docs.title: Answering only when it is sure
docs.text:
A model answers every text with its best label, however unsure it is. With Min score set, a request whose best score is under it is not answered with that label: the model abstains. It answers the Fallback label instead (such as unknown, scored at the min score), or no label when Fallback is empty, marks the answer "abstained": true and moves its own scores to "ranking", so nothing it said is lost:

{"model": "intents", "predictions": [{"label": "unknown", "score": 0.75}], "abstained": true,
 "ranking": [{"label": "lights", "score": 0.41}, {"label": "music", "score": 0.28}, …]}

At or over the min score the answer is the model's own with "abstained": false. Without a min score (empty, or 0) it is exactly as before, with no abstained key, and serving.json holds no minScore or fallbackLabel.

Under Min score the settings suggest a value from the model's last run: the lowest score at which its answers were right 95% of the time on that run's rows, answering a tenth of them at least (suggested 0.75: 95% right, answers 90%; its tooltip says more, and Use 0.75 puts it in the field). The scores tried are the gates the run kept, 0.05 apart, which the Metrics tab's chart of how far the scores can be trusted shows. A model right 95% of the time at any score needs none (97% right at any score), and of one that no score makes that right it says so (no score keeps 95% right): fine-tune or calibrate it first. A run of rows like the ones it will be asked suggests best; a calibrated model's scores mean what they say, so its min score holds better on new texts.

Abstentions are counted in the header's status tooltip, the console line says what it would have answered (-> unknown (abstained: lights 0.415 under 0.75)), and incoming.jsonl keeps the model's own label and score with "abstained": true.

docs.title: Who may ask and how much
docs.text:
Out of the box a listener answers anyone who can reach its address, which on the default host 127.0.0.1 is this machine alone. Before serving on another host (0.0.0.0, a LAN address) or to a web page, the Access fold of the gear panel sets four limits. Each is off while its field is empty, and then the listener behaves as it did before there were any:

Field (serving.json) What it does Past it Key (apiKey) A request must send the key as the header Authorization: Bearer <key>. New key puts a random one in the field (32 characters), Copy copies it; the field shows it as dots 401 {"error": "send the key as the header Authorization: Bearer <key>"}, with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="amie" Origins (cors) The web pages that may call the model from a browser, as the browser names them: https://app.example.com, http://localhost:3000, or * for any. A request from one of them gets the CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin with its origin, Vary: Origin, Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Retry-After), on errors too, and its preflight (OPTIONS) a 204 with the methods and OPTIONS, the Content-Type and Authorization headers allowed and Access-Control-Max-Age: 600. Without Origins an OPTIONS gets 405 a browser's request from a page not on the list: 403 {"error": "the origin https://elsewhere.example is not allowed"}. A request without an Origin header (curl, a server, another program) isn't a browser's and goes on Max bytes (maxBodyBytes) The most bytes a request's body, or a GET's text, may have. A body is read no further than one byte past it, and not at all when its Content-Length says it is over 413 {"error": "the request is over 4096 bytes"}, and the model isn't asked Per minute (rateLimitPerMinute) How many requests a minute it answers, every client together, counted over the last 60 seconds 429 {"error": "over 60 requests a minute; try again in 12 s"}, with Retry-After: 12

They are checked origin, method, key, per minute, then size: a request without the key uses up none of the minute, an oversized one does. A request turned away is logged in the console without its text, is never written to incoming.jsonl, and counts as refused in the header's tooltip. With a key set, Copy curl sends it:

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/models/intents/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer 3q2-7wEAAAB9pY1vX0dYb1JnS2hRcFdN' -d '{"text": "turn the lights on"}'

The key is kept in serving.json as it is, on this machine: Publish never sends it, and neither do the model's versions. Anyone who can read the AMP folder can read it, so a key guards the port, not the files. A new key, or none, applies after Stop and Listen, as every setting does.

docs.title: The HTTP contract
docs.text:
Request Answer POST <path>/predict with {"text": "…"} or a plain-text body 200 {"model": "intents", "predictions": [{"label": "lights", "score": 0.97}, …]}, best first GET <path>/predict?text=… the same a model with a Min score whose best score reaches it the same, with "abstained": false a model with a Min score whose best score is under it 200 {"model": "intents", "predictions": [{"label": "unknown", "score": 0.75}], "abstained": true, "ranking": […]}: the Fallback label scored at the min score, or [] without one, and the model's own scores under ranking no text (empty body, no text key, no ?text=) 400 {"error": "send text as {\"text\": \"...\"}, a plain-text body or ?text="} a method not in the model's Methods list 405 {"error": "PUT not allowed, use [POST, GET]"} with Access set: a browser page not in Origins, no key, too big, too many 403, 401, 413, 429 (above) with Origins set: a browser's preflight OPTIONS from a page on the list 204 with the CORS headers the model threw while answering 500 {"error": "…"}, and the page's errors count goes up nothing listens on the port the connection is refused (no HTTP answer at all) POST, DELETE, GET <path>/teach and POST, GET <path>/retrain the lessons: Teaching a model while it listens; a method not in that route's list is 405

Every answer is application/json, and one from a model whose module says its version carries it ("version": 2, the head that answered). The path is /models/<name>/predict unless Path was changed. /predict, /teach and /retrain are always appended, so a Path of /intents serves /intents/predict, /intents/teach and /intents/retrain.

docs.title: From a script
docs.text:
val url = serve("intents", port = 8765)          // null when it could not start; the console says why
log(url ?: "not started")
stopServing("intents")
serve("intents", minScore = 0.75, fallbackLabel = "unknown")   // abstains under 0.75
accessLog("intents", last = 5)                    // its last five access log lines, printed and returned

serve("name") with no other argument reuses what the page saved in serving.json; a port, host, path, methods, min score or fallback given here are saved there too, and the access settings saved on the page stay as they are. minScore = 0.0 turns a saved gate off, as emptying Min score on the page does, and fallbackLabel = "" takes a saved fallback away. The full example with the request code and every error handled is in the Cookbook. Four reasons a start fails, each one Error line in the console: a min score outside 0 to 1, the model cannot be loaded, the port is already taken by another program, or the path is already served by another model on that port.

docs.title: Running sessions
docs.text:
A session is a model or a package that the app holds open in memory so it can answer questions right away: the ONNX head of an intent model with its encoder, one instance of a package jar in its own class loader, or a bare ONNX Runtime session. A session is opened once, asked as often as you like with inference(text), and stays open until it is terminated: it survives the end of the script that opened it, the next run of the script, and switching pages. The Sessions tab of the Models page lists every open one, with its log and a Terminate button, and so does the Still open tab of the sandbox's console, where the console's free and terminate commands do the same by name (Close sessions).

This page is the practical guide: how to open a session, talk to it, keep it warm between runs, give it a scope, read what it did, and close it. The function reference is in Scripting API, the page itself in Models page.

docs.title: The five kinds
docs.text:
Kind Opened by How many What run(text) returns Intent model initMod("name") in a script, Open session on the Models page One per model. A second initMod("name") returns the session that is already open label:probability lines, best first (lights:0.91, weather:0.06, …); predict(text) is the label alone, scores(text) a label → score map Package initMod("name.jar") One per call. Every initMod makes a fresh instance of the jar's class in its own class loader What the package's run(text) returned, one line per element; answer(text) the first. No predict/scores: a package has no labels Session model sessionMod("name") in a script One per head. Everything asking for the same head of a model shares one snapshot, which goes when the last lets go label:probability lines, from the head it was taken on ONNX session importModelOnnx("file.onnx") One per call The raw model's output; no log is kept Model group group("name") in a script, Open swarm on the Models page One per group. A swarm over one session per model of the group (each the model's own session, reused if open); closing the swarm closes the sessions it opened The labels merged over the models, each with its best score; vote(text) the label most models give, each(text) every model's own label, ask(text) every raw answer. Logged to AMP/env/<env>/<group>.sessions.log; a group with a model that keeps no texts logs only each text's length, there and in its models' logs

The bundled NER model, initMod() with no name, is not a listed session: it is an ordinary object your script owns, so close it yourself when you are done, or open it in a scope function.

A template running in the background is listed with them as a background template, though it answers nothing and has no log: it is there so that it can be seen and terminated. See Templates in the background.

docs.title: Open one and ask it something
docs.text:
Every fresh AMP/ folder has the dummy model (labels greeting, lights, weather), so this script works before anything was trained:

val m = initMod("dummy")                              // opens the session, or returns the open one
log(m.predict("turn the lights on"))                  // lights: the predicted label
log(m.inference("turn the lights on").first())        // lights:0.61
m.inference("hello there").forEach { log(it) }        // every label with its probability
val scores = m.scores("hello there")                  // {greeting=0.65, weather=0.48, lights=0.36}
log(m.getStatus().toString())                         // the module manifest: encoder, dims, labels

predict is the label alone, scores every label with its score, inference the raw lines; all three are described in Reading a prediction.

Press Run. The console shows initMod: 'dummy' session ready (…), then your lines; the strip over it says Finished in 2s. Open Models (second sidebar icon) and the Sessions tab: dummy #1, intent model, 2 runs, open for a few seconds. The session is still there: the script ended, the session did not.

Run the script again. This time the console says initMod: 'dummy' is already open as session #1, that one is used, the run count goes up and no new session appears. A model has one session at most, on purpose: a script run ten times does not pile up ten copies of the model in memory.

A package behaves differently, because packages are bottles with their own state:

val echo = initMod("amie-demo-1.0.0.jar")             // the demo package: a new instance every call
echo.run("hello").forEach { log(it) }
log(echo.getStatus().toString())                      // id, jar, class, source, url, page, runs
echo.close()                                          // releases the instance and its class loader

Without the close(), every run of the script leaves one more amie-demo-1.0.0.jar #n open under Sessions. That is fine while you experiment (terminate them on the page, or packages.closeAll() at the top of the script), but a script you run often should close the packages it opens.

Where the jar comes from: the active environment, then AMP/pluginDir, then a path, then the GitHub repositories of AMP/github.json; a download is stored in AMP/pluginDir so the next open is local. packages.available() lists what those repositories offer. The Amie server is off, like accounts and Keycloak, until AMIE_ACCOUNTS=1 turns them on.

docs.title: Keep a session warm between runs
docs.text:
Loading a model takes a moment (the encoder is a BERT model); asking it takes milliseconds. Because an intent model's session outlives the script, the pattern for iterating on a script is simply to open the model at the top and not close it:

val m = initMod("intents")                            // first run: loads; every later run: instant
listOf("turn the lights on", "what's the weather", "hi").forEach { text ->
    log("$text -> ${m.predict(text)}")               // the label; m.inference(text) for every label:score line
}

Edit the texts, press Run, read the console, repeat. The session keeps counting runs across your edits. Close it when you are done (m.close(), or Terminate on the page) and the next initMod("intents") loads it again.

For a package, keep the session across runs by not closing it and reusing the same session on the next run:

val echo = packages.open.firstOrNull { it.jarName == "amie-demo-1.0.0.jar" && !it.closed }
    ?: initMod("amie-demo-1.0.0.jar")

(packages.open is the list of open package sessions, oldest first.)

docs.title: Scope functions
docs.text:
A script can say how long what it opens should live, instead of closing each session by hand. The four block functions take a name and a block, run the block and return its value, so val label: String = ortClosable { ... } works. A bare initMod outside any block behaves exactly as the rest of this page says, so scripts without them don't change.

Function What it does A session that was already open ortClosable(name) { } What the block opens is for that block alone. It is closed when the block ends, by a return or an exception, the last opened first. A handle kept past the block fails with is closed, which is what one-time use means Used and left open, with a console line saying so: the block frees only what it opened itself ortStatic(name) { } What the block opens stays open across runs until it is terminated or freed. Running the block again finds the same model session Adopted: the scope keeps it from now on. If a closable around the block held it, static wins and the closable no longer closes it ortRequired(name) { } Kept like ortStatic while anything else is in session: a model, package, group, template or background job that no required scope holds. Once nothing else is open it is freed, within a couple of seconds, and the block opens it again when next run. For what other models need beside them Adopted, and freed with the rest ortLimited(name, max) { } Kept like ortStatic, at most max sessions under the name: when one more is opened the oldest is closed first Adopted, and one of the max ortScopes.print() Lists what each static, required and limited scope holds, a limited one with how full it is, and returns those lines Listed once it is adopted; a session no scope holds isn't listed ortScopes.free("name") Closes what that scope holds, the last opened first, and returns how many were closed Closed if the scope adopted it ortScopes.freeAll() Closes what every static, required and limited scope holds, and returns how many were closed Closed if a scope adopted it; a session no scope holds stays open

A template called in an ortClosable block belongs to that block, however deep the call is. It runs inside the block, so what it opens is the block's too, and when the block ends the template ends with it: first its input closes so it can finish, then, if it still goes on after its grace time, it is cancelled. Only then does the block close what was opened. A template(...) called inside that template belongs to the same block, and so does a coroutineTemplate. An ortStatic block inside keeps what it opens, as the innermost block decides. A delegate used again in a later block starts a new run.

The names are optional for the first two: ortClosable { } and ortStatic { } go by closable and static. This is the starter Scope functions: ortClosable and ortStatic in the sandbox's Templates pane:

// ortClosable frees what its block opens when the block ends, so a handle is good for that one block.
// ortStatic keeps what its block opens across runs, until ortScopes frees it or it is terminated.
// ortRequired keeps it while anything else is in session; ortLimited keeps at most so many.

// A session open before a block is left as it is, so this starts with dummy closed.
initMod("dummy").close()

// The block's value comes back; the session is closed by then, however the block ended.
val (label, handle) = ortClosable("one time") {
    val m = initMod("dummy")
    m.predict("turn the lights on") to m
}
log("the block answered $label")

// One-time use: the handle the block gave back is closed.
try {
    handle.predict("hello there")
} catch (e: IllegalStateException) {
    log("after the block: ${e.message}")
}

// Kept under a name. Stop the script here and Models > Sessions says static search on its row.
val search = ortStatic("search") { initMod("dummy") }
log(search.predict("what's the weather"))
ortScopes.print().forEach { log(it) }

// Closes what search holds and says how many.
log("freed ${ortScopes.free("search")} session(s)")

// Kept while anything else is in session: once nothing else is open it is freed by itself, and opened again when next run.
val recent = ortRequired("recent") { initMod("dummy") }
log(recent.predict("hello there"))

// At most two under the name, the oldest closed when a third is opened. A model has one session, so this
// takes dummy over from recent; packages and ONNX files are new on every call, so for them it fills up.
val pool = ortLimited("pool", 2) { initMod("dummy") }
ortScopes.print().forEach { log(it) }

// Closes what every block keeps, so this script leaves nothing open.
log("freed ${ortScopes.freeAll()} more")

What to keep in mind:

  • Blocks nest and the innermost decides. A closable inside a static block frees what it opened and leaves what the static block holds alone. A static block inside a closable keeps what is opened in it after the closable has ended. The same goes for required and limited blocks, which keep like a static one.
  • What a block tracks is what the script opens itself: initMod("name"), initMod("name.jar"), initMod(), group("name") and importModelOnnx(...). initAmie stays a one-off inside a block, opened and closed for the call. serve("x") holds its own model, so a closable around it doesn't stop the listener.
  • Packages and ONNX files are new on every call. A static block keeps one more of them on each run, as a bare initMod("x.jar") leaves one more; a model has one session, so a model is held once however often it runs. That is what a limited block is for: ortLimited("pool", 3) { initMod("x.jar") } run again and again holds the three newest.
  • A required scope looks every couple of seconds. While a session no required scope holds is open, a model, a package, a group, a template or a background job, it keeps what it holds; once none is, the console says ortRequired 'recent': nothing else is in session, 1 closed, and the block opens it again when next run. What a model is made of doesn't count as something else: the encoders models share, an intent model's BERT encoder, and the encoder and decoders of a pair, which are all the pair's own. Two required scopes don't keep each other, a static or limited scope's sessions do. Nothing is freed while the scope's block is still going, while what it holds runs, or while a model.inBackground job waits on it.
  • A swarm answers for what it opened. Closing a swarm closes the sessions it opened, even one a kept scope adopted meanwhile, and a closable closes the swarm it opened with them.
  • A session is held by one scope at most. A second static, required or limited block that asks for it takes it over from the first.
  • A name is one scope. ortRequired("search") { } after ortStatic("search") { } makes search a required scope with what it holds, and the console says so; the kind and settings asked for last are the ones in force.
  • The block in force belongs to the thread. Work a block starts on another thread is not tracked: it behaves as a bare initMod and stays open, which is the safe direction.
  • ortForever is ortStatic now. A saved script that calls it still runs, and the console says the new name on each call; the editor no longer offers it.

The Sessions tab says what holds a session on its row, such as static search, timed search, 40s left, limited pool, 2 of 3 or closable. Terminate works on all of them as before, and the scope forgets what was closed, so ortScopes.print() doesn't list it again. A row a kept scope holds has Free beside Terminate, which frees the scope as ortScopes.free("search") would: everything it holds is closed, that session among them. The sandbox's Still open tab has the same rows, and free search typed into the console does the same without a script.

docs.title: Ask without touching the model: sessionMod
docs.text:
initMod("name") gives you the model's session, which is the model as it is: it moves to every new head and logs what it is asked. sessionMod("name") gives you a snapshot: the head and the labels the model has now, read together and kept in memory. It is a model to ask and nothing more, and works on its own, with nothing else open:

val m = sessionMod("dummy")                  // an object
log(m.predict("turn the lights on"))
log("v${m.version}, ${m.labels}")

val same by sessionMod("dummy")              // the same thing, as a delegate

val label = sessionMod("dummy") {            // for one block: its functions at hand, gone when the block ends
    log(scores("turn the lights on").toString())
    predict("turn the lights on")             // what the call returns
}
  • It can't change the model. It has predict, scores, predictions, run, answer, inference and getStatus, then name, version, labels and close. It isn't an InteractionModel, so m.fineTune(...) doesn't compile and nothing that takes a model takes it.
  • It stays on its head. A fine-tune, a build under the same name, a rollback, a rename or a destroy of the model doesn't reach it: it answers as it did, where a session moves to the new head. Take it again for the new head.
  • It leaves no trace on the model. What it is asked goes in no sessions.log and no run count of the model, and the model's session isn't opened. Its own runs are on its row on the Sessions tab.
  • It is cheap to share. Everything that asks for the same head shares one snapshot, on the model's shared encoder, so a snapshot costs its head and no more.
  • It goes by itself. The block form when the block ends, the others when the run ends or with .close(), the last to let go closing the snapshot. Terminate ends it for all who hold it. Neither touches the model.

A jar has no head, so sessionMod("x.jar") is refused. Use initMod for a session to keep warm between runs, with its log, and sessionMod for a script that must answer the same through a retrain or has no business in the model's log. The starters A model to ask, nothing more and sessionMod as a block are ready to run.

sessionMod was called sharedModel before. A saved script that still says sharedModel runs as it did, in all three forms, with one console line naming the new name; the editor no longer offers the old one.

docs.title: Read what a session did
docs.text:
Every intent-model and package session keeps a log of what it was asked and answered:

Line Written when open the session was opened (or reused: a model has one session) swap a new head of the model took the place of the one the session answered with, which was closed once its answers were done run each inference call: the text, the first three answers, how long it took error an inference call threw: the text and the exception close the session was closed, with the number of runs

Read it on the Models page, Log on the session's row, or in the file next to the owner: AMP/models/intents/<name>/sessions.log for a model, AMP/pluginDir/<jar>.sessions.log for a package. The file keeps the history of terminated sessions too; the page keeps the last 300 lines of an open one and Log shows the last 60 (with … n earlier lines in sessions.log).

2026-10-14T17:40:02.118Z dummy #3 open  opened as session #3
2026-10-14T17:40:05.402Z dummy #3 run   "turn the lights on" -> lights:0.61, weather:0.22, greeting:0.17 (14 ms)
2026-10-14T17:41:10.009Z dummy #3 close closed after 1 runs

From a script, packages.print() logs one line per open package session (#1 amie-demo-1.0.0.jar (org.example.Echo) · pluginDir · runs 4), and sessions.print() lists every ONNX Runtime session with its inputs, outputs, runs and whether it is busy; an intent model's head shows there as module:<name>. The Sessions tab shows the same at a glance: owner and #id, kind, inferring while it answers (a gray mark when idle), runs, open for how long.

docs.title: See what a script uses
docs.text:
Over the sessions, the tab lists Scripts: every script running, and each that ended and left something open, with the sessions it opened under it. A script goes by the template it is, word for word; anything else, an edited template too, is main.kts. Run again, it keeps its row and takes over what it left open. The row goes once nothing of it is left.

What a script uses
template · running 12s
holds 400.0 MB in 2 sessions · 8 answers · cpu 1.20 s · allocated 84.0 MB
Figure What it is holds What the sessions it opened weigh: heads, jars and encoders, as file sizes, since ONNX Runtime doesn't say what it holds.
